en: The Determination of the Meaning of the Root (Dhātvarthanirūpaṇa).

Following the sequence of the occasion (*avasara-saṅgati*), immediately after the preceding [topic] and before the subsequent one—because it is that upon which the latter depends—the author states "Now" (*atha*) to introduce the determination of the meaning of the root. In this regard—that is, concerning the subject matter of the meaning of the root to be determined—the followers of Prabhākara maintain: "Only the result (*phala*) is the meaning of the root; however, the productive operation (*bhāvanā*) is not directly denoted (*vācya*) by it, because a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*) having that as its object is never experienced in any instance. Rather, it is only the optative suffix (*liṅ*) that denotes it; yet even so, that [productive operation] is what is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*)."

That is not so. From the very rule "kṛt-affixes [denote] the agent" (*kartari kṛt*), the mention of the "agent" is favorable [to the view that] the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) in the rule "laḥ karmaṇi" (*laḥ karmaṇi ca bhāve ca akarmakebhyaḥ*) is the operation (*vyāpāra*), while the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha*) is effort (*yatna*). That this is the doctrine of the Guru (Prabhākara)—namely, that the factors of action (*kāraka*) are construed with the meaning of the verbal root—is obtained from the works of Vācaspati and others on the sūtra "tattu samanvayāt" (*Brahma-sūtra* 1.1.4). However, this is beset by the Naiyāyika refutation of the theory that effort is the meaning of the verbal suffix as stated by the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa*. Making this clear, he says: "In effort... (*yatne...*).

By this, it is indicated that effort is the purpose in all cases. He refutes the view of those following Maṇḍana Miśra with the words "yattu" (as for what [they say]). An objection is raised: "But surely, since the word 'agent' (kartṛ) refers to dharma, [the meaning] is obtained from that"; to this he replies: "kiñca apajati" (furthermore, it follows). The word "yataḥ" (since) is to be supplied. Thus, in all subsequent instances, the same applies as far as possible. An objection is raised: "But this [difficulty] is equal even in the established doctrine (siddhānta)"; to this he replies: "kiñca phūtkāra" (furthermore, [regarding] blowing). To the charge of begging the question (iṣṭāpatti), he says: "kiñca saṅketa" (furthermore, [regarding] convention). He removes this defect with the words "na ca" (and not). It is to be construed with the word "vācyam" (to be stated).

[Objection: But in this case, it would follow that the root *jñā* (to know) is not transitive, because no operation (*vyāpāra*) distinct from the cognition—which is the meaning of the verbal root—is experienced in Devadatta or others. To this, he says: "Even in the case of *jñā*" (*jānātāvapi*). "By way of being the object" (*viṣayatayā*) means: in the result [of the action] as delimited by its relation to that [object]. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: if the relation that delimits the status of being an operation were not introduced. "By a relation" (*sambandhena*) means: by a temporal relation (*kālika*) and so forth. "Of all" (*sarveṣām eva*) means: of all verbal roots. "The status of being an agent" (*kartṛtvam iti*).

Therefore, in expressions such as *ghaṭam bhāvayati* ("he brings about a pot"), the pot is the object (*karman*), whereas in expressions such as *ghaṭo bhavati* ("the pot comes into being"), it possesses the status of the agent (*kartṛ*) alone. This is because, in those cases, the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) is merely the activity of the agent which is coreferential with the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*). Furthermore, objecthood (*karmatva*) is simply the state of being the locus of the meaning of the verbal root that is non-coreferential with the activity denoted by the suffix-meaning; indicating this, he says "the pot" (*ghaṭam*). He says "the meaning of the causative suffix" (*ṇijartha*) in the sense of the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*).

The point is that even when the causative sense (*antarbhāvita-ṇyartha*) is included, there is no fault because the suffix itself indicates the meaning of the causative (*ṇij-artha*). He removes this objection as well with the words "And not... (*na ca*). Here, he says "by the principal [action]" (*pradhānena*) to show that the [causative] does not imply the absence of activity. By this, the opposite view regarding that case is also refuted. Now, one might object: "Is Yāska intending to convey that [the causative] does not imply [the activity], or is he referring to another school of thought? To this he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). This refers to the portion of the text beginning with "of this" (*ityasya*).

Even though the meaning [of the suffix] is obtained through the stated method, the grammarian teaches the meaning of the suffix again in the treatise for the sake of establishing its primacy (*prādhānya*). This is not a repetition of the cognition—as in the case of "two" (*dvau*) and so on—nor is it a restatement (*anuvādakatva*) of something already existing; rather, its fruit is precisely that primacy. Therefore, he says: "In the object" (*karmaṇi*). This means: "of *kṛt*-suffixes in the sense of the object, and of *kṛt*-suffixes in the sense of the object-agent (*karmakartṛ*). For this very reason, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in expressions such as "the cooker of rice" (*odanasya paktā*), as well as the connection with the kāraka (the object). To the objection that this is an accepted consequence (*iṣṭāpatti*), he says: "Furthermore. He states another fault: "Furthermore, the teacher... (*kiñca gurur iti*).

"—*anāpattiḥ* (no offense). This means the attainment of its absence. The same applies hereafter. Nor is the fruit (*phala*) the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) here; rather, the meaning of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) is the activity of the instigator (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*) conducive to the operation [of the agent]. In that context, the fruit is construed with the primary activity as being conducive to it. As for the *tiṅ*-suffixes, their meanings are tense, number, and the activity of the instigator. There is no repetition of the cognition, as in the case of "two" and so forth. Furthermore, by virtue of its primacy and the force of the sūtraic restatement such as *laḥ karmaṇi ca*, the substratum (*dharmin*) is implied solely through the activity of the instigator.

It should not be argued that there is no fault because the meaning of the phrase "anabhihite" (when not already expressed) and so forth, when implying power (*śakti*), is simply "not already denoted. This is because such a sense is not obtained from the rule *hetumati ca* [Pāṇini 3.1.26]. Since everything is consistent without strain according to our own view, there is no need for such a forced construction, and furthermore, it would be swallowed by the aforementioned defects. This is the direction of the argument. Thus he says: "ityanyatra" (elsewhere). The meaning is: in the *Gurumañjūṣā*. || 1.1 ||

He refutes the statement of the Prāñca Naiyāyikas with the words "yadapi" (even that which...). [The phrase] "karma" refers to the fact that it is cumbersome to postulate the capacity for the fruit in many verbal roots (*dhātu*) in dependence upon the object-denoting suffix (*karman-pratyaya*). Furthermore, if the verbal root were to convey the fruit, there would be no possibility of a direct syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between the meaning of the noun (*nāmartha*) and the meaning of the root through the relation of substratum-ness (*āśrayatā-sambandha*); therefore, the intention is that there is parsimony (*lāghava*) in the view that the meaning of the suffix is the state of being the substratum of the fruit, with "residence" (*vṛttitva*) as the relation. By the word "ādi" (etcetera), the co-occurrence with other [words] distinct from both [the noun and the root] is included.

—Regarding "abandonment" (*tyāga*): the sense is that a single [action] alone is the generator of both conjunction and disjunction. Since that same fault applies in each respective definition, he says "therein" (*tatra*). This is to be construed with the rule beginning "of the two fourths" (*caturthyor*), etc. —Regarding "action" (*karman*): the meaning is as in examples such as "the rice is cooked by itself. He states "he abandons" (*tyajati*) because the causality of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) is also difficult to explain. Now, one might object that this fault does not arise if one introduces the property of "belonging to that person" (*tatpuruṣīyatva*); therefore, he says "the state of being an effect" (*kāryatā*).

He refutes the statement of the Naiyāyika with the words "yattu" (as for what [they say]). Regarding the denotation of an operation delimited by a fruit (*phala*), in the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) consisting of the knowledge of the sentence "he goes to the village," the cognitive representation (*upasthiti*) produced by the verbal root (*dhātu*) having as its object an operation delimited by a fruit must be included within the obstructiveness (*pratibandhakatā*) toward the inference whose object is the Sāman. In this regard, that [representation] is included either as possessing a qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) regarding the operation qualified by a mode-ness (*prakāratā*) residing in the fruit, or as possessing a mode-ness regarding the fruit qualified by a qualificand-ness residing in the operation.

The meaning is as follows: because there is no decisive criterion (*vinigamanāviraha*), the view that the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) possesses a greater degree of obstructiveness involves a cumbersomeness of the delimiting factor (*avacchedakagaurava*). In my view, the presentation of the result produced by the second [word] is included within the causal complex itself, serving as the substitute for the presentation produced by that [word] established in your own system; thus, there is parsimony (*lāghava*).

Although, given that the verbal causal complex (śābdasāmagrī) such as "the second [case-ending]" and so forth exists when the meaning of the verbal root is a *vyāpāra* delimited by the result, such an inference (*anumiti*) does not arise—and thus, for the sake of accounting for that, such a relation of the sublated and the sublator (*pratibadhyapratibandhakabhāva*) is necessary even for you—nevertheless, he states the actual excellence [of his own position]: "But that, being such... The sense is that it has been established that a subverting cognition (*bādhakabuddhi*) lacks the status of a sublator with respect to cognition in general. He states this as a secondary point: "In the case of inference... etc.

Between those two, there is no causal relationship at all, because even without it, that [cognition] arises; thus, its status as a cause is useless. How the process of inference is [established] has already been explained above. By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the knowledge of pervasion (vyāptijñāna) and so forth are included. — Regarding the phrase "as in the case of the crow" (kākavat):

The meaning is: "How many teeth does a crow have? How many palas is a ram's egg? and so forth. This has been stated even while granting [the opponent's position for the sake of argument]. However, in reality, it is simply impossible; thus he says, "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). Since, according to the opponent's view, the mind is atomic (*aṇu*), he says, "the mark of the mind" (*manoliṅga*). He says, "directly" (*āñjasyena*), because [such a mark] is impossible without relying on the opponent's own doctrine. He precludes total non-existence by saying, "through experience" (*anubhava*). Thus, this is a refutation directed against the opponent.

Having thus refuted the view that "it is so," he states another defect in the position under discussion at the end with the words "Moreover, by you... [and] "as the meaning of the suffix... [and] "connected with that... and so forth. The sense is that "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) consists precisely in the absence of such [an object]. [And] "by being the meaning of the verbal root" refers to [the argument based on] positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), and so forth. [The phrase] "because it is obtainable" should also be understood to include "due to its complexity" (*gaurava*).

Furthermore, in cases such as "one sacrifices to Viṣṇu" (*viṣṇuṃ yajate*) or "Viṣṇu is to be sacrificed to" (*viṣṇuryaṣṭavyaḥ*), since the accusative case ending prescribed by Pāṇini’s rule [P. 2.3.2] would express Viṣṇu only as the *uddeśya* (the intended object), it would follow that the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is intransitive. Moreover, because Viṣṇu would not be the object of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvartha*), there would be no occasion for the application of suffixes such as the *laṭ* or *tavya* to denote that object. If it is argued that Viṣṇu is the "object" of the sacrifice by way of being the "object" known as *uddeśyatā* (intendedness), then even the root *bhuji* (to eat), when used in the sense of "desiring to eat," would result in being transitive.

Nor should it be argued that being transitive (*sakarmakatva*) consists simply in being different from what is intransitive (*akarmaka*), and that in this context, distinctions such as between the roots *kṛ* (to do) and *jñā* (to know) need not be introduced in accordance with usage. For even transitive roots would then incur the impossibility [of being called transitive] when they are intransitive in another sense. By the same logic, intransitivity must also be defined as being different from being transitive, since no other definition of it can be stated. And thus, due to the consequence of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*), rules such as "laḥ karmaṇi" (Pāṇini 3.4.69) would result in being unintelligible; this is the general direction of the argument. He states this with the words "ityanyatra" (in another place); the meaning has been explained. 1.2.12.

He states the distinction with the words "herein" (*atre*). This means: regarding the domain of verbal roots (*dhātu*). First, he states the opinion of the wise, such as Dīkṣita and others, with the words "separately" (*pṛthak*). Now, one might object: in this way, there would be no syntactic connection (*anvaya*) between those two, because in that case, presentation by distinct words (*bhinnapadopasthiti*) is the governing factor. To this he replies: "by a single [word]" (*eketi*). Thus, the sense is that this [restriction] pertains to a domain other than the verbal root. He further states that this is also accepted by others with the words "of others" (*pareṣām*).

[Objection: Surely, since the connection with the substratum of the accusative case-meaning cannot coherently apply to its single part, namely the *phala* (result), one should not accept a separate [verbal] power (*śakti*). This is because, according to the grammatical rule "the second case is used for the object" (*karmaṇi dvitīyā*) and due to the diversity of linguistic usage, such a meaning is easily obtained. To this he says: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*). The meaning is: if a separate power is not admitted. "In that manner" (*tathā*) means: by way of that form. Even though the two powers are equal in their production, he says: "Heavy" (*guru*). [Objection: Even so, there would be the undesirable consequence of the cognition that "going with the aim of a result" is not an action (*vyāpāra*). To this he says: "Here" (*atra*).

The meaning is "in the view that [the action] has a distinct power" (*pṛthakśaktipakṣe*). Or, the meaning is "among the [verbs] that are co-occurrent" (*anvayānām madhye*). He states this by distinguishing between verbal suffixes expressing an object (*karmapratyaya*) and those expressing something other than that—namely, "the fruit" (*phala*). Being "internal" (*antaraṅgatva*) consists in its being the first to be presented [to the mind]. Precisely for this reason, the fruit does not present itself independently. Now, even so, one might object that there would still be the undesirable consequence of such usage based on the intention that the fruit is qualified by the operation; therefore, he says "the aspect of the fruit" (*phalāṃśa*). The meaning is "the aspect consisting of the fruit. "In general" (*utsargataḥ*) means in cases other than those involving verbal suffixes expressing an object.

And thus, from the word "going" (*gamana*), there is the cognition of such an activity itself as the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), and not its opposite; therefore, that [undesired] consequence does not arise—this is the sense. To indicate that this is the general rule (*autsargika*), he says: "But in some cases... He states the scope of this [rule] because it is not well-known: "For example... Incidentally, he states the meaning of the term "result" (*phala*) according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) right here: "And being a result... Since [the result] is not actually produced in the previously mentioned examples such as "he lies on his husband," he says: "produced by... (*janya*).

In cases such as "the leaf falls" (*parṇaṃ patati*), if the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is simply the conjunction produced by disjunction, then although disjunction possesses the status of a qualificand (*viśeṣya*), the positive condition (*satyanta*) is not met; and although conjunction possesses that status, it is not the qualificandum. Thus, both are mentioned, as he says: "of disjunction and conjunction. The word "mutually" (*mithaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder. He states the result of the phrase "by the agent-affix" (*kartṛpratyaya*) as: "action" (*karma*). 1.3.

He states his own conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "pare tu" (But others). He says "param etenaiva" (But by this very [reasoning]) and "pṛthak" (separately); the sense is that in their view, that [instrumentality] is not dependent on that [object]. Since that is absent in cases such as "the king's servant" (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*), he says "autsargikī" (default/primary). [The phrase] "tattadbodhasya" refers to the presentation of the fruit and the operation. He refutes the lack of systematic restriction with "kartṛkarma" (agent and object). Now, the ancients have already stated that the heaviness resulting from the delimitors of the capacity for being a denotative power (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) is indeed a fault; therefore, he says "gauravaṃ ca" (and heaviness). This too is said while conceding the point.

Even though it is so in reality, he states that there is indeed simplicity here [in our position] by saying "Furthermore, one... (*kiñcaika*). Otherwise—that is, if one does not accept the third hypothesis—[this difficulty would apply] elsewhere as well, namely, even in the case of universals, individuals, and so forth. (1.4)

Intimating that action (*karman*) is the sole commonality among all [factors], he says "all" (*sarva*). He states "in the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthe*) because the established doctrine of the ancients—that the eight [kārakas] possess their status through action alone—and that of others—that it belongs to the states (*bhāva*) of the *kārakas*—is also restricted solely to the meaning of the verbal root; the sense is "in the operation delimited by the fruit" (*phalāvacchinna-vyāpāra*), etc. The intention is that this applies in any way whatsoever, whether directly or indirectly.

He states that the conventional power (*sāṃketikī śakti*) of the word "action" (*kriyā*) resides in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*), whose nature will be described later—saying, "And this very [is it]. The word "very" (*eva*) serves to exclude other opinions. To dispel the charge of being groundless, he says, "beginning with *bhū*," which means: according to the established doctrine of the *Bhāṣya*. For therein it is said: "This thing called action is absolutely imperceptible," and so forth.

The second verse (*kārikā*) makes known the unifier (*anugamaka*) of the delimiters of capability (*śakyatāvacchedaka*), such as "residing in the intellect" (*buddhisthatva*), but it does not make known the essential nature of the action itself. Thus, [the author] explains [the verse] by reversing the order—despite having previously mentioned specific properties (*dharma-viśeṣa*) and so forth—in order to highlight the inconsistency of the *Bhūṣaṇa* and other works. He says: "of those whose birth occurs in sequence," meaning those [actions] residing in the intellect, such as placing the pot on the fire (*adhiśrayaṇa*) and so forth; the syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is with the phrase "the aggregate (*samūha*) of these. He states "with reference to the aggregate" (*samūhaṃ prati*) because of proximity (*pratyāsatti*).

Regarding the phrase "by those that have become qualities" (*guṇabhūtaiḥ*), the meaning is "by those that have become non-attached" (*asaṅgabhūtaiḥ*); otherwise, there would be the fault of tautology. Therefore, he explains that the word *guṇa* refers to *dharma*, while the word *bhūta*—based on the rule that roots meaning "to reach" (*prāpti*) can take the present participle suffix *-kta*—refers to *jñāna*. Thus he says: "in the form of this or that. Regarding the term *prakalpita*, he states that it is a *karmadhāraya* compound and not a *bahuvrīhi* as suggested by Bhūṣaṇa and others; thus he says: "having a form in which difference is imagined. He resolves the contradiction with the words "here," meaning "in the definition of action" (*kriyālakṣaṇe*).

For this very reason, he states "by this" (*eteneti*) that there is no contradiction with the Bhāṣya on the *sarūpa* sūtra. The meaning is: "by means of the unity residing in the aggregate. Regarding the statement "it has been said by means of cognition" (*buddhyetyuktam*), he explains that in the compound *prakalpita*, it is a *karmadhāraya* and not a *bahuvrīhi* as stated by the *Bhūṣaṇā* and others; thus he says, "having the form of an imagined non-difference" (*prakalpitābhedarūpa*). To resolve the contradiction, he says "herein" (*atrety*); the meaning is "in the definition of action" (*kriyālakṣaṇe*). For this very reason, he states "by this" (*eteneti*) that there is no contradiction with the Bhāṣya on the *sarūpa* sūtra. The meaning is: "by means of the unity residing in the aggregate" (*samudāyāśritaikatvena*).

Regarding the statement "it is said by means of cognition": its application extends even to a collection (*samūha*). The linguistic usage of a "collection" is produced by cognition and is purely conceptual (*vikalparūpa*), not real. Thus, the meaning is that action is a single entity consisting of a collection of various parts—past, future, and present, existent and non-existent—which are sequentially ordered and in a state of being accomplished. He states this in a way common to both philosophical systems with the words "in that manner. "Manner" (*prakāra*) here means distinction (*bheda*). An objection is raised: "In that case, [the agent] would not be said to 'construct' [the object] part by part"; to this he replies: "one by one. As it has been said:
"The verbal roots such as *pac* (to cook) apply either to a single part or to the entire collection of operations."

"They proceed by their own nature, relying upon a common form. According to Kaiyaṭa’s view, he says "an aggregate" (*samūha*). The phrase "placing on the fire" (*adhiśraya*) is an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*). In reality, even "placing on the fire" and so forth do not consist of a single moment; for that too has parts such as the stretching out of the hand, the taking up of the vessel, and the placing it on the stove, each of which likewise consists of multiple moments. Thus, even that [act] is indeed of the nature of an aggregate.

Furthermore, it should be understood that even those parts of theirs which resemble atoms are neither denotable nor perceptible, due to their inherent nature as the power of words (*śabdaśaktisvabhāva*). For this very reason, he states [the following] in common with both systems: "adhyāsa..."—that is to say, when that which is superimposed (*adhyasta*) is the denotation of the verbal root (*dhātu*). The sense is that such a thing is superimposed, because it is a word whose meaning is relative (*sambandhiśabda*). By this, it is shown that action (*kriyā*) is that immediately following which the production of the result occurs without interruption; for example, in the case of "he cooks rice," the softening (*vikledana*) is the action. Since acts such as placing the pot on the fire are the generators of that [softening], their status as action is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). As it has been said:

"The action for which a subsequent fruit is determined is known as the primary [action]; because it exists for the sake of that [fruit], other actions receive its name. This [definition] is refuted, because in that case, the [primary action] would incur the status of being secondary (gauṇa). Furthermore, even when the cooking has begun, since the action is yet to come into being, there would be the undesirable consequence of the usage "he will cook" (pakṣyati).

In this context—namely, regarding the state of being the object to be accomplished (*sādhyatva*) which constitutes the body of action (*kriyāśarīra*)—the author first states the opinion of the *Bhūṣaṇakāra* and others with the words "some" (*kecit*). Therein, he first states what must be expressed as that which is to be excluded (*vyāvartya*) with the words "the state of being accomplished" (*siddhatvam*). "Heterogeneity" (*vaijātyam*) means the state of being a substantive entity (*sattvabhūtatvam*). The term "pūrvāpara-" is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the seven [cases] beginning with the vocative are included. He states that this very point is what has been said by others with the words "in another action" (*kriyāntara-*). "Heterogeneity" here means the state of not being a substantive entity (*āsattvabhūtatvam*).

[Objection: But if this is so, then the treatment of indeclinables such as *hiruk* and others as being primarily expressive of action—which is established in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *taddhitaśca*—would be untenable, because their meaning is not apprehended as such [i.e., as action]. To this he says: *hirugādi*. [The phrase] *kriyāmātra* [is to be understood] as beginning with *like words ending in -ktvā*, etc. Thus, the sense is that the designation there is figurative (*gauṇa*). He states precisely what is excluded by the word *mātra*: *svarādīnāṃ tu* ("but in the case of *svara* and so on"). For this very reason, the particle *tu* indicates a distinction. By the word *api*, the conjunction of actions in examples such as *svaḥ paśya* is included.

[Objection: "Surely, on the basis of the stated commentary, let that meaning be the primary reality itself; for what purpose is its status as secondary (gauṇatva) asserted? To this he says: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). [The word] "of them" (*teṣām*) refers to those meanings which possess the sense of "rising up" (*hirudadyarthānām*). The reading is *ākāṅkṣā ceti*. Both [terms] exclude both [meanings] respectively. Thus, the sense is that because it does not appear with a specific distinctness (*vaijātya*) that serves as the delimiting condition (*avacchedaka*) for not giving rise to an expectancy for another action, it does not possess that [primary] reality. "In that regard"—that is, between those two. For this very reason it has been said: "The action, in its state as something to be accomplished (*sādhyatvena*), is there based upon the verbal root (*dhātu*);
but that aspect of it which is an established state (*siddhabhāva*) is based upon the suffixes such as *ghañ*."

Regarding the word *ced*: it should be understood that even in the case of *bhuktvā* (having eaten), because it occurs in conjunction with the suffix *-ktvā* prescribed for the connection of verbal roots (*dhātusambandha*), there is no fault. This is because, in examples such as *pacati bhavati* ("he cooks [and] exists"), although there is no mutual expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) between *pacati* and the like, the latter (*bhavati*) requires a subject or other factors; thus, by virtue of semantic compatibility (*yogyatā*), the connection occurs through the expectancy of only one of the two. || 1.6 ||

He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "in reality" (*vastutaḥ*). He explains that the meaning is etymological (*yaugika*) with the words "that which is to be produced" (*niṣpādya*); the sense is that it is precisely the state of being currently in the process of production. By the word "only" (*eva*), the aforementioned exclusion is indicated. Regarding the objection raised in the *Bhāṣya*—"this defect applies even to nominal stems"—he says "even though" (*yadyapi*) to show how this is resolved by the very statement in the *Bhāṣya*: "but substance is established by its own nature" (*svabhāvasiddhaṃ tu dravyam*). "But by itself" (*svatastu*) means when there is no co-utterance (*asamabhivyāhāra*) with that [verbal root]. Now, one might object that the establishedness (*siddhatva*) of a substance in its gross form is indeed contradicted; therefore, he says "and establishedness" (*siddhatvaṃ ca*).

He speaks from the perspective of the Satkāryavāda (the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause), saying "even though" (*yadyapi*). "In that way" (*tathā*) means "in a subtle form" (*sūkṣmarūpeṇa*). Regarding the phrase "of the substance" (*dravyasya*): by this, the literal meaning of the aforementioned Bhāṣya—"Substance, established by its own nature as the nature of the potency for sound, is precisely that which is denoted by the word while remaining in its established state in a subtle form"—is indicated. Thus, the sense is that although action (*kriyā*) is a reality, it does not possess the same status of being denotable by a word; this is the distinction. He states the defect according to the view of certain [opponents] with the words "pacati-bhavati" ("he cooks—becomes").

Because the word *pacati* (he cooks) lacks expectancy, he says "it becomes" (*bhavati*). Here, although it lacks the nature of an action (*kriyātva*), it certainly exists as an agent (*kartṛtva*); thus he says "expectancy for an action. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) is as before, intending examples such as *bhuktvā* (having eaten). He states another fault with the words "in this way" (*evam*). The particle *api* is used in the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*) of *ktvā* and so forth. "In that way" (*tathā*) means when there is an expectancy for an action that has been raised [by the suffix]. He says that even here there is no fault in his own system with the words "separately" (*hiruk*). This is the ablative case (*pañcamī*). The phrase "of exclusion" (*varjanādeḥ*) is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). "Not" (*na*); the phrase "in its meaning" (*tadarthe*) is the ellipsis.

By this, the following argument of theirs is also refuted: "Nor is there a lack of evidence for denoting [the root meaning] as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), because in cases such as *pacati* (he cooks), *pākaḥ* (cooking), *karoti* (he does), and *kṛtiḥ* (action), although there is no difference in the understanding of the root-meaning, we observe the presence or absence of an expectancy for another action; this very observation is the proof. He says "the direction" (*dig*) because it will become clear later how, in this view, there is no fault in cases such as "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. 1.7.

"In that regard"—that is, between those two. "By the two *kārikās*": by those which demonstrate meanings established by universal experience; by this, the exclusion of the general form is indicated. He states that very point with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). The sense is that otherwise, even if there were a cognition in a general form, because there would be no cognition in a specific form, there would be an absence of certainty regarding either alternative, resulting in doubt. "It is indeed accepted": by this, the claim that [the general property] is not the delimitor of the denotable capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*)—on the grounds that it serves as a unifier (*anugamaka*) for the delimiters of denotable capacity such as "being present in the intellect" (*buddhisthatva*) according to the maxim of "that and so forth" (*tad-ādi-nyāya*)—is refuted.

In that context—among those various operations—that which is the operation [is what is denoted]. By this, the lack of a fixed rule (*avyavasthā*) is refuted. For this very reason—precisely because the substratum of that [operation] possesses agency (*kartṛtva*). By this, the following objections are rejected: [the claim] that if the action of the wood (*kāṣṭhakriyā*) were denotable, the third case-ending (*tṛtīyā*) would not occur; or that if it were not denotable, the first case-ending (*prathamā*) would not occur, and that by rule the third case-ending would necessarily occur.
[The phrase] "because of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*), etc."—by "etc.," [is meant] being a verb in the *parasmaipada* voice, and so forth.

By this, the view that "the delimitor of the expressive power (*śaktatāvacchedaka*) is simply the status of being a verbal root (*dhātutva*), which is common to all [roots], because it is perceived as having the operation of bringing about what is to be done (*kṛtyaniṣpādakavyāpāra*)" is also refuted. With the words "by this" (*etena*), he refutes the statement of Dīkṣita and others in both ways. The word "only" (*mātram*) signifies entirety. This was stated by them so that there would be no multiplicity of meanings (*nānārthatva*). And that [activity] is a specific universal (*jātiviśeṣa*) residing in the same locus as the state of being denotable by a verbal root (*dhātuvācyatva*). Furthermore, it is established as the delimitor of the expressive power of the word "action" (*kriyāpada*), etc., since the universal "water-ness" (*jalatva*) is established as the delimitor of the denotability of the word "water" (*jalapada*), as seen in the *Lolāvatyupāya*.

The universal (jāti) [of dhātutva] is established through recognition and linguistic usage, and its status as being denoted by words is stated in the Bhāṣya on the *sarūpa-sūtra*. Furthermore, "dhātutva" (the state of being a verbal root) contained therein is a specific universal. The intended meaning is that the *bhūvādi-sūtra* serves as the indicator of that [universal]. To prevent the undesirable consequence that all actions would be understood from every verbal root, he says: "and in their respective forms. Thus, the intended meaning is that the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with words such as *pacati* acts as the regulator for the understanding of those respective [actions].

He states the meaning of the phrase "by this" as "due to complexity" (*gauravāt*); that is, due to the postulation of both [the relation and the universal]. He states another defect with the words "of such a kind" (*tādṛśa*); that is, having the nature of a universal (*sāmānyarūpa*). And [he says] "because it would have only the perceived object as its referent" (*udṛṣṭamātrārthatvāt*); that is, because it would result in the loss of reality (*tattvāpatti*). The point is that since the capacity of co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) to determine cognition cannot be maintained if it produces a cognition not connected to its object, such a connection must be postulated by you as well.
Furthermore, because no cognition is experienced in that form; and furthermore, because cognition is indeed experienced in its respective specific forms.

By this, the view that—even if it is impossible to state another single common property shared by all [the instances]—the property of "being conducive to softening" (*viklitty-anukūlatva*) itself is such [a property] is also refuted; for that which is over-extended (*atiprasakta*) cannot be a delimitor of denotability (*śakyatānavacchedaka*). Furthermore, since it is supported by valid means of knowledge (*prāmāṇika*), the postulation of multiple [denotable properties] does not constitute a fault. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of the destruction of the very notion of "denotability" (*tattva*) even in cases like the word *saindhava*, because one would have to postulate a single property residing in horses, salt, and so on, as the delimitor of denotability for those words. If it is argued that the cognition of those [objects] occurs precisely through [properties] such as "horseness" (*aśvatva*) and the like, [we reply:]...

The same applies to the subject under discussion (*prakṛta*). For this very reason, the universal "all-pervasiveness" (*vibhutva-jāti*) is not established as the delimitor of the denotative capacity (*śakyatāvacchedaka*) of the word "all-pervasive" (*vibhu*), because the cognition [of all-pervasiveness] arises from [the property of] "supreme great dimension" (*paramamahat-parimāṇatva*) or simply from "being in conjunction with all corporeal things" (*sarvamūrtasaṃyogitva*); such is the direction of the argument.

[Objection: But surely, when rice is produced by a flame already established through another action residing in Caitra—even without blowing upon the fuel with that specific form—the usage ‘caitraḥ pacati’ (Caitra cooks) would not occur; therefore, he says: “only by blowing. By the word “only” (eva), it is indicated that even in that case, such [usage] is indeed desired [by him]. He states that this is necessary for you as well: “by blowing,” etc.

[Objection: Even if this were so, there would be no disagreement among disputants as to whether [the object] is a desire for sacrifice or a cognition, because one of the two alternatives would necessarily be determined. To this he says: "yāga" (sacrifice). [He specifies] "tattatpuruṣīya" (belonging to such-and-such a person); there is an alternative reading, "svīya" (one's own). The point is that this is not a doubt, which would require the knowledge of both alternatives by a single person. These two defects should be understood as stated by the Mīmāṃsakas. [Objection: Even if this were so, there would be no occasional cognition in a general form; to this he says: "dhātūnām" (of verbal roots).

By this, the view that [the suffix *kta*] functions through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) to mean "that" is refuted. Now, one might object: even so, by the mere fact of the blowing being past, one would have to say "he cooked" (*apākṣīt*) at a time when another operation was currently taking place; therefore, he says: "blowing," etc.—"of the state of having become past," etc. This will become clear later. (1.8)

[Objection: But in that case, would not verbs such as *asti* (to be) fail to qualify as verbal roots (*dhātu*), since they denote mere existence and thus lack the expression of an action consisting of an operation (*vyāpāra*)? To this he says: "It is *asti*"; "itself" (*ātman*); the meaning is that it has become the very nature of the action. Where there is this observation of time, the sequence is also inherent in its very self—this is the syntactic connection. He states that very point with the words "prior," etc. By the word "etc.," the state of being a collection is included. Here, because of the contradiction with what was stated previously, he says: "Or else" (*yadvā*). The prefix *ā* in "up to the sixth" (*āṣaṣṭhāt*) indicates a limit (*maryādā*). It should be understood as "immediately after birth."

Although the entity exists even in a subtle form during its origination and destruction, he says "existent" (sat) in order to exclude that [state]. He states its specific nature by saying "having that as its object" (tad-viṣaya); the reading is "its own nature" (sva-svarūpa). He clarifies this very point by saying "the Self" (ātma). He states the result of saying "existent" by saying "and that [is]... (sā ca). He states the result of saying "up to the sixth [day]" (ā-ṣaṣṭhāt) by saying "let him die" (mriyatām). Here—in the four [days]... This is clear; the meaning is that it refers to the second view.

In this regard, it has been stated [by the author] to dispel the following doubt: "If, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), 'action' (*kriyā*) is defined as 'the specific mode of activity of the factors of action' (*kāraka-pravṛtti-viśeṣaḥ'), then since actions such as eating possess mutual distinctions due to their nature as specific modes of activity, while this is not the case for roots like *as* (to be) and so forth, the status of these as verbal roots (*dhātu*) would remain unestablished. To resolve this, he says: "If this is so, then the designation of verbal root is established for *as* and the others; otherwise, indeed, they proceed differently when applied to the factors of action, and differently when applied to death (*mriyati*)."

The literal meaning of the verse beginning with "those two [exist] as denotable agents of action, while activity is otherwise" is as follows. This has been stated: "let him die. In that context, "maintaining that" refers to maintaining the gross form. Thus, the intended meaning is that since the sense of the verb "to exist" (asti) indeed possesses the nature of a specific activity in relation to "dies," its establishment is secured.

"Vārṣyāyaṇi said that there are six modifications of being (*bhāvavikāra*): it is born, it exists, it transforms, it grows, it diminishes, and it perishes. To indicate that the subsequent commentary aims to demonstrate further reasoning for the fact that words such as *asti* (it exists) denote action (*kriyā*), he says: "taduktimiti" (referring to his statement). [The name] Vārṣyāyaṇi; the word "said" (*āha*) is to be supplied. He cites the passage from that commentary beginning with "bhāvasya" (of being), etc. These are the varieties of action. He states the result of the term "without a prefix" (*nirupapada*) in the phrase "anyatra" (elsewhere).

The explanation of this very point is: "In Pradhāna and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), [the states of] Īśvara and others are included. Therefore, the meaning is that they are not denotable by the term *bhāva* alone. — In the *Mokṣadharma* section of the *Mahābhārata*: "O twice-born one, your Veda shall be established in its entirety, together with the Upaniṣads and the Khilas," and so on. — [Regarding the phrase] "it will come to be":

"He shall attain that designated state desired by Sāṅkhya and Yoga"—thus ends [the verse]. Since "priority" (pūrvatva) is relative, he says: "six. Regarding "of birth"—that is, of the entity whose nature is origination—"beginning" means the commencement. Being thus, he dispels the charge of deficiency by saying: "approaching the beginning. "Apavarga" means its completion. He states this with the words: "having been born. Because there is no interval [between them], he says: "it is described. Now, one might object: since it is non-existent at that time, it cannot be described; therefore, he says: "of the non-existent. Otherwise, the consequence would be the origination even of things like a hare's horn—this is the intended meaning.

[Objection: "In that case, let him simply state its negation by means of that [negation]. To this he says: "Nor... (*nāpi*). The explanation of the term *sattvasya* is "of that which possesses existence" (*sattāvataḥ*). Since it exists even previously in a subtle form, he says: "of such a kind" (*tādṛśa*). This means "having arisen. He states that here "holding" (*dhāraṇam*) does not mean "ascertainment" (*niścaya*). And thus, the meaning is as follows: the very existence of Brahman (*brahmasattaiva*), consisting of the manifestation (*vivarta*) of various actions, appears in the form of birth and so forth, having the nature of an effect (*sādhya*) determined through its connection with the causal factors (*kāraka*). Therefore, that [existence] is also the reality (*tattva*). || 1.9 ||

[Objection: "In that case, why is this not clearly understood even in sentences such as 'the jar exists' (*ghaṭo 'sti*), just as it is in 'he makes a jar' (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*) and so forth? To this, he says: "bhāvanā" (the efficient force). The term *krama* (sequence) is placed first according to the rule that the producer precedes the produced. Thus, the meaning is that its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [existence] would be a defect if it were to be clearly manifest in that manner.

Thus, having established that the meaning of those [roots] is action (*kriyā*) according to the method stated in the *Bhāṣya* and other texts, he says "āsanna... (proximate...), because even the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the general and the particular—which serves as the proof for the action-nature of the meaning of roots such as *pac-*—as presented through the form of question and answer in the *Bhāṣya* and elsewhere, is not universally applicable here. [In the phrase "praśne,"] the word "kṛte" (when made) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. And from the answer—as well as because the answer is accepted by all—it follows that if this were the case, then just as "pacati" (he cooks) is an answer to the question "kiṃ karoti? (what does he do?), the answer "asti" (it exists) would also have to be possible. This [objection] is thereby refuted.

[Objection: "If this is so, why does it not happen likewise in other cases as well? To this he says: "In other cases" (*anyatra*). The meaning is: "distinct from that which is on the verge of destruction. In reality, even though it is distinct from that, since [the desired result] is intended even when it is not known as such, he says: "by way of being well-established" (*susthatayā*). This too is clear in the Bhāṣya on that very point. He says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca ca*), because even the technical (śāstrīya) [application], like the worldly one, is non-pervasive (*avyāpaka*) and serves to establish that [principle]. With the intention that the establishment of the state of being *ṣatva* is also achieved through semantic force (*sāmarthya*), he says: "in the case of the agent" (*kartari*). He states the reason for that: "because of the object" (*karma*).

The meaning is "whatever [is produced]"; the intention is that only that which is artificial (kṛtrima) is understood there, in accordance with the specific object to be characterized (*lakṣya*). In this way, the establishment of the *laṭ* and other tenses is also to be understood as having been stated in the Bhāṣya by the words "even that" (*tasyāpi*) and so forth, as they serve to establish that very status. He states another meaning of that [term] with the word "ghaṭa" (pot). Here, however, the nature of action (*kriyātva*) in the form of a specific activity (*pravṛtti-viśeṣa*) is quite clear. The proof for this is: "Rohita was born from Lohita; Dhundhu was his son."

And so forth. Now, one might object: even if it is designated as such by way of its true nature (*tattva*), since it is unitary in its form as a property (*dharma*), and because there is no relation of priority or posteriority [between its parts], how can it be a "true nature"? To this he says: "Pātañjala" and so on. "In that regard" (*tatra*) means: in the existence (*sattā*) consisting of the apprehension of the gross form, [it refers to] the activity residing in Caitra which brings about that apprehension. "Of that" (*tasyāḥ*) means: of that existence. He says "state of being" (*bhāva*) because the difference [of the parts] is not established. This means: the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as it exists in its accomplished state (*siddhāvasthā*). And those [states] are described as: "actionless, partless, tranquil, faultless, and stainless."
The supreme bridge to immortality, the witness, the conscious one, absolute and devoid of qualities.

And so forth. One should also consider such Smṛti texts as: "The Supreme Lord is the cause, who, though pure, [appears so] by way of metaphorical designation. Regarding that—namely, the state of being an entity—he says "pure," according to the manner previously stated. "As elsewhere"—meaning as in passages such as "That thou art. "By negation"—the meaning is as in passages such as "There is no diversity here. He states the second view already mentioned: "by negation. "In this very way"—that is, solely through superimposition. By the word "etc.," number is included. ||1.10||

In accordance with the views of the predecessors, he states what is [already] established in the Siddhānta: "And [the definition of] transitivity (*sakarmakatva*)," and so on. He says "or else" (*yadvā*) because if only the fruit or only the operation were denoted, there would be an over-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition of intransitive verbs in certain cases. The sense is that the first [definition] alone is the intended meaning, while the second is obtained by implication. As for the example: in that case, both [the fruit and the operation] are denoted as being in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*); therefore, the absence [of the definition] there is due to the absence of their being in different grammatical relations (*vyadhikaraṇatva*).

Otherwise—that is, if the operation (*vyāpāra*) were not denotable there and only the result (*phala*) were denotable—since rising, which consists of conjunction with a higher location, would be the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) in that context, the suffix *kta* would have to denote that very [result] as having occurred (*bhūtatvena*). Consequently, while that [result] exists, the state of having already occurred (*bhūtatva*) would be absent; thus, by the rule "after roots meaning 'motion' or 'intransitive' [the suffix *kta* denotes the agent]," the *kta* suffix could not denote the agent in the past tense. To this, he says: "having risen" (*utthitaḥ*). But for me—who maintains that both [the operation and the result] are denotable there—the [suffix *kta*] denotes that [conjunction with a higher location]. [Note: The term *tattvābhāvāt* refers to the absence of the state of being already accomplished (*bhūtatva*), which is required for the application of the rule regarding the agentive *kta*.]

[Objection: "In that case, let it be that only the operation (*vyāpāra*) is the denoted meaning (*vācyatva*) there, and not that [result]; to this he says: "These very [same ones]. The meaning is: precisely because that [result] is also denoted. By the word "even" (*eva*), the view that being intransitive consists in denoting only the operation, while being transitive consists in denoting both the result and the operation, is rejected. Demonstrating the fruit of formulating a different definition, he says: "In some cases. The meaning is: the absence of that [transitivity] is caused solely by the absence of that [result]. He states the illustrative example for this definition: "And thus... (*evaṃ ca*).

By the word "kevala" (exclusive), it is indicated that [the action] possesses the nature of being a non-operation (*avyāpāra*) rather than a result (*phala*), because it is difficult to maintain the previously mentioned status of being a result in that case. By this very point, the previously mentioned view beginning with "yadi vā" (or else) is refuted. Since the *Bhāṣya* and other texts can be easily reconciled here as well, he dispels the aforementioned contradiction by stating "nirukta" (as defined). He says "dravyasya" (of the substance) to show that the meaning stated in that *Bhāṣya* regarding "sattāvataḥ" (that which possesses existence) is not intended here; rather, it means "that which is obtained through the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*) of this system. [He then states] "svarūpa" (essential nature).

By this, the meaning of the Bhāṣya and Kaiyaṭa is also indicated. "Tasyā api" means even by its existence (sattā). In the reading "tasyāpi," the meaning is "even of existence and so forth. "Upapāditam" (it has been established) means either by the passage beginning with "satkārya" and so on; for this very reason, there was no tautology previously with the passage beginning "sattāyām iva. And thus, it should be understood that the previously stated view—that the meaning of a verbal root (dhātvartha) is an operation delimited by a result—is merely a general rule (prāyika). As it is said: "A verbal root is transitive (sakarmaka) when its meaning, through direct deviation [from the agent], partakes of an object; but it is intransitive (akarmaka) when [the connection to the object] is through a succession [of steps]."

He refutes the Mīmāṃsaka position—which results from the statement of Bhaṭṭa in the *Bhāvārthādhikaraṇa* and which maintains that [the object] is the living being who wards off the mountain—by means of the verse beginning with *yaddhātū*. The words "of its meaning" (*tadarthasya*) are to be supplied as the remainder. The phrase "being other than that" (*tadanyatvam*) is understood by implication to mean "the state of being intransitive" (*akarmakatvam*). Furthermore, even among roots that have the same general meaning, that root is transitive (*sakarmaka*) in which there exists a specific connection to a particular action; thus, there is no fault even if the root *kṛ* (to do) has the meaning of mere effort, just like the root *yat* (to strive).

The point is this: although that which is presented by words such as *karmatva* (the state of being an object) lacks a requirement for an action (*kriyākāṅkṣā*), it is nonetheless possible for the effort (*yatna*) presented by the root *kṛ* to have a requirement for an object, just as that which is presented by the accusative case-ending (*dvitīyā*) has such a requirement. Furthermore, the qualifier to be mentioned later should also be understood here in order to avoid the over-extension (*avyāpti*) of the definition to cases where the object is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣitakarman*). In this way, it is established that the very same [root] can be both transitive (*sakarmaka*) and intransitive (*akarmaka*) depending on the difference in meaning.

The point is this: since the definition of a transitive verb (*sakarmaka*) is that which, for its own meaning, possesses an expectancy for an object qualified by the absence of non-intention to speak, [the definition] applies as a consistent rule. Thus, although [the expectancy] exists in cases such as *pacati* ("he cooks"), it does not exist elsewhere; this is what he states in the phrase "in *gacchati* etc. (he moves, etc.).

The Naiyāyika position—that because all verbal roots (*dhātu*) denote some result (*phala*) and so forth, it would follow that they all possess their own respective meanings (such as *svartha-phala* etc.), leading to a lack of systematic consistency (*ananugama*), and therefore "being distinct from intransitive roots" must be what is denoted; and that in this regard, distinctions such as *janayati* and so on need not be included according to usage, meaning that those [roots] do not participate in the conventional usage [of "transitivity"]—is refuted by the phrase *akarmaka*. The meaning is that, including those [intransitive roots], "intransitivity" (*akarmakatva*) should be defined as being one or another of these [categories], while "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) is being other than that.

Because a distinction within itself is impossible, he says: "asambhava" (impossibility). Regarding "sakarmaka" (transitive): this is intended merely as a definition of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) and is not included within the formal definition (*lakṣaṇa*). The meaning is that, having subsumed those [verbs], one must state that "transitivity" (*sakarmakatva*) is the state of being one or another among them, and "intransitivity" (*akarmatva*) is the state of being other than those. By the word "etena" (by this), in the first case the meaning is "due to impossibility," and in the latter case the meaning is "due to the defect of under-extension" (*avyāpti*). || 1.11 ||

In accordance with the purpose of the yoga, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) beginning with "vastutas tu" (but in reality). He says "etad" (this) in order to exclude that [interpretation] which resides in other systems (*tantrāntara*) due to its proximity. Indicating the fault in the previous definition of the transitive (*sakarmaka*), he says "tena" (by that), meaning by the acceptance of this [position]. Since the form "māsa āsyate" (the month is sat through) is established even there, he says "ādhyāsitāḥ" (sat upon). Because it is transitive, the suffix *kta* is applied to the object in the past sense according to the rule "niṣṭhā. Indicating the lack of establishment [of the previous view] in this context, he says "atra" (here).

[Objection: But in this way, there would be over-extension (*ativyāpti*) to cases such as *jīvati* ("he lives") and so on, because they have meanings such as "he maintains his life-breaths" (*prāṇān dhārayati*). To this, he says: "And the connection... The meaning is: that which has the nature of the relation [between the agent] and that which is presented in such a manner. By the word "and so on" (*ādi*), dancing and other such acts are included. With the intended sense of the present context, he says: "From the meaning of the verbal root" (*dhātvarthāt*). And this is clear; for in that case—even when a suffix denoting the abstract state (*bhāva*), the agent (*kartṛ*), or the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) follows a desiderative in *-san*—there is no [designation] in the object (*karman*), because "that object, being already expressed, is included within [the meaning of the root], and thus becomes part of the meaning of the verbal root."

It has been stated: "In that case, there is no other action by which [the root] could be transitive. This is because, like the root *jīv* (to live) and others, a desiderative form ending in *kyac* is intransitive. In that regard, this same fault applies even to the definition of a transitive verb given previously. Indicating that the result—such as the maintenance of life or the movement of limbs—is present there, and because that result resides in a locus different from the [agent's] activity (*vyāpāra*), he states the flaw in the method of exclusion proposed by the *Bhūṣaṇa*: "pūrva... etc. For this purpose—that is, to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) in this context—the "result" (*phala*) refers to the maintenance of life and so forth.

"—Its substratum is *prāṇa* and so forth. Since the previously mentioned parsimony (*lāghava*) applies here as well, there is no resulting complexity (*gaurava*) caused by its absence; thus he says 'here' (*atra*). The meaning is 'here too. In passing, he sets forth Kaiyaṭa’s view in order to refute it, saying 'and not' (*na ca*). The sense is that there is a difference in words due to a difference in meaning. 'By observation'—the remainder is 'given that [it is] a reality' (*tattve sati*). 'Cognition' (*pratyaya*) means knowledge. And this is clear."

For in that [context], the section refuting the extension (*atideśa*) rule—"Let it be established that roots having time as their object are treated like those without an object"—states: "'It is said: 'of those without an object. But there are no roots whatsoever that are without an object when [used with] time, state (*bhāva*), or distance.'"

"We shall understand those very ones as 'intransitive' (akarmaka) who [are so] in some instances"—having raised this objection in the *Bhāṣya* that the status [of being intransitive] might be based on the non-intentionality of the object (*avivakṣitakarmatayā*), [the author] provides the resolution: "In this treatise, only those entirely devoid of an object are grasped by that term, and not even those whose object is not intended; otherwise, in the case of roots such as *pac* ('to cook'), when the object is not intended, there would result the occurrence of the *lādi*-suffixes in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*). Furthermore, it is maintained that for the word *akarmaka*, the verbal roots (*dhātu*) themselves are taken as the referent of the external member of the compound, and not their meanings.

If one relies solely on the meaning (*artha*), then when the action (*karman*) is not intended to be expressed, the meaning itself would receive the designation "intransitive" (*akarmaka*). However, if the verbal roots (*dhātu*) themselves are relied upon, then because they are observed to be connected with an object in some instances, they cannot—due to their identical form (*sārūpya*)—be designated as "intransitive" based on the cognition of their true nature, thinking "these are the very same [roots]. Rather, since meanings are indeed distinct due to differences such as the factors of action (*kāraka*), the designation of "transitive" (*sakarmaka*) and "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) is made with reference to those specific meanings. Thus, some are transitive and others are intransitive. This is the correct designation.

But when there is the view that "even the object (*artha*) has no inherent difference," then there is no fault regarding objects as the referents of other words; this was established by him [Patañjali] with the example "of the mother" (*mātuḥ*). For in that context, it was stated in this way to refute the portion of the *Vārttika* beginning with "as if intransitive in the case of transitive objects, etc. (*karmādiṣvakarmakavat*). He explains that: "For in that [context]" (*tatra hi*), which means "because. He states another fault therein: "Of the verbal root" (*dhātoḥ*). The word "of the object" (*karmaṇaḥ*) is connected with the preceding three [words]. To show that [the reading] is not the work of the Sage (*anārṣatvāt*), he says: "by the learned" (*abhiyukta*).

The term *akarmaka* is a bahuvrīhi compound. He states that distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) is in relation to the first [type of root]—namely, "according to your way. That is, according to Kaiyaṭa’s way itself. There he states another defect: "Furthermore, because of the qualifier," etc. This is in accordance with the manner of Śeṣa’s statement, namely "and not," etc. He expresses the intention of that author (Śeṣa) as follows: "But if," etc. "As stated" means in the manner of Śeṣa’s statement; that is to say, precisely because there is an absence of denoting the result (*phala*) in those [roots]. Kaiyaṭa’s way of explaining, however, is indeed questionable, because it is difficult to justify even in the case of rules such as *laḥ karmaṇi*.

In examples such as *kṛtapūrvī*, since the object (*karman*) of the past participle suffix (*kta*) is not intended to be expressed, it is established that the suffix denotes the abstract action (*bhāva*); this is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and other sources under the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*. Furthermore, the argument beginning with "because [the root] is intransitive" (*akarmaka*) is also untenable as an explanation for that, because since the technical designation *karman* (object) is a designation based on meaning (*arthasaṃjñā*), it is more appropriate that the meanings themselves constitute the external referent (*anyapadārtha*) of the compound. Moreover, the view that even the meaning itself possesses no inherent distinction is also incorrect, as it would lead to the undesirable consequence of abolishing the polysemous nature (*nānārthatva*) of verbal roots. It should be understood that the intention of the *Bhāṣya* will become clear immediately following this.

Now, he states another defect common to both the previous and the current definitions, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). "Because it is not obtained"—that is, because that [definition] does not apply to that [object]. An objection is raised: "But surely this is its definition, just as possessing a dewlap and so forth is the definition of a cow. To this he replies: "Even if it were a definition. He says "likewise" (*tathā*) to show that experience also is not such [as the definition]. "By means of that instrument" (*tatkaraṇa*) means by means of the instrument of the definition. He concludes the established position (*siddhānta*) with "Therefore" (*tasmāt*); the sense is that such an object is obtained only through the power of *yoga*. 1.12.

[Objection: But how is the non-intentionality (*avivakṣā*) of that [object] compatible with the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) as found in the *kārikā*? To this he says: "In the *kārikā*"—meaning "by way of specification" (*viśeṣya*). The sense is: because of the abandonment of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) which is capable of being construed with it. By the phrase "in cases such as ‘it is not cooked here’ (*neha pacyate*)", etc., [he includes] "it is eaten," and so forth. Regarding "by way of qualification" (*viśeṣaṇa*): the meaning is "having that form. The sense is that while that very same object exists, when there is no intention to construe it as an object (*karmatva*), one intends to construe it as a mere relation (*sambandhitva*).

In the phrase “*mātuḥ smaryate*,” etc., the expression “etc. includes “*pituḥ smaryate*,” and so forth. Regarding that as well, he states the specific detail with the words “*kārya-,*” etc.; by the expression “*kaṭam*,” etc., the phrase “*anubhūtapūrva-*,” etc., is included. To avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he says “*kṛta-,*” because [the application] is not expressed [in such cases]. This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *kartṛkarmaṇoḥ*. By this, those who accept [the application of the genitive] in such instances as *gaṅgādharasya* (of Gaṅgādhara) are refuted. Incidentally, he provides an example for that [rule *dhātoḥ*] which was not previously mentioned, saying “*dhātoḥ*.”

He states "according to the opinion of the ancients" by means of the maxim *yakṣānurūpa* (the offering corresponds to the deity), using the term *adhyāhāreṇa* (by ellipsis). However, the true nature [of this] should be understood as previously stated. He refutes what was stated by the ancients with the words *prasiddheḥ* (from common usage). The implicit meaning is that even the property of having a function other than the well-known one must be provided as a qualification for the result (*phala*). The verbal [meaning], however, is indicated by the very fact that the action is obtained through common usage; thus, it is shown that the verb is intransitive (*akarmikā*) when it is conveyed by a sentence devoid of the use of that [specific] word.

He states the reason for abandoning the literal meaning of the word with the words "But not... (*na tv iti*). Regarding the phrase "in the Bhāṣya": the meaning is that the Bhāṣya does not state that [the verb] is intransitive merely by accepting the connection of that [meaning] as it presents itself. For this very reason, Kaiyaṭa has explained the Bhāṣya statement, "The river flows is intransitive" (*nadī vahatīty akarmakaḥ*), as having the sense of "the river flows" (*nadī syandate*). It is precisely to indicate this that this very example was provided.

But if this is so, how is the critique of the extension (*atideśa*) in the Bhāṣya regarding the example "māsam āsyate" and so forth? To this he says: "In the Śāstra. The intention is that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) depends on the general rule. [He adds: "By virtue of the force [of the context]."

The intended meaning is as follows: regarding the term *akarmaka* (intransitive), does it mean those verbal roots (*dhātu*) which, by way of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*), lack that meaning which serves as the basis for the technical designation "object" (*karma-saṃjñā*)—that is, roots whose expressed meaning lacks the factor that triggers the application of the term "object"—or does it mean those which, by way of secondary indication, convey a meaning devoid of an object? Of these two alternatives, the first has been refuted [by the statement] "And not in any case... (*na ca kvacid api*). Thus, if the meaning were "those roots whose expressed meaning lacks the factor that serves as the basis for the designation 'object'," then since all roots could potentially possess such a meaning, there would be no possibility of providing examples for the category of "intransitives" (*akarmaka*). This is the sense.

In the final case, it should be stated that the possibility of the example arises from the fact that the object (karman) is not intended to be expressed (*avivakṣita*). Nor is it impossible for time to be unintended because it is required by action alone; for since the requirement for time is satisfied by the time denoted by the verbal suffix itself, it is possible for an external temporal object to be unintended.

And this being the case, since the restriction [of the definition] in the *gatyādi* sūtra depends on its application to verbs of the same class, its scope would be restricted to transitive (*sakarmaka*) verbs; thus, in the case of intransitive (*akarmaka*) verbs, that [restriction] would be established by the rule "that which is most desired by the agent" (*kartur īpsitatamam*), making the mention of "intransitive" (*akarmaka*) redundant. Bearing this implication in mind, it was said: "Thus, etc. (*ta evam*, etc.). The meaning of the word "in some cases" (*kvacid*) is: in a sense devoid of the status of object (*karmatva*) due to factors such as time (*kāla*), etc., and lacking [the verbal roots] beginning with *āpti*. The essential point is that by virtue of that implication, in that state, [roots] are understood as being devoid of an object. — "Thus" (*iti*) means: in such passages [as the one cited]. 1.13.

Having thus defined the general meaning of the verbal root (*dhātu*), he defines the specific meanings of certain roots in order to refute the views of others, beginning with the word "of *pac*" (*paceḥ*). Indicating the purpose of this further explanation, he says: "And that [meaning] is manifold" (*sa cānekaḥ*). By this, the view that the meaning of *pac* is merely an activity conducive to conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is refuted; for if it were so, the usage "he cooks" (*pacati*) would be impossible in the case of one who possesses a flow of water conducive to the softening of rice-gruel (*bhaktaviklitti*) but lacks an effort (*kṛti*) conducive to conjunction with fire. — [Regarding the phrase] "the absence of the causal complex for destruction" (*dhvaṃsāsamagrī*).

The meaning is "the collocation characterized by the state of being a counter-correlate" (*pratiyogitva*). Although it would have been sufficient to say "conforming to destruction" (*dhvaṃsānukūla*), he states the purpose of using the term "non-perception" (*adarśana*) as follows: "separated" (*vyavahita*). Regarding that, he provides the proof for the second [case], since the first is well-known: "when it has arisen," etc. "Destroyed" means not ascended to the intellect (*buddhyānārūḍha*). Regarding the word "carried away" (*hṛta*): there was a king named Kārtavīryārjuna who possessed a thousand arms.

"By the mere recollection of that," and so forth. By this, the view that there is *lakṣaṇā* (indication) in that case is refuted; for even one who does not perceive the semantic incompatibility (*anupapatti*) understands it from that [recollection]. "In that case"—that is, between those two. "By this"—by the connection with time in that instance. "Of destruction"—of the non-perception produced by annihilation (*dhvaṃsa*). "Because of its eternity"—because, even if it were produced, it would be indestructible.

Since the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) everywhere consists simply in the operation conducive to destruction (*dhvaṃsa*), there is no need to postulate two separate powers (*śakti*). Out of parsimony (*lāghava*), he states the final conclusion according to the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) with the words beginning "And destruction... and ending with "others. *Śakti* (power) refers to a subtle state (*sūkṣmāvasthā*). [Objection: But in that case, there would be a contradiction with the previously stated etymologies and so forth, because in reality there is an absence of both production (*utpatti*) and destruction (*dhvaṃsa*). To this he replies: "From that" (*tataḥ*). This means "from the prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) of that form. To exclude a second day [of the same action], he says: "manifestation" (*abhivyakti*). To establish its status as an action (*kriyā*), he says: "having been obtained" (*labdha*).

For this very reason—that is, precisely because [the mind] resides in that [self] by way of its true nature—he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) for the sake of establishing conjunction: "And the self" (*ātmā ca*). In that context—that is, such being the case—he points out the flaw in the Naiyāyika position: "The mind" (*manaḥ*). The conscious individual soul (*jīva*) is the substratum of cognition. The phrase "due to the impossibility of conjunction" implies that the statement "the mind knows" is clearly untenable; this is the remainder [of the sense]. By the term "substratum of cognition," it is indicated that even with a substratum of cognition, that [conjunction] is not possible. Making this clear, he says: "He accepts that" (*tad-abhyupeti*).

The mind is atomic in nature because multiple cognitions do not arise simultaneously; it is not all-pervasive (*vibhu*). Thus, even if one does not accept its conjunction with two all-pervasive substances, there is no contradiction in accepting it [with others]; however, the intention is that its non-pervasive occurrence (*avyāpyavṛttitva*) refers specifically to its conjunction with external objects. Regarding the phrase "approaching" (*upayan*): it means possessing origination and destruction. "It transforms"—that is, it brings about the cognition of that destruction. He says "the Self" because the mind is composed of eight principles (*tattva*). The implication is that, in doing so, one's own established doctrine (*siddhānta*) would be undermined.

In connection with the usage "he goes to space" (*ākāśaṃ gacchati*) and so forth, he says "thus" (*evam*). This means [the distinction] between the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and the mind (*manas*). He provides the consensus for all cases by saying "that which has been stated" (*taduktim*); this means by Śrī Harṣa. Regarding the phrase "without pervading" (*avyāpya*), the meaning is that [the action] coexists with its own absence due to the difference in delimiters (*avacchedaka-bheda*). By the word "consensus" (*saṃmata*), his lack of dispute [on this point] is indicated.

The meaning of "that which is one" (*tadeka*) in the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is precisely this: when there is a question regarding a location that possesses a conjunction whose form exists in one part of that [location]. Indicating that the following is the statement of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the previously mentioned case, he states the *cūrṇikā*: "Therefore... (*tasmāt*). To the question, "How does this prove the point at hand? he replies: "Even in that which is partless" (*niraṃśe’pi*). He explains that the word "completely" (*nitarām*) connects with what follows, saying: "in every respect" (*sarvathā*). By the word "even" (*api*), the permanence accepted by the opponent is refuted.

[Objection: But surely, since [the atom] is imagined to have parts even if it is partless, why was the explanation provided by supplementing the text with the word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*), rather than following the meaning as it appears in the literal reading? For in that case, the desired conclusion would not be established. To this, he says: "Kaṇāda. *Pārimāṇḍalya* means the atom (*paramāṇu*). And thus, because all things possess parts, the previously stated proof is established. By this, the Naiyāyika claim—that creation arises from the conjunction of two atoms delimited by their respective spatial directions—is refuted, for the aforementioned reasoning applies, and because even space (*dik*) is non-existent at the time of the initial creation. Thus ends the discussion. 1.14.

On July 1, [the author] continues to refute the arguments of Bhūṣaṇa and others: "Now, even though the removal of the veil (āvaraṇabhaṅga) possesses the nature of being an object (viṣayatā) as defined by the aforementioned result, it lacks the nature of being the reality (tattva); therefore, he says: 'And of the object-nature' (viṣayatāyāśca). The word 'and' (ca) in 'and the determination' (vyavasthā ca) has the sense of 'for' (hi). The phrase 'the meaning of this' (asyārthaḥ) is to be construed with the word 'established' (vyavasthita) within the compound. He states that the word 'where' (yatra) has both meanings by saying: 'in the object' (karmaṇi). He says 'it is so stated' (ityucyate) because it is not his own established tenet."

Therefore, he says that in the second half [of the verse], the particle *tu* indicates its status as the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) by way of its distinction from what was previously stated. By the restrictive particle *eva* in the phrase "by words alone" (*śabdair eva*), there is an exclusion of perception (*darśana*). For this very reason, he says: "in the view" (*mate iti*). Where it is expressed (*ākhyāte*): *saḥ* refers to the verbal root (*dhātu*) that constitutes it; the same applies hereafter. *Tatra* means "among those. *Evam* means that it resides in both [the word and the object] through a difference in relation. *Na ca* means "certainly not. *Evam* means "residing in both. *Katham api* means "by whatever relation serves as its delimiting factor (*avacchedaka-sambandhena*)."

The reading is "nayanti" (they lead). Here, he states the agreement with the Bhāṣya: "ata eva" (for this very reason). The meaning is: precisely because the doctrine stated in the second half [of the verse] is the established conclusion (siddhānta). "Teṣām" refers to those roots whose action resides in the agent (kartṛsthabhāvaka). He states that the referent of the other word (anyapadārtha) is "dhātu" (the verbal root), saying "dhātūnām" (of the roots). He states that the meaning of the genitive case is the relationship between the signified and the signifier (vācyavācakabhāva), saying "vācyāyāḥ" (of the signified). He says "phalarūpa" (in the form of the fruit/result), as in the expression "pariniṣpattiḥ kriyāyāḥ" (the accomplishment of the action), meaning its employment [is indicated]. Its status as such has already been demonstrated previously.

Since, according to the method stated above, existence (*sattva*) and so forth are likewise inconsistent with the literal reading [of the text], he says "in mere action" (*karmamātre*), following the maxim that "every statement [must be consistent]. This means "only in action. Now, since the commentary as it stands is common to both sides, why not take it as referring only to the meaning stated in the first half? To this he replies: "The verse (*kārikā*)," etc. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in "knowledge, etc.," there is an inclusion of the agent of differentiation (*bhidā*) and so forth. Therefore, that [interpretation] is indeed not the established doctrine (*asiddhānta*); thus, what was stated by the *Bhūṣaṇa* and others is simply incorrect—this is how it should be understood. 1.15

"Thus" means "as if one knows. Now, one might ask: since it is difficult to specify the substratum [of knowledge] in the case of the past and so forth, how can that [knowledge] be real?
