To this he says: "The past," etc. This should be understood in the same way for expressions such as "he makes a pot" and the like. However, in the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), there is no suspicion of any defect whatsoever. Now, even so, one might ask: how can the Self itself be the reality in that context? To this he says: "The Self," etc.—[and] "the object," etc.

And thus, the sense is that because the fruit and the operation reside in different loci due to the distinction between the imagined selves, the verb retains its transitivity (*sakarmakatva*). Regarding the phrase "like the object" (*karmavat*): for it is stated there, "There are two selves: the bodily self (*śarīrātman*) and the inner self (*antarātman*). The bodily self performs that action by which the bodily self experiences pleasure and pain. By this, the statements "the self slays the self by means of the self" and "the self creates the self by means of the self" are also explained.

Now, one might object: while the operation consisting of the contact between the self and the mind—which is conducive to the production of the fruit in the form of knowledge (jñāna) as qualified by the relation of objectivity—is possible in the cases mentioned, how can this be established in instances such as "he knows Brahman"? For in that case, there is no knowledge distinct from its own nature, and since that [nature] is unproduced, and because the contact between the self and the mind is absent, how can [the action] exist? To this he says: "Brahman... This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* and *Bhāmatī* on the Sūtra: "Because of seeing, [Brahman] is not that which is not based on scripture" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*). In the same way, the explanation of passages such as "He thought" (*sa aikṣata*) is established.

In this regard, it should be understood that the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is as follows: first, there is the observation of indeterminate name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*); then, the desire to manifest that in a general way; then, that same desire in a specific form; and finally, its manifestation. He states, "it is transitive" (*sakarmaka*), because even though there is a difference in the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) due to the difference in the resulting fruit—namely, conjunction with a subsequent location—the status of being transitive remains the same since the relation of having a different locus (*tadvyadhikaraṇatva*) is equal in both cases. He provides an example from the rule *dvitīyā-śrita-* [Pāṇini 2.1.24]: "hell" (*naraka*).

He states "merely the conjunction produced by disjunction" (*vibhāgajanya-saṃyoga-mātra*) in order to explain such cases as "the leaf falls from the tree. By the word *mātra* (mere), there is an exclusion of the operation conducive to that [conjunction]. Even though that [conjunction] lacks the status of being the result mentioned therein, there is no inconsistency because it is an action (*kriyā*) according to the aforementioned method. By this, the view that [the root *pat*] is intransitive because its meaning is merely an operation is refuted. Indicating that its meaning is an operation co-located with arising—just like the root *jan*—he says "co-located with arising" (*utpatti-samānādhikaraṇa*). He refutes the position of the Naiyāyikas and others by stating "merely effort" (*yatna-mātra*).

And likewise, expressions such as "he makes a pot" (*ghaṭaṃ karoti*) would not be possible. He states another defect with the words "furthermore" (*kiñca*). By the phrase "the *ya*-class [suffixes] and so forth," he includes the *taṅ*-class suffixes and others. Now, one might ask: how is effort (*yatna*) understood in the word *kṛti*? To this he replies: "The word *kṛti*. By "and so forth" (*ādi*), he includes the instrument (*karaṇa*) and other factors. By this, the view that there is a secondary figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) in those cases is set aside. Indicating that this too has been stated according to the system of others, he states his own established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "or rather" (*yadvā*). The reading is *kṛtiyatnaśabdayor api*. Otherwise, if the reading were different, it should be understood as a copulative compound (*dvandva*) meaning "effort (*yatna*) and the word *kṛti*."

Regarding the phrase "while being told": the word "she" (*sā*) is the agent (*kartṛ*), as is understood from the context. The meaning of the root *jan* (to be born) is an operation (*vyāpāra*) that has the same locus (*samānādhikaraṇa*) as the act of origination (*utpatti*). Among these, the nature of origination has already been explained previously. Roots such as *sraṃs* (to fall) are intransitive (*akarmaka*), like *jīv* (to live), whereas roots such as *dhā* (to place) are transitive (*sakarmaka*) because their nature is otherwise; thus he says: "Enough of this. (1.16)

Having thus defined, both generally and specifically, the pure meanings of certain particles for that purpose, he now defines them when mixed with other words, in order to refute the views of others, ancient and modern, regarding objects that are not free from fallacy—beginning with the words "anubhūyate" (is experienced). He says "sākṣāt" (directly) in order to establish the equality that will be stated hereafter. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), examples such as "alaṃ kriyate" (enough is done) are included. He states this by way of commonality to both cases: "of particles. "Sākṣātkāra" means "tadādi" (that and so forth).

However, only that much has been stated here in accordance with the context under discussion—the implication being that there would be no transitivity (*sakarmakatva*) even if the fruit such as "experience" were the meaning of a particle (*nipāta*). [The phrase] "only in the fruit of the verbal root's meaning" is used because of proximity (*pratyāsatti*); otherwise, the intention is that in cases such as "he abandons the new [village]," there would result transitivity even with respect to the village and so forth. Now, by way of occasion, he defines that [meaning] for that purpose—starting with "and the state of being a manifestor" (*dyotakatvam*). On this point, some say: "There is a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of each respective verbal root in its respective meaning, and the particles (*nipātas*) serve to indicate the intended sense (*tātparya*); this very thing is what constitutes 'being a manifestor'."

Others, however, say: because verbal roots have multiple meanings, they possess the capacity (*śakti*) for that meaning as well; the co-occurrence with a prefix (*upasarga*), however, is the awakener (*udbodhaka*) of such a capacity. And being an awakener of capacity is precisely what constitutes "indicative function" (*dyotakatva*). This very thing is expressed by the term "bestowing of capacity" (*śaktyādhāyakatva*) in cases such as *vyatiṣe*. [The phrase] "awakening of the function" (*vṛttyudbodha*) means this. By this, when victory has its capacity established [in the root], their [the prefixes'] role is to delimit the capacity regarding excellence (*prakarṣa*). Their nature is merely being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatva*) within that which delimits the capacity (*śaktatāvacchedaka*).

And thus, there is a capacity for excellence by virtue of being preceded by *pra*; nor is there a capacity by virtue of being preceded by *ji*, because that would entail the fault of postulating an additional [denotation] and because it would result in the non-connection with the meaning of the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). Since "indicative power" (*dyotakatva*) consists precisely in being a delimiting factor of the capacity—this is the specific point he states with the word "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*). He states its result with the word "sometimes" (*kvacid*). Now, one might ask: why is it not treated here like the example "he sits drawing on the ground"? To this he says: "having first delimited" (*prādeśam*), meaning having measured out.

The word "vi-" [is used] because the speaker’s intention is precisely as indicated by the employment of the term "prādeśa" (span); otherwise, the propriety of that statement would be clearly untenable. This is because the root √likh, like the root √jīv and others, is intransitive (akarmaka), since the object in the form of "syllables" (akṣara) is already included within the meaning of the verbal root itself. Nor should it be asked how this applies to the illustrative example.

In that context, regarding the friend’s words to the woman who has been waiting for many days—"He is to be protected by us as much as your own life"—the phrase "on the ground" (bhūmim) and not "on the ground" (bhūmau) suggests that the intended action is not the primary object of reference. By saying "he was writing" (likhan) rather than "he was writing" (likhatī), it is suggested through *dhvani* that the act of writing is secondary, being unintentional. By saying "outside" (bahis) rather than "inside" (madhye), it is suggested that the hero is in a state of extreme agitation.

It is *āste* (he sits), not *āsīt* (he sat); by this, the fact that such a state culminates in grace (*prasāda*) is suggested—this is because, due to the polysemous nature of verbal roots (*dhātu*), there is no fault here, as the root [in this context] signifies an action conducive to drawing a line (*rekhā*). He states the third [type of *karmapravacanīya*] with the words "between speech and mind" (*vac-citte*). This means a specific relation (*sambandhaviśeṣa*). And this is clear in the *Bhāṣya* on the term "karmapravacanīya. For in that [section], regarding the statement "those who have expressed an action (*karman*) are *karmapravacanīyas*," the *Bhāṣya* says: "Those which do not currently denote an action..."

Regarding the statement, "Those which express an action (*kriyā*) when [the action] is not being performed are *karmapravacanīya*s," it is stated that this is a designation based on its etymological meaning (*anvarthasaṃjñā*).
In this regard, Hari says:
"This [term] indicates (*dyotaka*) an action, but it neither expresses (*vācaka*) nor denotes a relation."
Nor does it imply a verbal action, but rather differentiates the relationship itself. Thus [it is said].

And thus, the sense in the Bhāṣya is that the verb [in the sūtra] refers subsequently to its connection with that [object]. He states another example for the second [case] with the words "atha" (now). Kaiyaṭa says: "Even though the instruction on words (*śabdānuśāsana*) has many actions as its object, the fact that it is being commenced is understood through the proximity of the word *atha*. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he includes the statements of Miśra and others. In every respect, he says "evam" (thus) to indicate the lack of such a restriction. Now, since there is no distinction in that regard in common usage, he says "aḍ-ādi" (the augment *aṭ*, etc.). By "etcetera," he includes reduplication (*dvirvacana*). He refutes the view of the Naiyāyikas with the words "etena" (by this).

The intended meaning is as follows: in expressions such as *prajayati* ("he conquers excellently"), excellence (*prakṛṣṭa*) and so forth are not denoted by the prefix (*upasarga*). For if that were the case, since it would not be the meaning of the verbal root (*prakṛti*), it could not be construed with the meaning of the verb (*ākhyāta*), because of the grammatical rule: "suffixes [denote their own meanings] in relation to the meaning of the base. Nor can it be argued that "conquering" is the meaning of the root and "excellence" is the meaning of the prefix *pra*; for according to the rule that the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a root cannot be directly construed through a relation of difference without mediating the meaning of a case-ending, even in this view, its construction with the meaning of the root remains impossible.

Furthermore, "qualified victory" (viśiṣṭajaya) is not the meaning of the verbal root (dhātvartha), because the cognition of this very meaning would arise even without a prefix, just as it does for other meanings. Therefore, the previously stated passage from "since the capacity [for denoting] victory is already established [in the root]" up to "this is the conclusion" should be understood.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "what pleasure is experienced," if that [prefix *anu-*) were to denote it [the pleasure], then because the verbal root would be intransitive (*akarmaka*), the application of the *la*-suffixes (tense/aspect markers) in the sense of the object (*karman*) would be impossible; for being transitive (*sakarmaka*) consists precisely in denoting an operation whose locus is distinct from the locus of its own primary fruit (*svārthaphala*). Otherwise, since some degree of distinction of locus from the fruit exists everywhere, there would be the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) of transitivity in all cases. Therefore, prefixes (*upasarga*) are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), whereas particles such as *ca* and others are indeed denoters (*vācaka*).

In expressions such as "is directly perceived" (*sākṣātkriyate*), since words like *sākṣāt* can denote the result—perception and so forth—which possesses the relation of objectness (*viṣayatā*) [with respect to its object], the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) is the operation conducive to the production of that [result]. Thus, in cases such as "the teacher is directly perceived," the understanding is: "an operation conducive to the production of a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) which resides in a locus non-different from the teacher, by way of the relation of objectness. He states this with the words "taditara... (in the verse). To provide proof for its being such [a result], he says "sākṣāt...": [the word *sākṣāt*] denotes reaching, ornamenting, sufficiency, and warding off.

It should also be understood that *uraryūri*, *corarīca*, and *vistāre* (in the sense of expansion) and *aṅgīkṛtau* (in the sense of acceptance)—these three [are formed]. Now, an objection: since the classification of roots as intransitive (*akarmaka*) and so forth is based on the inclusion of specific meanings, how can there be the *la*-affix (the optative/imperative suffix) in the sense of the object (*karman*) here, in the case of [roots meaning] perception and the like? However, it is not correct to say that being transitive (*sakarmakatva*) consists merely in denoting an operation whose locus is distinct from the result; for that would incur the fault mentioned immediately below starting with "kiñca" and so on. Thus, since that [result] is part of the root-meaning, it is necessary that these [prefixes] are merely indicators (*dyotaka*); why then is this the case? To this, he says: "And being transitive... *Note: The text provided contains some orthographic irregularities typical of older manuscripts, such as the use of *ca* instead of *vā* in certain contexts, and the sandhi forms.*

[Objection: Even so, in order to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), [the definition of] *karmatva* (objecthood) must consist precisely in being the locus of the fruit of the verbal root's meaning (*dhātvarthaphala*). Since that is absent here, how can there be *karmatva* for that [word]? To this he says: "Even objecthood..."—that is, "of such a kind. This means: the fruit which is the meaning of either the word itself or the particle (*nipāta*) connected with it. He states the meaning of the phrase "by this" as follows: "In the case of disparity. According to the method stated in the passage beginning "between the meaning of a noun and the meaning of a verbal root," since it is so there, it is so here as well. Consequently, the derivation of that [term *karmatva*] conforms to this [definition], and its scope is restricted to cases other than particles (*nipāta*).

Even in that case, it is more appropriate [to consider the suffix] as a denoter (*vācaka*). The sense is that the usage "he cooks a little" (*stokaṃ pacati*) would otherwise be inexplicable without its being an indicator (*dyotaka*). Thus he says: "It is experienced. He states the flaw according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*): "The object," etc., and "of the cognition," etc. The sense is that it is not perceived through the natural capacity of the word (*śabdamaryādayā*). The reason for its extreme heaviness is its difficulty to understand;

and because it is constituted by a distinction (*bheda*), it depends upon multiple cognitions distinct from both of those [the object and the cognition], and because such a [comprehensive] cognition is impossible, it is neither real nor unreal—this is the meaning. (1.17)

He refutes the argument concerning the Kaustubha jewel and so forth with the words "As for what [was said]..."—the prefix is denoted by that word; therefore, there is no identity between the reason and the delimiting property of the subject. [This is done] by means of inference, specifically a negative inference (vyatirekin). By "by another"—namely, by the Naiyāyika—the phrase "in the proof" is to be supplemented by "stated due to a fault. Regarding the view that there are four types of words, he says "śakti... (power...); regarding the view that there are three types, he says "or an indivisible [entity]."

Even if the meaning were "that which has the form of an *upādhi* (limiting adjunct) or the form of a *jāti* (universal)," a delimited (*sakhaṇḍa*) nature—consisting in being listed in the *ca*-group and so forth—would still be possible; nevertheless, because that [delimited nature] lacks a commonality (*ananugatatva*) due to the differences between the *ca*-group and other such lists, it is abandoned. — "By being a particle alone" means "by being the denotable object of the word 'particle'. By this, the objection that "this is incorrect because there is no reason accepted by both parties to establish that [property] under the delimitation of a general [term]" is refuted.

In this view, because there is an absence of expressiveness (*dyotakatva*) in that [case], there is a deviation (*vyabhicāra*); therefore, he says: "due to the absence of denotative power" (*vācakatvābhāva*). And thus, the sense is that when [denotation] is possible, expressiveness is overridden by the "convergence of meanings" (*arthasamājagrasta*). He states the reason for its being logical: "of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇānām*). The sense is that for instruments of knowledge (*pramākaraṇa*), the presence of a pervading property (*vyāpakadharma*) is necessary. The essential point is that when a means of valid cognition operates under the delimitation of generality, the principle of parsimony (*lāghava*), assisted by the absence of any subverting factor (*bādhaka*), is the underlying cause. [He concludes with: "because it would result in the establishment of that" (*tatsiddhyāpatti*).

This is not an acceptable conclusion (*iṣṭāpatti*), because it would result in the undesirable consequence (*anāpatti*) that particles (*svarādi*) could also be used independently (*svātantryeṇa*). For this very reason, he refutes the statement of the *Bhūṣaṇa* and others with the words "the status of being a particle" (*nipātatvam*). The meaning is "that form. The intention is that [this is so] by virtue of pervasiveness (*vyāpakatvena*) according to the aforementioned reasoning. And thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply; this is the intended sense (*tātparya*). Since the apprehension of the general [category] is useless, he says "each respective" (*tattad-*) and "occurring therein" (*tadvṛtti*). The meaning is "occurring in each respective [instance]."

[Objection: But surely, by the maxim "that which [is established] for two specific cases," that [principle] is also applicable; therefore, he says: "the proponent of the nipātana view. The sense is this: while such an admission might be accepted in other cases where there is no subverting evidence (*bādhaka*), here, because such subverting evidence exists, it is not so. He refutes another argument from the *Kaustubha* and other works with the words: "as for what was also said..."

Just as in the case of *dhātu* (verbal root) and *ghañ* (nominal suffix), where there is no relation between the action (*kriyā*) and the agent (*kartṛ*), so too in examples such as *rāmāu* (Rāma-du), since number (*dvitva*, etc. is a qualifier of the subsequent element, the rule regarding suffixes being indicators (*sādhaka-pratyaya*) applies. However, because here there is a relationship of denoter and denoted (*gamya-gamaka-bhāva*) and the meaning presents itself independently from the word, this [objection] is unavoidable; thus, to avoid inconsistency with the *Bhūṣaṇa*, he says: "By the power of the word (*śabda-śakti*). The sense is that, according to the maxim "the meaning of a word [is what is understood]," it cannot be construed there as the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*). Having accepted the possibility of the application of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhī*), it was refuted in the latter [case].

In reality, that [objection] is not valid; thus he says, "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). The term "second" (*dvitīyā*) refers to the accusative case and so forth. To avoid an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), he states the intended meaning with the word "therein" (*tatra*); the sense is "in the qualifier. The phrase "of the jar" (*ghaṭasya*) means "of that very [jar]. And thus, since there is no syntactic connection (*śābdānvaya*) of that [jar] with respect to that [qualifier], the aforementioned undesirable consequence does not follow; this is the point. He expresses this with the word "where? (*kva*). [The objection] "But even so... is stated while accepting the view of the ancients that "the meanings of nouns [are connected] with each other. However, he states that this is actually incorrect with the words "In reality" (*vastutaḥ*).

—At the beginning—in this very section immediately following. —For this very reason—because they (the particles) are eternally independent and thus lack the status of being qualifiers such that there is no verbal connection (*śābdānvaya*) of a jar or the like with them; whereas in that case [with the jar], there is indeed a verbal connection of it [the jar] with them. However, in the case of *dvandva* compounds and the like, it should be understood that multiple words are employed for the sake of expressing mutual conjunction (*samuccaya*). By this, the defects alleged by the *Kaustubha*, the *Bhūṣaṇa*, and others—namely, that if particles were denotative (*vācaka*), there would be the consequence of non-difference connection (*abhedānvaya*), and that there is no evidence for providing the qualification "being other than a particle"—are also refuted.

Because there is no distinction in the nature of the word’s expressive power (*śabdaśakti*). According to the perspective of others—that is, following the opinion of others—he says "or rather" (*yadvā*), because of the parsimony (*lāghava*) resulting from the absence of that [relation]. The sense is: in the case of "that jar is a collection" (*sa ghaṭaḥ samuccayaḥ*), since the connection occurs through non-difference (*abheda*), there is no genitive case based on difference, nor is there the presentation of a specific portion of it, nor is there a connection with "beautiful" (*śobhana*) and so forth, because it is a single part (*ekadeśatvāt*). Now, if this were so, since it would have existence as its meaning, there would be the undesirable consequence of hearing a case-ending; therefore he says "by its very nature" (*svabhāvataḥ*). This refers to the phrase beginning with "the expressive power of the word. He says "the proponent" (*vādī*).

If there were no provision for the compounding of particles (*nipāta*), then case endings would not arise at all, because those particles lack semantic content and thus do not possess the designation of *prātipadika*. Furthermore, the established rule that in negative compounds (*nañ-samāsa*) and the like the meaning of the subsequent member is predominant would not hold, since the preceding member, such as *nañ*, would be semantically void. Therefore, it is necessary that the meaning of the particle be presented by its own form; however, in that context, it exists as something non-existent (*asattvabhūta*). But when presented by the word "samuccita" (collected), it exists precisely as something existent (*sattvabhūta*).

Regarding this, he states the consensus of Hari (Patañjali): "It has been said," etc. [The point is that] although suffixes (*pratyaya*) possess denotative power when combined, they are not employed in isolation;

such is the meaning of the verse beginning with *ityādi*. Even though their status as "subsequent" (*para*) is not traditionally taught in the same way as the status of suffixes, they are not used alone because the meaning to be conveyed by them lacks syntactic connection (*anvaya*) without a related term. The particle *ca* is used in the sense of "also. By this, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) with the previous opinion. For this very reason, he himself stated:
"Even when expressing a combined meaning, those [words] which denote a qualified object..."

"The connection of words is through their qualities (guṇas), whereas particles such as *ca* and others are dependent. Even so, since the cognition [of the meaning] would remain incomplete without the specific presentation of those two [the particle and its referent], they are eternally dependent; thus, the sense is that there is no separate usage [of the particle]. This is also necessary in the previous view. And so, while the former view relies on two natures, this one relies on only one; this is the more parsimonious [theory]—this is the hidden intention (*gūḍhākūta*). —Regarding the "substratum aspect" (*dharmyaṃśe*), it says "conjunction" (*samuccaya*).

The meaning is that [the word] "of the jar" (*ghaṭasya*) cannot be construed with [the word "potter"] without the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhaktyartha*), because otherwise there would be no connection between the two due to their difference; for otherwise, an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would result, as a connection would be impossible. The sense is that it is like the specific capacity (*viśiṣṭaśakti*) of a jar and so forth. || 1.18 ||

Having thus refuted the objections raised by others regarding their denotative capacity (*vācakatva*), and having accepted the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) that their function is necessarily indicative (*dyotakatva*) according to the reasoning stated previously, he resolves the two objections raised by others starting with the words "nipātānām" (of the particles). The word "ādāyaiva" (having indeed accepted) has the word "bodhyam" (is to be understood) as its ellipsis. By this, it is indicated that the justification for the grammatical rule (*anuśāsana*) beginning with "sākṣāt" (directly) and so forth is likewise established in this very manner. Now, an objection may be raised: since the definition of "meaningfulness" (*arthavattva*)—which consists in being a generator of the cognition of a meaning through one of the two functions (*vṛtti*), namely direct denotation (*śakti*) or indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—is included in the rule *arthavat-sūtra* to avoid over-extension (*anatiprasaṅga*), how can the resolution [of the objection] be achieved from that?

As for what is stated in the *Bhūṣaṇa* and other works—that although there is no over-extension [of the rule], either because of the absence of number-suffix application (*saṃkhyānvayābhāvāt*), or by the maxim of the reduplication of a single vowel (*ekāj-dvirvacana-nyāyāt*), or because there is no fault due to elision (*luk*), or because forms like *rāmaḥ* are compounds (*samāsatva*) like *rājapuruṣaḥ*—nevertheless: in the first case, since even particles (*nipāta*) lack number and so forth, the case-ending would not occur; if one accepts the universal application of the singular number (*ausargikaikavacana*), then that same consequence would apply to *rāmaḥ* and the like as well. Furthermore, the maxim of the reduplication of a single vowel is not applicable here, because the parts are not assisted by the operation belonging to the whole.

And thus, what has been stated by Kaiyaṭa and others should be considered; for in the third case, since [the suffix] is not a constituent part of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), the elision (*luk*) would not apply, resulting in the undesirable consequence of hearing the case-ending and the occurrence of *jaś*-substitution and *na*-elision in forms such as *dhanaṃ*. Therefore, even the fourth alternative is inconsistent. Consequently, some hold that there is no production of case-endings precisely because of the indicator (*jñāpaka*) in the rule "avyayād āpsupaḥ" (Pāṇini 2.4.82).

Others hold that it is due to the Vārttika "nipātasya... (Vārttika on Pāṇini 2.4.82). Still others maintain that when that [Vārttika] is rejected on the basis of the indicator in "adhiparī" (Pāṇini 1.4.93), its establishment is achieved by resorting to its being dependent upon a general category (*sāmānyāpekṣatva*).

Regarding the statement that Dīkṣita says the truth is that those [suffixes] are included under the rule *kṛttaddhita* by means of the particle *ca* (and) for the purpose of collecting what was not explicitly mentioned, that is incorrect. For the general singular number is accepted only when there is an indicator (*gamaka*). Therefore, there is no occurrence of *jaś*-substitution and so forth. This is because, by virtue of its association with *dhātu* (verbal root) in the rule *supo dhātu*, the *sup* (case-ending) is accepted as belonging only to a nominal stem (*prātipadika*) that consists of more than one element; furthermore, the Vārttika [which would otherwise justify such an inclusion] has been rejected, and there is no evidence for its being dependent on a general [application], and because it has been stated in the Bhāṣya and elsewhere that the particle *ca* serves to collect items that are otherwise meaningless [in that context].

Making this very point clear, he says: "śakti" (power). The meaning is that it is precisely such possession of meaning (*arthavattva*) that is included in that sūtra. It was stated previously that the acceptance of the function of suggestion (*vyañjanā-vṛtti*) is for this very purpose.

By this [objection], it is refuted that there is no fault in that case by including "being the locus where the subjecthood (*viṣayatā*) is fully resident" (*paryāptyādhikaraṇatva*), because that [possession of meaning] exists only in the qualified [word]. However, in the present case, since prefixes (*pra-* etc. themselves convey the intended meaning (*tātparya*), they are the causes of the cognition of meaning according to the aforementioned method; thus, since there is indeed the status of being the locus where the subjecthood is fully resident in the cognition that causes that [meaning], the objection is dismissed.
Because [the alternative] would be afflicted by defects, such as the undesirable consequence that one would be "cutting across" (*vyatilunati*) and so forth.

Now, if it is objected: "Even if they are nominal stems (*prātipadika*), how can there be an inflection (*vibhakti*) given the absence of number and other factors?"—we say no. This is because of the *jñāpaka* (indicative evidence) in the rule "after an indeclinable, [the suffix] *āP*" (*avyayād āP*), and because of the statement in the Bhāṣya on the sūtra "and the secondary suffixes" (*taddhitaśca*), which accepts the singular number for all case-endings. Thus, although it has been stated that prepositions (*upasarga*) and other particles (*nipāta*) are established as being either indicators (*dyotaka*) or denoters (*vācaka*), prepositions are exclusively indicators in every respect; otherwise, in the case of *pratiṣṭhate*, there would be no cognition of the action in the form of "going."

If the root *sthā* has the meaning of "cessation of motion" (*gati-nivṛtti*) and the prefix *pra-* signifies "absence," then the cognition would necessarily arise as "there is no absence of motion. However, there is not even the possibility of such a cognition here, because [the absence] is not presented as being related to the absence of motion; otherwise, such a cognition would also arise in the case of "the absence of a jar" (*ghaṭābhāva*). Furthermore, when used in conjunction with the negative particle *nañ*, there is no fault, because we accept an innate linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*) established from time immemorial. Nor is there any actual experience of such a cognition. Therefore, for them [the prefixes], they function solely as indicators (*dyotaka*).

Suggesting this very point, he also cites the consensus of the Bhāṣya thereon: "pratiṣṭhate" (he stands). The meaning is "even here. "tadartheti" refers to the rule beginning with "dhātoḥ" (Pāṇini 3.1.91). "tadgatāditveti" means "the state of having motion as its culmination," etc.; that is to say, "initial action" (*ādikarma*). "bhūvādīti" [refers to the rule beginning with *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*].

In that context, while refuting the *vārttika*—"There is a prohibition [of the designation 'verbal root'] regarding a root denoting action when a prefix (*upasarga*) or suffix (*pratyaya*) is present"—it is first established that "the base (*prakṛti*) occurs in the sense of the base, and the suffix occurs in the sense of the suffix. Then, having stated that "a prefix qualifies the action; in the case of *pacati*, the action is understood, and the prefix qualifies it," and having resolved the issue by showing that just as there is deviation of the root from the prefix, there is likewise a deviation of the prefix from the root in cases such as *adhīte*, it is said: "In this case, then..."

"It is clearly understood that there is a different meaning [in each case]: in 'tiṣṭhati' (he stands) there is the cessation of the act of going (*vrajikriyā*), while in 'pratiṣṭhate' (he sets out), there is the act of going; therefore we consider this to be produced by the prefix (*upasarga*), by which the act of going is understood here. This is an observed deviation: [the prefix] *pra* is used in the sense of the commencement of an action (*ādikarman*). If one says, "This is not so, for roots have many meanings," [we reply: just as it is in the case of *vap* and other roots, so it is here as well; it has been stated that "the root *sthā* itself expresses both the act of going and its cessation."

"Because this [word] is used elsewhere as well; therefore, it is inferred that whatever meaning is expressed by it elsewhere is the very same here too. Kaiyaṭa explains that because verbal roots have multiple meanings, the root *sthā* itself signifies "motion. To state a specific point, he says "even though," etc., presenting the previously mentioned [view] as the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya, preceded by a doubt. Regarding the word "separately" (*pṛthak*), it was stated by Hari: [The text continues with the verse: "The root *sthā*, which is established in its own form, is taught as having the sense of 'remaining' (*avasthāna*). However, when it is connected with another [root], it is seen to signify motion (*gati*) and so forth. Thus, even though the root *sthā* is established in its own form as signifying "remaining," it is taught as such; yet, when it is joined with another [verbal element], it is observed to express motion and other meanings. For example, in the case of *pratiṣṭhate*, the prefix *pra-* is understood to signify "going forward" (*pragati*), while the root *sthā* signifies "remaining. When these two are combined, the resulting meaning is "going forward" (*pragati*). Similarly, in the case of *adhiṣṭhānam*, the prefix *adhi-* signifies "superiority" (*aiśvarya*), while the root *sthā* signifies "remaining"; when these are combined, the resulting meaning is "sovereignty" (*aiśvarya*). Likewise, in the case of *abhiṣṭauti*, the prefix *abhi-* signifies "repetition" (*vīpsā*), while the root *stu* signifies "praising" (*stuti*); when these are combined, the resulting meaning is "praising repeatedly" (*vīpsā-stuti*). In the case of *anuṣṭhānam*, the prefix *anu-* signifies "similarity" (*sādṛśya*), while the root *sthā* signifies "remaining"; when these are combined, the resulting meaning is "acting similarly" (*sādṛśya-kriyā*). In the case of *pariṣṭhānam*, the prefix *pari-* signifies "surrounding" (*pariveṣṭana*), while the root *sthā* signifies "remaining"; when these are combined, the resulting meaning is "remaining after surrounding" (*pariveṣṭana-anuṣṭhāna*). In the case of *samavasthānam*, the prefix *samava-* signifies "coming together" (*saṃgama*), while the root *sthā* signifies "remaining"; when these are combined, the resulting meaning is "remaining after coming together" (*saṃgama-anuṣṭhāna*). In the case of *vyavasthānam*, the prefix *vyava-* signifies "distinction" (*viśeṣa*), while the root *sthā* signifies "remaining"; when these are combined, the resulting meaning is "remaining with distinction" (*viśeṣa-anuṣṭhāna*). In the case of *upasthānam*, the prefix *upa-* signifies "nearness" (*sāmīpya*), while the root *sthā* signifies "remaining"; when these are combined, the resulting meaning is "remaining near" (*sāmīpya-anuṣṭhāna*). In the case of *pratiṣṭhānam*, the prefix *prati-* signifies "counter-action" (*pratidvandva*), while the root *sthā* signifies "remaining"; when these are combined, the resulting meaning is "remaining in counter-action" (*pratidvandva-anuṣṭhāna*). In the case of *anuṣṭhānam*, the prefix *anu-* signifies "following" (*anugamana*), while the root *sthā* signifies "remaining"; when these are combined, the resulting meaning is "remaining in following" (*anugamana-anuṣṭhāna*). In the case of *pariṣṭhānam*, the prefix *pari-* signifies "surrounding" (*pariveṣṭana*), while the root *sthā* signifies "remaining"; when these are combined, the resulting meaning is "remaining after surrounding" (*pariveṣṭana-anuṣṭhāna*). "In the grammatical treatise, the separate conceptualization of roots and prefixes is for the sake of establishing the rules for *aṭ* and so forth; however, in reality, the root alone is such [as the meaningful unit]."

Such [an entity] is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*). He states this very point with the words "and thus" (*evaṃ ca*). The meaning is that in common worldly usage, since a qualified cognition arises only from a qualified [word], and since difference is merely postulated for the sake of grammatical operation (*kāryārtha*). — For this very reason—namely, because it is internal (*antaraṅga*) and precisely because it has that as its meaning. — "Thus" (*iti*): [this refers to] examples such as *ityādi*. By this, the inclusion of examples such as *tenānubhūyate sukham* is intended. By this, the refutation of the view of Sīradeva and others—that this is an independent technical rule (*paribhāṣā*)—is accomplished. By the term "report" (*pravāda*), its non-Vedic origin (*anārṣatva*) is indicated.

He states that reality [is established] precisely through the order of proximity by saying "and external" (*bāhyaśca*). For this very reason—namely, by virtue of their being internal and external respectively. And thus, the sense is that the rule "even when there is intervention by *a* or *śas*" (*aśyāsavyavāye’pi*) need not be formulated. Now, an objection: if this were so, forms such as *adhyayanam* would be unestablished. For if the prefix were joined first, the long vowel caused by that [prefix] would occur, and subsequently, with the suffix *lyuṭ*, the *guṇa* substitution would result in the undesired form *adhayanam*; therefore, he says "adhyayanam. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), the rule "after the root *ṇī*, [the suffix *lyuṭ* becomes *a*] in the sense of study" (*ṇeradhyaye*) and others are included.

To avoid an over-extension [of the principle], he says "kvacit" (in some cases). The particle "eva" is as before. And thus, even its status as a *dyotaka* (indicator) is merely conceptual (*kālpānika*), intended for the sake of establishing that [function] during the stage of grammatical analysis (*prakriyā-daśā*); such is the intended meaning. — The "New School" (*navyāḥ*) refers to Dīkṣita and others. ||1.19||

With the intention that such an arrangement is not tenable when a single unified statement (*ekavākyatva*) is possible in every respect, he states the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) beginning with "In reality, however" (*vastutastu*). Its connection is with the word "is to be understood" (*bodhya*) here. The word "stated" (*ukta*) is connected with "thus" (*iti*) and so forth. Having stated in response to the question "What is internal (*antaraṅga*) and what is external (*bahiraṅga*)?"—namely, "Whatever is stated, that alone should be resorted to"—he shows what is indeed reasonable by saying "The verbal root... (*dhātūpa-*) and so on.

And thus, because the *suṭ* augment is not *asiddha* due to its being *antaraṅga*, there is no occurrence of a long vowel on account of the absence of *laghutva* (lightness); furthermore, the *guṇa* substitution is established because of the word beginning with a *saṃyoga*. This is the intended meaning (*bhāva*). The word "hi" means "since. The purport is that this [rule] is for the sake of establishing forms such as "upāsyate guruḥ," which require the *ārdhadhātuka* suffix. Since no fault would arise if it had the meaning that will be stated later, and since *antaraṅgatva* would not be established otherwise, he states the meaning differently with the word "upa": the sense is that there is an absence of *bahiraṅgatva* and so forth caused by meaning.

He states that being an *upasarga* (prefix) is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and not a mere incidental characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*) by saying "by that which is designated as such. He uses the present tense in "he says" (*āha*) according to the rule "the present tense is used for immediate past time" (*vartamānasāmīpye*). The same applies hereafter. "This is not so"—this refers to the intention that is about to be stated. He provides the reason for this by saying "for previously," where "for" (*hi*) means "because. Demonstrating its lack of substance, he shows the correctness of the statement "for the verbal root [is mentioned] first" by saying "for the instrument (*sādhana*)."

For by means of the *sādhana* (the instrument of accomplishment), there is the cognition of the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*), since the state of being "to be accomplished" is dependent upon its relation to an instrument of accomplishment. And the status of being a prefix (*upasarga*) occurs when it is in conjunction with such an action; this is the intended meaning. He states this with the words "that [action]"—namely, "he performs the state. Thus, in the stage of the form *saṃskṛti*, because it is caused by the word *saṃ* which has a more internal meaning, the *suṭ* augment and so forth are more internal than even reduplication (*dvitva*) and the like. This is the sense.

And thus, the sense is that when a suffix denoting an instrument (sādhana) is joined to a verbal root (*dhātu*) meaning "to go" (*prā*) in its primary sense, the understanding of it as an action (*kriyātva*) occurs first, and only then does the connection with a word termed a prefix (*upasarga*) take place. He states the refutation for the contrary view with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*); the meaning is "in the absence of that [prior connection]. He explains according to the aforementioned method with the passage beginning "by the instrument" (*sādhanena*) and ending with "that is its purpose" (*tadartha*). And thus, the sense is that the rule "first the root [is joined] with the prefix" (*pūrvaṃ dhātur upasargeṇa*) is not sound. — "The other" (*itara*).

The meaning is: while accepting this very point, he says [the following] in order to demonstrate its internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*). "Previously" means prior to the connection with words bearing the technical designation *upasarga*. "Because of non-termination" means because of uncertainty; the sense is that the state of being an object-to-be-accomplished (*sādhyatva*) is dependent upon the determination of the means-of-accomplishment (*sādhana*). "How then? refers to cases such as *saṃcaskāra*, where [the augment] *suṭ* and so on [would apply]. Since it is not desired [that the *suṭ* augment apply] in that manner, he says: "That which for you... Because [the root] necessarily requires an object [of action] prior to the verbal root, he says: "Due to the connection with the means-of-accomplishment (*sādhana*)."

In that context—"in a qualified sense"—and "kriyāyoga" (connection with action)—these are two *bahuvrīhi* compounds. "Root" (*dhātu*) means the root alone. "By way of meaning" means by way of its own inherent meaning. "By a means" (*sādhanena*)—the meaning is that it is joined with a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) for the purpose of making known its status as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). This is the intended sense of the phrase "then [it is joined] with a prefix" (*tata upasargeṇa*). As stated by Kaiyaṭa regarding the rule "a motion [is elided] before a motion" (*gatir gatau*): "The very qualified action is manifested by the means."

And thus, "the agent employs the combination of root and prefix (*dhātūpasargasamudāya*) in order to convey the connection with the means (*sādhana*) of a qualified action," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "he who thinks": the meaning to be understood is that for him who thinks, the connection with the meaning also occurs subsequently, just like the connection with the word. [This is] to be understood. Regarding "of the root" (*dhātoḥ*): it refers to *bhū* and other roots which are intended as such by their very nature. Regarding the word "from the outset" (*prakramāt*): the meaning is that one first resorts to its being expressive of an action caused by that [prefix]; thus he says: "by resorting to."

The phrase "having resorted to" (*āśritya*) is to be understood as "at the beginning," etc.; the intention is that this refers to the rule *bhūvādayo dhātavaḥ*. He explains "and the status of being an object" (*karmabhāvaśca*) with the words "as for example" (*yathā ca*). The intention is that in forms such as *pipaṭhiṣati*, [the status of being an object] is established by the rule *dhātoḥ karmaṇaḥ* (Pāṇini 3.1.7). He explains "likewise another [instance]" with the words "so too, when there is a prefix" (*tathābhāvyupasarge*). This means "by that word. He clarifies this very point by means of the second verse, saying "root and prefix," etc. The ellipsis for the phrase "having made [something] the object" (*viṣayīkṛtya*) is "by what is uttered" (*uccāritena*). That [prefix] is a qualifier of the root.

Regarding the word *bhede* (in the case of difference), the explanation of the term *tathā* (so) as it occurs there is "produced by the meaning of the prefix. The meaning of *bheda* is "distinction" (*viśeṣa*). By implication, he says "by the verbal root itself"; the meaning is that it is accepted as being [the primary] meaning. The meaning of the phrase *padakāle* (at the time of the word) is "at the time of the employment of the word. Its purpose is stated as "the prefix," etc. Since the speaker exists prior [to the listener], he says "of the listeners. He states another interpretation with the word *tathā*; the meaning is "in that same way. [The phrase] "by qualifiers"—meaning by prefixes such as *pra*, etc.—[is explained by] "priorly," etc.
Even if the reading were *prāk ca*, the meaning would be the same: the sense is that she (the action) is not perceived as something to be accomplished (*sādhya*). || 1.20 ||

He states the contradiction with the views of other [schools of] Hari (the Grammarians) in the words "yadyapi" (although...). The portion ending with "śāstre" (in the treatise) connects with what precedes. "Tu" (but) means "in reality. He states the view of another [school of] Hari in the words "kriyā" (action). Regarding "saṃghātair" (by aggregates): the meaning is that specific actions, consisting of operations conducive to experience and so forth, are understood by means of [words for] experience and the like at the very outset. Regarding "kāryāṇām" (of effects): the meaning is that, this being the case, their status as internal (antaraṅga) is established for those two. "Tathā" (so too) means "only by means of what is understood through the aggregate."

The reading is "kriyeti cetyapi. Now, one might ask: if this is so, how can that which was stated regarding its being *antaraṅga* (internal) be accepted as the opinion of the Bhāṣya? To this he says: "dhātūpasarga... [referring to the fact that the application of an affix depends on both the root and the prefix]. Because it is not caused by the meaning, he says: "pūrvopasthita... [meaning it is established first].

And thus, there is no relationship of *antaraṅga* (internal) and *bahiraṅga* (external) between these two [rules], but rather between their respective operations. Consequently, in forms such as *upāsyate*, the status of the object (*karman*) is established; and in forms such as *saṃcaskāra*, when the connection with the prefix occurs after the connection with the suffix (the *sādhana*), the rule *sa kṛti* being established, its [the object's] establishment follows because it is *antaraṅga*. Thus, there is no fault—this is the sense. The meaning is "of the previous Hari" (*pūrvahareḥ*). This very thing is what was stated regarding the *antaraṅga* nature of that operation. Regarding "in the case of *guṇa*": this refers to the rule *ādguṇa*.

— *Pararūpa* [is taught] by the rule "omāṅośca. He states the meaning of the word *hi* (for/indeed) as "from the root" (*dhātoḥ*). — [He says] "there is no connection with *āṅ*" because the prefix (*upasarga*) has no independent meaning on its own. Even when it exists, he says "by the meaning of the root" (*dhātvartha-*) etc. He states the underlying intention of the doubt: "only with *āṅ*" etc. — "By the aggregate" means "by the meaning of the root conjoined with the meaning manifested by the prefix. He expresses this as "of *āṅ*" etc. And thus, the intended sense is that the operation involving the root and the prefix is *antaranga* (internal), because it is conditioned by words whose meanings are internal. He expresses this with "therefore" (*tena*).

The meaning is that it indicates [this]. He states, "And thus," in order to show that what was previously said regarding the ornaments (*bhūṣaṇa*) and so forth is incorrect; the sense is that the meaning is that the connection with the means (*sādhana*) occurs prior to the verbal root. The point is that, in his view, the fact that the root alone depends on that [the suffix]—and not what is stated by him—is such that the inconsistency with the *Bhāṣya* is quite evident. To demonstrate that the *Bhāṣya* on the two aforementioned rules does not contradict the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "upapadam" (Pāṇini 2.2.19), he speaks, refuting the arguments of Dīkṣita and others, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).

—Regarding *upasargāṇām*: the meaning is "of those having that designation" (i.e., *upasargas*). That is to say, they are those which indicate a specific quality pertaining to the action (*kriyā*). — For this very reason: because they are indicators (*dyotaka*), their connection [with the verb] occurs only subsequently. Indeed, it has been stated there in the rule *upapadam* and in the rule *gatiḥ*: by excluding *atiṅ* [from the rule *sup-supā*], and thus setting aside the *paribhāṣā* "of *gatis*, *kārakas*, and *upapadas*," [it was asked]: "If this is made known [by the *paribhāṣā*], by what means will the compound now be formed? By that which is semantically capable (*samarthena*)."

If this were so, a compound would also result for a root and a prefix—according to the rule: "First the root is joined with a prefix, and afterwards [the prefix] with the suffix. This is not the case. Rather, it is said: "First the root is joined with the *sādhana* (the grammatical factor), and afterwards with the prefix. For the *sādhana* brings about the action (*kriyā*), and the prefix qualifies that action. Furthermore, a qualification by a prefix can only be stated regarding an action that has already been brought into being.

The meaning of this is as follows: regarding the phrase "yadi etad" (if this), the question arises because the word *atiṅ* is a qualifier of the compound (*samāsa*), and thus the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) is not explicitly mentioned by the word itself. Regarding the phrase "samarthena" (with a capable [word]), since the *upapada* is a form ending in a case-suffix (*subanta*), either the term *sup* is supplied by way of *anuvṛtti*, or—since this is a rule concerning words (*padavidhi*)—the general paribhāṣā concerning semantic compatibility (*samarthaparibhāṣā*) applies. He states the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) that would occur if *sup* were not supplied by *anuvṛtti*, with the words "yadi evam" (if it were so), referring to the rule "kugatiprādayaḥ. The intended sense is that by the rule "atiṅ," there is a prohibition specifically of that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*).

Consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence [of the rule applying] even to cases where the suffixes have the same phonetic form (*ekasvarya*). Nor can it be argued that there is no fault because the term *atiṅ* is a *paryudāsa* (exclusion), meaning "a compound ending in a suffix other than a *tiṅ*," since this would still lead to the unavoidable fault of compounding the prefix with the verbal root in forms such as *prapipaṭhiṣati*—which means "an intense desire to read"—where the desiderative suffix (*san*) ends in a *tiṅ*-like element. Furthermore, there is no evidence that *atiṅ* refers exclusively to a *kṛt* suffix; for if that were the case, the author of the *Aṣṭādhyāyī* would have simply formulated the rule as *upapadaṃ kṛt*.

Furthermore, there is no commonality (*sājātya*) other than that which consists in being of the nature of a verbal root (*dhātuprakṛtika*). As for the status of being a suffix (*pratyayatva*), it is indeed over-extended to *sup* endings as well. To indicate this very point, he will say here: *prapipaṭhi*. [The word] *upasargeṇa* means by a word bearing that designation. Consequently, there is a functional capacity (*sāmarthya*) between those two, because of the connection with the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) of an action qualified by the meaning of the prefix. The phrase "this is not so" means that the rule "first the root [is combined] with the prefix" does not exist [in this context]. Otherwise, he would have simply said, "this fault does not exist."

By means of the *sādhana* (the instrument), which is a *kāraka* in the form of agent (*kartṛ*) or object (*karman*). Since the relationship with that [instrument] is internal (*antaraṅga*)—because the requirement for an instrument arises first for that which is perceived as the *sādhya* (the goal to be accomplished)—therefore, first there is the production of a suffix denoting the instrument; subsequently, the verbal root, being already conjoined with the instrument, is joined with the prefix (*upasarga*), and not alone. Consequently, due to the absence of semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*) between them, there is no compound (*samāsa*). In that regard, a compound certainly occurs with a word ending in a *kṛt* suffix, but it does not occur with a word ending in a *tiṅ* suffix because of the prohibition "not with a *tiṅ*" (*atiṅ*).

He states the logical justification for the connection with the *sādhana* (the means of accomplishment) prior to the verbal root (*dhātu*), saying: "For the *sādhana*... [The *sādhana*] brings about or accomplishes the action (*kriyā*) and the cognition thereof. This is because the cognition of the state of being accomplished (*sādhyatva*) is dependent upon its relation to that [action]. Furthermore, when there is a connection with a meaning perceived as something to be accomplished, those [words] possess the status of prefixes (*upasarga*) and so forth. Nor does the cognition of that [action] arise from a verbal root whose power has been grasped through grammar—such as "√bhū in the sense of existence"—because that [cognition] is to be accomplished through the connection with the factors of action (*kāraka*).

However, because a prefix (upasarga) is designated as such on the grounds that it is connected to an action—specifically, by manifesting a particularity residing in the action—the connection [between the prefix and the verb] occurs only after the action-ness [of the root] has been cognized; for it is only after that that the restrictive rule "they [prefixes] precede the verbal root" (te prāgdhātoḥ) becomes operative. [Tām] means "that which is apprehended as having the nature of an action. [Upasargaḥ] refers to a word bearing that designation. It qualifies [the prefix] by way of its being a manifester (dyotaka). He provides the reasoning for this: "of that which is already accomplished" (abhinirvṛttasya), meaning of that which is known to have been produced.

The distinction—the qualifier such as excellence (*prakarṣa*) and so forth—is capable of being indicated by a prefix (*upasarga*) in expressions such as *prajayati* ("he conquers excellently"). The phrase "with respect to the cognizer" is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).

Intending this very point, he states it briefly: "of the root and the prefix. Indicating the aforementioned meaning of the phrase "for this very reason," he states its distinction [from other cases]: "the preceding one" (*pūrvām*). He raises an objection: "not so" (*na ca*), even though [the prefix] is merely indicative (*dyotaka*); the word "only" (*mātra*) excludes the verbal suffixes (*tiṅ*). The meaning of "thus" (*iti*) is as follows: since it is established by the treatise that even the *lakāra*s (verbal suffixes) have the sense of the factors of action (*kāraka*), when there is a connection with a prefix during the comprehension of the meaning of the suffixes through that very connection, [the objection applies] to the state of being a suffix (*lāvatā*) of the roots (*inām*).

"—*tasya*" means of that which is delimited by the state of being *l*. "*Vibhaktīnām*" (of the case-endings) means of their substitutes. The argument—that because those [substitutes] also possess the property of expressing a state (*bhāva*), they cannot be the determinants for the cognition of that [state]—is not tenable, since the determination occurs through *tātparya* (intentional focus). Indicating this, he says: "*sādhanasya*" (of the instrument/agent). For this very reason, in forms such as *adhyaiyātām*, even though the augment *āṭ* is present in the state of *l*, the *vṛddhi* (vowel strengthening) does not occur first.

Some maintain that because the operation of the means (*sādhana*) necessarily precedes [the operation of] that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*), the former is more internal (*antaraṅga*) due to its fixed requirement for a means; therefore, by the rule "vārṇādāṅgam" (an *āṅga* operation takes precedence over a *vārṇa* operation), the desired result is achieved through the application of *iyaṅ*, then *yaṇ*, and finally *vṛddhi*.

In reality, according to that view, because [the substitution of] *vṛddhi* is *antaraṅga*, this form would be unestablished (*asiddha*). Even if one somehow resorts to the rule "after a phoneme, [the augment] *āṭ* is applied before *ām*" (*varṇādāṅgam*), there would still be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of applying *yam* because the root has more than two vowels (*anekāctva*). Therefore, forms such as *adhyaiyātām* are Vedic (*chāndasa*). For in that case, due to the inclusion of the word "frequently" (*bahulam*) in the rule "frequently in the Veda, even when *amāṅ* is not used," one should understand that after the substitution [of *iy* for *e*], *iyaṅ* applies by virtue of being subsequent (*paratva*), and then *āṭ* is added, resulting in *vṛddhi*. — Regarding "tiṅ": in order to state the intended meaning of this Bhāṣya, he raises an objection with "nacaivamapi" (even so...).

The meaning is: "even in the case of preventing a compound (*samāsa*) of that which ends in a verbal suffix (*tiṅanta*) and that which ends in a *tiṅ*-derived suffix (*tiṅbhāvilānta*). Regarding the word "compound" (*samāsa*): the idea is that the absence of a single unified meaning (*ekārthībhāva*) when roots and prefixes are extracted separately does not trigger compounding and the like; rather, since the parts themselves possess that [unified] state when there is a unified meaning in the whole (*viśiṣṭa*), [the whole triggers the operation]. He states this intention with the words "to be mentioned later" (*vakṣyamāṇa*). The sense is: at the occasion of defining the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅartha*). "Of the qualified" (*viśiṣṭasya*) means: of that which is qualified by tense, number, case-role (*kāraka*), and so forth. The sense is that the meaning of the root (*dhātvartha*) consists of five factors (*pañcaka*). "Of that" (*tasya*) refers to the lack of semantic connection (*asāmarthya*) with respect to the parts.

The meaning is this: there is no formation of a single unified meaning (ekārthībhāva) with a finite verb (tiṅanta), because of the prohibition [by Pāṇini] stating "not when it ends in tiṅ" (atiṅ). Nor can there be such a formation with a part of that [verb], since the prefix (upasarga) connects only with a meaning already conjoined with a grammatical factor (sādhana). Thus, finite verbs possess only a signifying function (dyotakatva).

[Objection: But in this way, because of the connection with a prefix (*upasarga*), before that connection, the simple root *bhū* and others lack transitivity; consequently, the *l*-affixes and so forth would not occur in the sense of the object (*karman*). Furthermore, in forms such as *sañcaskāra*, the internal nature (*antaraṅgatva*) of the augment *suṭ*—as stated in the Bhāṣya on the rule "suṭ kātpūrvaḥ"—would be violated. To this he says: "In that case too" (*tatrāpi*). This means: even though the tiṅ-affix is merely indicative (*dyotaka*). "The meaning of the prefix" (*upasargārthaḥ*) refers to the meaning indicated by it. As for "even though it is to be indicated" (*dyotyo'pi*):

since the sequence of presentation follows the sequence of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) here as well, just as in the "five-fold" (*pañcaka*) view there is the sequence beginning with the root-meaning (*svārtha*). How this is so has been explained previously.

By this, the following objection is refuted: "Even if prefixes (*upasarga*) are merely indicators (*dyotaka*), in cases such as *uṣāsya-te*, since the root must necessarily express the meaning indicated by the prefix prior to its connection with a grammatical factor (*sādhana*) in order to account for its transitivity, and since the prefix must necessarily be joined with the preceding [root], the capacity (*sāmarthya*) exists; therefore, a compound between the root and the prefix would be unavoidable. This is rejected because—[the capacity does not exist there].

As it was stated by Kaiyaṭa under the rule *upapadam* as a resolution to the objection raised regarding the nominative case: "In examples such as *anubhūyate sukham* (pleasure is experienced) and *upāsyate guruḥ* (the teacher is worshipped), the verbal root alone expresses the action accompanied by an object; the prefix (*upasarga*), however, is merely indicative (*dyotaka*). It is connected only later for the sake of the listener's understanding; thus, there is no fault whatsoever in this view. (1.21)

Reiterating what has already been stated, he prevents the possibility of compounding in other instances as well—such as *prapipaṭhiṣati*—in order to avoid the deficiency [of the rule] since it was not mentioned in the Bhāṣya and other works. The meaning is "even in cases such as these. The phrase "by the suffix *san*" implies "of the base" (*prakṛteḥ*). Thus, the sense is that there is no semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) between the prefix and the root alone; therefore, the compound does not apply to those two. Now, one might object: "Even so, let the compound be formed with the *san*-ending form itself"; to this he replies: "tattadviṣaye" (in each respective case). This means that [the compound occurs] after the primary operation (*pradhānakārya*) has taken place.

The intention of this [statement], namely "this is the meaning," has already been stated in the commentary (*vyākhyāna*). Nor is it the case that "because of the mention of 'object' (*karman*), the mention of 'root' (*dhātu*) in the rule prescribing *san* is redundant; for if [it is argued] that the object is that which is accompanied by a prefix (*sopasarga*), then since the prefix serves to qualify the object, the object itself is that which is without a prefix. For if that which is accompanied by a prefix were the object, then even though there is the governing context of 'root,' because *san* must convey a desire specifically directed toward a qualified [action], it would not be prescribed, as [the root] would not have an object. This point is correct here: that the object is indeed that which is accompanied by a prefix.

Nor should it be argued that there is the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of the suffix *san* not applying because of the genitive case in the rule *karmaṇaḥ*; for the meaning is "from a root which is a part of the object" (*karmaṇo 'vayavād dhātoḥ*). However, in cases such as *mahāntaṃ putram icchati* ("he desires a great son"), the suffix *kyac* does not apply after a nominal ending (*subanta*), even by virtue of the principle of "behaving like the principal" (*vyapadeśivadbhāva*), because of the lack of syntactic competency (*asāmarthya*) due to the presence of a relative requirement (*sāpekṣatva*). Thus, one should not claim that this contradicts the Vārttika and Bhāṣya on the *san*-sūtra.

Regarding the term *sopasargam* (with a prefix), since its meaning is "qualified by the sense manifested by the prefix," the aforementioned fault does not apply; furthermore, the subsequent passage refers to a partisan view (*ekadeśin*), so that too is not a fault. This was stated by Kaiyaṭa: "The verbal root alone expresses the qualified action, while the prefix is merely indicative; thus, there is no lack of independence [between them]. Making this very point clear, he says: "For this reason also. He explains the meaning of this with the words: "Of the qualified..."

By this [argument], it is established that here the objecthood of the root (*iṣ*) must be predicated of a qualified action alone; thus, because of the prior connection with the prefix, there would be the undesirable consequence (*āpatti*) of *san* following from the qualified [root] even in the absence of the mention of the verbal root (*dhātu*). However, the Bhāṣya has been explained in such a way as not to contradict any of the aforementioned statements in the Bhāṣya.

[Objection: Even so, in cases such as *niviśate*, there would still result a compound (*samāsa*) of those two [the prefix *ni-* and the verb], because the prescription of the Ātmanepada suffix depends precisely upon their mutual relationship; therefore, that [the status of being a preverb] must necessarily precede it. To this, he says: *ner viśaḥ*. By the word “etc. (*ādi*), one includes rules such as *parivyavebhyaḥ* and *viparābhyāṃ jeḥ*. Although in this case the matter could be resolved by taking the genitive [in *neḥ*] to mean “from a word expressing a specific meaning manifested by *ni-*”, nevertheless, in accordance with the subsequent sūtra, he says: “by virtue of being after *ni-*”.

—This is the meaning; that is, the meaning of "in sequence" and so forth. And thus, since the application of the *ātmanepada* occurs precisely before the connection with those [prefixes], there is no fault. In that regard, however, assuming the ablative case (*pañcamī*) in the sense of the genitive (*ṣaṣṭhyarthe*) would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). This is clear from the *Bhāṣya* on the rule "nerviśaḥ. By this, it is indicated that even for the augment *suṭ*, its status as *antaraṅga* (internal) is established—either by the meaning "of that which is preceded by *sam* and *pari*" or by the meaning "of that which is capable of being subsequent to those two"—such that *suṭ* occurs precisely before the conjunction with *sam*.

[Objection: Even so, since there is an absence of case-endings (vibhakti), when the two are pronounced as a composite unit, they would incur the status of a compound (samāsa) due to their connection with the rule [of *sampṛca* etc.]. To this, he says: "Also of *sampṛca* etc. The intention is that, in order to avoid contradiction with the aforementioned Bhāṣya, the rule [for *sampṛca* etc. is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) based on the imitation (*anukaraṇa*) of both [the root and the prefix] according to the stated method. However, although that [status of compound] might exist in cases such as *āyatastūḥ*, *kaṭaprūḥ*, and *ajasrapam*, the point is that it never occurs between a verbal root (*dhātu*) and a prefix (*upasarga*).

He states that even what is desired is established in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) according to the aforementioned method and according to the method of the *Bhāṣya*—namely, the rule "saṃprasāraṇācca"—by saying "gosandāya. [The term] "from the qualified" means from that which conveys a meaning qualified by that [suffix]. He says "residing in the intellect" because there was no prior connection. The overall purport is that in such cases, this alone is the method for explaining grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Thus, with the passage beginning with "even though" and ending with "is established as the final conclusion," he resolves the contradiction with Hari within the *Bhāṣya*’s final conclusion accepted by Hari, using Hari’s own words.

Because the reality [of the meaning] is already clear, he provides an illustration consisting merely of the expressive word (*vācaka*), saying: "as it is established" (*yathā pratiṣṭhate*). This is exactly as stated in the Bhāṣya on the *bhūvādi* sūtra. Regarding "of *tiṣṭhati*": the meaning is "of the root *sthā*. Regarding "by that which has such a meaning"—that is, by that which has such an intended sense (*tātparya*)—this is a conjunction with the phrase "it is understood as qualified by a conscious agent. Thus, even though positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) exist, they do not constitute expressiveness (*vācakatva*), because those two are accounted for simply as indicators (*dyotakatā*); this is what he says: "In that case"—the meaning is "in the object of that cognition."

—From two kinds: the positive-negative (anvayavyatirekin). That which was stated previously is exactly of this nature. He says "in some cases" (*kvacid*) to show that prefixes (*prādi*) are indeed prepositions (*upasarga*). —The "divisions" (*bhedāḥ*) are the specific qualities (*viśeṣāḥ*), such as excellence (*prakarṣa*) and so forth. He states the reason for this with the words "because of the prefix," etc. (1.22).

[Objection: But even so, in cases such as *pratyaya* (suffix) and *jñāna* (knowledge), where they are abstract nouns (*bhāvapratyaya*), the aforementioned method is impossible; thus, those two would necessarily incur the same fault. To this, he says: "But where... (*yatratu*). The word "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction from what was previously stated. The meaning is: in a case where the means (*sādhana*) is expressed within the same word, it is so [as described]; but here, because the suffix has the sense of an abstract action (*bhāva*), it is more internal (*antaraṅga*). Therefore, by necessity, according to the very method explained for *van* and other suffixes, once the status of being an action (*kriyātva*) is understood through its connection with an external means, then there is the connection with a prefix (*upasarga*). He states this: "Because of its internality" (*antaraṅgatvāt*).

— provided that there is no further expectancy (*nirākāṅkṣatva*). And thus, by the maxim *vārṇādāṅgam* ("an internal operation [āṅga] takes precedence over a phonetic operation [vārṇa]"), the form *yaṇ* is established through *guṇa*; this is what he states with the words *ata eva*. The meaning is: precisely because of the acceptance of that [principle] in that context. By the word *ādi* ("and so forth"), one includes [the rule regarding] suffixes (*pratyaya*) and others. As for the commentary on the sūtra *samprasāraṇācca*, it concerns cases where the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is expressed within the same word-base (*samānapada*); therefore, there is no contradiction with that.

By this, Haradatta’s argument—that even when there is a prior connection with a prefix (*upasarga*), the application of the grammatical operation regarding the *sādhana* (the agent or object) is desired first, as indicated by examples such as "adhyayanena"—is refuted. Likewise, the view of the Navya (modern grammarians)—that prefixes possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) themselves, and that the status of being an object (*karmatva*) or having an object (*sakarmakatva*) is experienced as such, thereby establishing the *la*-suffixes in the sense of the object in cases like *anubhūyate*—is also rejected. For in those very instances, it would result in the undesirable consequence of compounding (*samāsa*) between the verbal root and the prefix.

[Objection: Is it not true that in examples such as *adhyāgacchati*, the prefix *adhi* and others are devoid of meaning; therefore, [your] explanation here is inconsistent? For without expressing a specific relationship determined by an action (*kriyā*), it is difficult to define the status of being a *karmapravacanīya*. Furthermore, if that were the case, "connection with an action" (*kriyāyoga*) would consist solely in expressing a meaning that serves as a qualifier of the action, and since that is absent here, it would be difficult to maintain that this [category] is an exception (*apavāda*) to the rules for *gati*s and so forth. Therefore, he says: *adhyāgacchati*. He states *āgacchati* to show that the prefix *āṅ* possesses the function of indicating a specific quality pertaining to that [action].

By this, the opposite view is refuted. He removes the inconsistency regarding its application by saying "in common usage" (*laukike*). Otherwise, there would be no application of words such as *kalaśa* (jar). Regarding the contingency of [the prefix] being a "motion" (*gati*) and so forth, he says "having come together" (*sambhūya*). The word "of two things standing" (*sthitayoḥ*) is to be supplied; the sense is that it applies when those two are used together. Regarding "of the preverb" (*upasargasya*), the meaning is: of either *adhi*, *pari*, or another [preverb] that signifies "reality" (*tattva*) and so on, or of *āṅ* which possesses that [quality of reality]. Regarding "in another meaning" (*arthāntara*), the meaning is: having a meaning other than that which is signified by *āṅ*.

The intended meaning is that the designation *karmapravacanīya* [is applied] by virtue of the force of the explicit statement. Thus, it has been stated that prefixes (*upasarga*) possess a suggestive function (*dyotakatva*), and that this is on an equal footing with other particles (*nipāta*). He clarifies this with the words "But in some cases... This refers to instances such as *ghaṭaśca* ("and a jar"). The term "particles" (*nipātānām*) is used to include prefixes (*prādi*) as well. By the word "also" (*api*), the suggestive function is likewise included. That [function] should be understood as being established [on a case-by-case basis]. He strengthens this very point by showing another example with the words "For this very reason...". The meaning is: "precisely because they possess denotative power" (*vācakatva*).

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is with the word "is seen" (*dṛśyate*). By this, it is indicated that experience (*anubhava*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) in this context. The locative case in "in the word" (*śabde*) is a locative of the object (*viṣaya-saptamī*). To make his statement regarding "of particles" (*nipātānām*) fruitful, he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*). Regarding the phrase "it would not be so" (*na syāt*): the sense is that if that were the case, since [the meaning] would be the primary meaning of the base (*prakṛti-artha*), there would be no connection with it because it is a word such as *tad-* and so forth. Now, one might object: let its status as such be due to the very meaning it illuminates (*dyotya*), as stated previously; to this he replies: "of that" (*tasya*). This means "of the word *arvāk*. (1.23)

[Objection: But even if [gender] is what is to be expressed (*dyotya*), why is it not the qualificand (*viśeṣya*)? To this he says: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). The meaning is: precisely because it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). Regarding the rule *striyām* (P. 4.1.3), the meaning is: in the context of the fourth chapter (*cāturthika*). He states that it qualifies the suffix because of its predominance: "the word 'strī' being subordinate" (*strītyavasya*). This is according to the maxim: "Between the base and the suffix, the suffix is subordinate. Regarding the word "number" (*vacana*): since it is of a non-substantial nature (*asattvabhūta*), it cannot be construed with number. Otherwise, the resolution [of the objection] would clearly be inconsistent. He also cites another passage from the Bhāṣya: "And for this very reason... (*ata eva ca*).

Now, one might object that the position regarding [the particles] being *dyotaka* (illuminators) was not explicitly stated in the first [view]; therefore, he says: "In the case of the feminine... He states that this too is the opinion of Hari (Patañjali): "His statement... Having set aside the first [view] because it is obscure, he presents the second: "Some say... With the intention of explaining [examples] such as *adhyāgacchati*, he says: "Some are meaningless. This is derived from the analogy. In the phrase *sambhūya*, the word *sthitāḥ* (situated) is to be supplied as an ellipsis. The term *vācaka-pada* (denotative word) refers to that which produces cognition.

In some places, the reading is exactly as it stands. Thus, the meaning to be understood is that those [words] which, having arisen together, exist as indicators of meaning, might therefore be like the Āgamas—namely, entirely devoid of meaning. Regarding the term *prātiśākhya*: this refers to the conclusion of the second chapter. *Jātam* means a collection. Those very [terms] were stated at the beginning. In all these instances, the agent (*kartṛ*) is the user (*prayoktṛ*). *Sattvam* means substance (*dravya*). By this, it is clearly stated that indeclinables (*avyaya*) lack the status of being nouns (*nāman*). He clarifies what has already been said with the words "that which expresses an action" (*kriyāvācaka*), and so forth.

By the word *kriyā* (action), the category of "being" (*bhāva*) is expressed. It has been clearly stated that the status of being denotable by a verbal suffix (*ākhyātapada*) belongs not to the suffix alone, but to the [stem-suffix] complex as a whole. Regarding the phrase "by the first," the meaning is that the speaker expresses the action by means of the verbal root together with [the suffix].
