He states that the phrase "by the other two" refers to what has been introduced [previously], namely, "by the noun" (*nāman*). He explains the meaning of the word "other" (*itarābhyām*) as "by the noun. This is obtained through the logic of the "Brāhmaṇa-Vasiṣṭha" maxim. Likewise: "those which denote an object along with those two."

He states a distinction from what precedes with the words "upasarga" (prefix). By the word "api" (also), the inclusion of [prefixes] as indicators (*dyotaka*) and so forth is intended. He says "thāl" (the suffix *thāl*) to refute the objection that the state of being a qualifier (*prakāratva*) of the indicated meaning is inconsistent. He clarifies that very point in detail with the words "na tu" (but not). The meaning is: "having a function qualified by a qualifier. The word "pratyayam" (suffix) is used in the singular to denote the class (*jāti*). He states the first type of deviation with the words "yo hariḥ" (who is Hari). He states the second type of deviation with the words "ākare" (in the authoritative source). By the word "etena" (by this), it is meant: "by its not being an indicator (*adyotakatva*)."

In that context—referring to the domain of *thāl* and other suffixes—he dispels the misconception of deviation [from the rule] elsewhere as well: "from another class" (*jātyantāt*). The particle *tu* indicates a distinction from what was previously stated. "The substratum" (*āśraya*) means that for a universal (*jāti*), the individual (*vyakti*) alone is its relative. Regarding "if," the meaning is that even suffixes such as *yadā*, which are prescribed by that [rule], express purpose and so forth. He states the evidence for their being generally [of that nature] by completing the phrase with "mostly" (*prāyeṇa*) and so on: "that being the subject matter" (*tatprakṛta*).

For in that [work], having stated one position—that "the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs in its own sense after a word in the nominative case denoting abundance"—another alternative position is stated: "the suffix *mayaṭ* occurs in the sense of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) after a word in the nominative case denoting food and so forth that is presented in abundance. By this, the form "bhavanmayo dhyāyati nāvanīpatiḥ" (the lord of the earth meditates, consisting of you) is established. The intention is that the purport of the rule lies in both meanings through the device of *tantra* (simultaneous application), as shown by the commentary. He makes his statement fruitful with the words "śaraiḥ" (with arrows); for this very reason, the particle "tu" (but) is used.

Otherwise—that is, if [the suffix] functions as a denotative (*vācaka*)—in that case, the meaning is "one who is similar to the counter-correlative" (*pratiyogiviśiṣṭasādṛśya*). Therein, the connection (*anvaya*) of the "sun" (*usra*) occurs with the counter-correlative through non-difference (*abheda*), and the connection of the "similar" occurs with the arrows through non-difference. As for the third [interpretation], it follows from the rule that the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) must possess identical case-endings. And thus, the meaning in that view is "by means of arrows which are non-different from that which is non-different from the similar, which is itself qualified by a counter-correlative non-different from the sun," etc.; he states this with the words "of that which is similar to the sun" (*usrasadṛśasya*).

The meaning [of *iva*] is similarity (*sādṛśya*). In that case, there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) with the two correlates (*pratiyogin*), and its connection with the arrows occurs by way of being their locus; the third case ending (*tṛtīyā*) is as before. In that view, the particle *api* serves to conjoin that [similarity] with its absence. Since meaninglessness is accepted in other contexts, he says: "and because of ungrammaticality. Regarding the first position, he says: "as *iva*. [He explains: "the third case ending. The word should be split as "by means of non-existence" (*abhāvena iti cchedaḥ*). Now, one might object: "Its existence is established by the indicator (*jñāpaka*) 'after an indeclinable' (*avyayāt*); therefore, its cognition follows from that. To this, he replies: "after the word *iva*."

He says "elision" (*lug*) to prevent the occurrence of the suffix *ṇatva*. The intention is that because it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), [the case ending] is dropped by that very rule. By the word "even though" (*api*) in the phrase "even though there is existence" (*sattve 'pi*), there is a conjunction with the absence of the plural number even when the singular number exists for that [suffix]. However, the instrumental case following the word *usra* cannot convey the instrumentality residing in the object of comparison, because it is not the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*). Therefore, the intention is that its function as a mere indicator (*dyotaka*) is more appropriate. || 1.24 ||

He states the consensus of their commentaries regarding both cases with the word "bhāṣya" (the commentary). How this is so is clear from that [commentary] itself. Therein, in the first instance, it is said: "The treatise entitled *Śabdānuśāsana* (Instruction on Words) is to be understood as the subject under discussion. In other instances as well, it should be understood from that very source. For this very reason—that is, precisely because they are expressive—so it is further below as well. Since it is an indeclinable (*avyaya*), he says "pūrva" (preceding).

The point is that even if [the prefix] functions as a dyotaka (indicator), its status as the meaning of the prior member (*pūrvapadārtha*) makes its predominance (*prādhānya*) difficult to establish, according to the method previously stated. This is precisely why the reading is *ca* (and). In the sense of "congested" (*saṅkaṭa*), the suffix *kaṭac* is applied by the rule *saṃprodaśca*. In *udvataḥ*, in the sense of "gone up" (*udgatāni*), the suffix *vati* is applied by the rule *upasargācchandasi*. — Regarding *udvataḥ* and so on: by the rules beginning with *samādeḥ*, the inclusion of *ni* and others is intended for forms such as *nivataḥ*. This connects with the word *rūpam* (form) in the process of its grammatical derivation (*sādhana*). — [Regarding the word] *bhāvaye*.

The intention is that [this is established] in such sūtras as "gatiśca" (and the movement). Since it is difficult to explain that [movement] without that [sūtra], even though it was not stated prior to it, it is indicated after it by the maxim of the needle and the pot; thus, by the maxim of the lion’s backward glance, he raises an objection regarding the established conclusion (siddhānta) with the words "nanu" (but surely). The meaning is: "in this sense. The intention is that there is no inconsistency in the sense that will be explained hereafter. He speaks according to the view of word-formation (pada-saṃskāra-pakṣa) with the word "usmā" (the sibilant). He refutes the opponent's statement with the word "upamā" (comparison). He speaks according to the view of sentence-formation (vākya-saṃskāra-pakṣa) with the words "yadyapi" (although). [He refers to] "sā" (that).

Even what has been stated by others is not obtainable through mere instruction; rather, it is based solely on the relation of non-difference (*abhedānvaya*) with the object of comparison (*upameya*). This is because of the pervasion (*vyāpti*): "that which has attained non-difference with another possesses a power equal to that [other]. And thus, the meaning is that the second alternative mentioned previously is indeed inconsistent. Regarding the word *uktā* (stated): the meaning is according to the method previously stated, namely, that the meaning to be illuminated (*dyotya*) is indeed the contextual factor (*prakaraṇa*). Furthermore, since the aforementioned cognition is impossible, he says "not merely that" (*na tāvanmātram*), adding "by way of being the standard of comparison" (*upamānatvena*). This refers to the phrase "of that which is co-occurrent with itself" (*svasamabhivyāhatasya*), and so forth. Regarding the word *tādṛśa* (such):

The meaning is that the object of comparison (upameya) is qualified by a property common to both [the object of comparison and the standard of comparison]. The intention is that its very essence (*tattva*) consists precisely in that [qualification]. Now, one might object: since the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamānatva*) is defined in relation to the object of comparison, it would be untenable without the cognition of that [object] alone; however, it does not depend on the cognition of it as qualified [by the common property]. How, then, is the final [proposition] established? To this he says: "And the status of being a standard of comparison... The meaning of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyārtha*) is "qualification" (*vaiśiṣṭya*). For this very reason, because it is impossible for it to be identical in every respect, he says: "slightly" (*īṣat*). Now, what is the proof for this very point? To this he says: "This... (*idam*).

In that context, having raised the question—"Does the relationship between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*) exist in total difference or in non-difference?"—and having dismissed the consequence of the word *iva* (and other terms expressing comparison) becoming redundant in cases such as "cow like cow" or "cow like horse" due to the impossibility of a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) in either case, [the author] states: "It exists where there is an apprehension of difference in its specific form and an apprehension of non-difference in the form of a common property. Then, in response to the doubt, "How has this come about?", he says: "This is determined from the conventional usage of the term 'comparison' (*upamāna*), which signifies that which measures (*mimīte*) but does not measure absolutely (*atyantāya*)."

The meaning of this is as follows: for a measure such as a *prastha* is a complete measure; therefore, it is a determiner [of the object] only through absolute difference, as in "a *prastha* is the measure of this" or "the rice is a *prastha*. But this [simile], on the other hand, is a determiner by means of both difference and non-difference, as in "this is inferior. The indeclinable *atyantāya* has the sense of "absolutely"; thus he says "elsewhere," meaning in the *Uddyota*, the *Guru*, and the *Mañjūṣā*. By this, the view that "being a standard of comparison" (*upamānatva*) consists in being intended as the determiner of the simile, while "being the compared" (*upameyatva*) consists in being intended as its substratum, is refuted.

He states that this is also accepted by the latest rhetoricians with the words "in both cases. The meaning is "the cognition of that. Regarding "liṅga," the meaning is "a defect of simile consisting of a difference in gender and so forth. By "and so forth" (*ādi*), a difference in number is included. Regarding "in the *Prakāśa* and other works"—there too, by "and so forth," the *Pradīpa* and others are meant.

For it has been stated there as follows: "Even if there is a difference in gender or number between the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the subject of comparison (*upameya*), if the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) were to take a different form [in one of them], then because that attribute would be understood as connected to only one of the two, the status of being either the object of comparison or the subject of comparison would be perceived only for that [one] along with its qualification. Thus, since the intended meaning is not clearly sustained even by means of an implied attribute, that constitutes the fault of 'broken uniformity' (*bhagnaprakrama*). For example: 'O God, you have fallen from my hand like the *cintāmaṇi* jewel; fie on my wretched fortune! O God, pure roasted flour (*saktavaḥ*) has been eaten by me, like a virtuous wife. " In this verse, the word *cyutaḥ* (fallen) is masculine, while *bhakṣitāḥ* (eaten) is plural and feminine. Consequently, the intended meaning—that the speaker’s misfortune is as great as the loss of the *cintāmaṇi*—is not effectively conveyed. Thus, it is an instance of broken uniformity.

In that context, indicating the cognition [arising from] the individual [words], he states the cognition [itself] with the words "and thus" (*evaṃca*). The meaning is: when that [compound] serves as the indicator of that [cognition]. The word "etc. (*ādi*) includes such cognitions as: "The face is beautiful, being non-different from the lotus which is the beautiful object of comparison," as in the expression "The face is beautiful like a lotus."

By this, such cognitions as "the face is non-different from that which possesses the delight which is the cause of the similarity defined by the moon" and "the mouth is non-different from that which possesses the beauty which is the cause of the similarity defined by the lotus" are refuted. He states its necessity with the words "evañca" (and thus); the meaning is "in the presence of words such as *iva*."—"Vibhaktikatvam"—this refers to the rule regarding case-endings. He explains its meaning with the word "tena" (by that). He specifies [the nature of] the qualifier with the word "sādhāraṇa" (common).—"Iti bodhaḥ" (such a cognition).

Therefore, the intended meaning here is that even in this case, those two possess identical case-endings (*samānavibhaktikatā*). This should be understood similarly in examples such as "Caitra walks like an elephant" (*gaja iva gacchati caitraḥ*).

In such instances as "The hero goes to the battlefield like an elephant to the forest," the cognition is: "The hero’s going to the battlefield is non-different from the elephant’s (the standard of comparison) going to the forest. Here, because the common property—going—is the predicate (*vidheya*), the cognition has the simile as its predicate. In such instances as "The man who is like a tiger goes," the cognition is: "The going is performed by the heroic man, who is non-different from the tiger (the standard of comparison). Here, because the common property—heroism and so forth—is the subject (*uddeśya*), the cognition has the simile as its subject, and so on. (1.25)

He refutes the view of others with the words "ye tu" (but those who...). The reading is "vadantīti-bodham. By this, the following [opponent's] position is rejected: that in the sentence "The face shines like a lotus," the cognition is "the face is the object of a cognition whose qualifier is a similarity as characterized by the lotus."—[The phrase] "is not perceived" means:

by this, it is shown that here, just as particles such as *vā* function as *upasargas*, they possess only an indicative (*dyotaka*) function; otherwise, how could there be the grammatical agreement of the third case (*tṛtīyā*) and so forth following words such as *usra* in expressions like "with rays (*usra*) that are bright"?

The Vaiyākaraṇa position—that the word *usra* (bull) functions as a dyotaka (indicator), whereby the phrase "by arrows similar to bulls" (*usrasadṛśaiḥ śaraiḥ*) serves as an adjective to "arrows" (the instrument)—is not tenable. This is because the word *usra* cannot function as an instrument with respect to the action of extracting [an arrow] from a bull; furthermore, since it lacks the status of being an adjective to "arrow"—which is the actual instrument—due to its connection with similarity (the sense of the particle *iva*). In the case of dyotakatva, the word *usra* would refer to something similar to a bull, and thus the instrumental case ending would be properly applied as an adjective to "arrows" (meaning "by arrows similar to bulls"). However, this is incorrect because there is no counter-argument (bādhaka) against the denotative power (*vācakatā*) of prefixes such as *upa* in examples like "the teacher is worshipped" (*upāsyate guruḥ*), whereas such a counter-argument exists for the denotative power of particles like *iva*. Thus, the Vaiyākaraṇa view is untenable.
Because of the diversity of examples: when there is grammatical agreement (samānavibhaktikatā) between the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) and the qualified (*viśeṣya*), it is said:
"Where the qualifier has the same referent as the qualified, the gender and other attributes [of that qualifier] generally follow those of the qualified."
For even when there is a difference in gender and number, the relationship of standard of comparison and object of comparison remains;
moreover, the case-ending of both the standard and the object of comparison is indeed the same.

Furthermore, since this instruction exists, the use of the third case-ending following the word of comparison is justified as being for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*). Therefore, particles such as *iva* possess denotative power (*vācakatva*) itself. Otherwise, if the status of being "expressed by the word" (*śrautī*) were to lose its significance despite the use of the word *iva* being unanimously accepted by all theorists of poetics (*alaṃkārika*), there would arise the fault of "forced meaning" (*neyārthatva*), characterized by the prohibition of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇika*), because neither conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) nor a specific purpose (*phala*) would exist for the indication of similarity.

Furthermore, Vaidyanātha’s argument—that if particles such as *eva* function as indicators (*dyotaka*), there would be an impossibility of the connection of the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) with a part of the referent of the standard of comparison (such as the moon), and that if it were admitted to connect only with the object of comparison, the fault of "difference in gender and number" (*liṅgavacanabheda*) would be untenable—is refuted.

Even if the first verse were established according to the view of the sūtra beginning with *viśeṣaṇānāṃ ca*, it would result in its being merely a conceptual construction (*kalpita*) rather than possessing authoritative status (*prāmāṇika*), and it would lead to the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Furthermore, since the *Paspaśā* section and the natural sense of the Bhāṣya on sūtras such as *adhi-pari-*, *nañ-*, *avyayam vibhakti-* etc.—which teach that particles (*nipāta*) other than those conveying a specific modification of action (*kriyāgata-viśeṣa*) [are indeclinables]—and because of the reasoning [of the commentators], the doctrine that "both" [the particle and the verb are indeclinables] is the position of the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*). Consequently, your stated position does not exist at all, as it is merely a fabrication based on some arbitrary assertion.

For this very reason, even the statement that "the view of the Grammarians is not tenable" is rendered like the maxim of "how many teeth does a crow have? Therefore, in cases such as "with arrows" (*śaraiḥ*), there is only indication (*dyotakatva*) according to the aforementioned method. Consequently, the proposition that "therefore, particles (*iva* etc. possess only denotative power (*vācakatva*)" is merely charming when left unexamined, like the cognition "this is silver" in the case of mother-of-pearl.

Furthermore, the claim that "there is a disparity with the example because there is no sublation [of the meaning] in the case of the denotative function of words such as *iva*—as in the expression 'the guru is worshipped thus (*iva*)'"—is merely a manifestation of ignorance regarding the established doctrine (siddhānta). Moreover, when words like *iva* are employed, since the simile consisting of the relation to a common attribute is the expressed meaning (*vācya*), its status as *śrautī* (verbal) is established according to the consensus of all theorists of poetics (*alaṅkārika*). It will become clear later that the cognition of similarity itself is purely *ārthī* (implied).

For this very reason—just as the fault of resulting in a prohibited metaphorical usage (lākṣaṇikatva) according to the rule "there is no metaphorical indication [of a word] in its similar," the aforementioned fault beginning with "furthermore" (kiñca) does not apply either; such is the direction of the argument. In that regard, [the comparison is made] by means of the two expressions "the moon-like face. Now, even if identity is perceived through both [terms] possessing a common attribute, how is the explanation [of the figure] achieved from that? To the question "How then is there a cognition of similarity? he says: "The moon... and so on.

Surely, when a meaning is understood through implication (*pratīyamāna*), it would be understood as being produced by an indefinite property, because what is produced by a property already present is alone cognized. In examples such as "the hero goes to the battlefield as if an elephant goes to the forest," there is no simile (*upamā*) because the particle *iva* and others, when used in conjunction with a verb, have the sense of possibility (*saṃbhāvanā*). The cognition [there] is: "The action of going, whose agent is the hero and whose object is the battlefield, is the object of the possibility of the action of going, whose agent is the elephant and whose object is the forest."

Nor should it be argued that the cognition "he sees the difference from the jar" (*ghaṭabhedam paśyati*)—which would otherwise follow from the sentence "the jar does not see" (*ghaṭo na paśyati*)—is precluded because the cause of such a cognition is the mental presence (*upasthiti*) generated by a word ending in a heard case-suffix, where that suffix is related to a qualificand-ness (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of the verbal root; for if this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence that words such as *dadhi* (curd), *tūṣṇīm* (silently), *ārāt* (near), and *pṛthak* (separately) could not be construed with the meaning of the verbal root.

However, expressions such as "the jar does not see" do not possess grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*) in the sense already described; for the negative particle (*nañ*) denoting difference requires a substratum (*adhikaraṇa*), and thus one employs the expression "the jar is not a cloth" (*ghaṭo na paṭaḥ*) in that context. This is because the meaning of "difference" cannot exist without the employment of a substratum. Furthermore, there is no such syntactic connection (*anvaya*) even with a jar-ness that is superimposed (*āropita*). This is because, in the cognition where the relation of difference has both the meaning of the verbal root (denoting existence) and the meaning of the noun as its objects, the cause is the awakening of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) triggered by the apprehension of the word's power (*śaktigraha*) regarding the case-ending.

Furthermore, because a relation other than that between qualifier and qualified (viśeṣaṇa-viśeṣya-bhāva) cannot be understood without a word expressive of that relation, this will become clear later in the section on the genitive case (ṣaṣṭhī-prakaraṇa).

By this [principle], in expressions such as "hesīva" ("like him"), the similarity (*sādṛśya*) is construed with the substratum (*āśraya*) which encompasses all the parts of the body, and not with the act of plunging (*avagāhana*), which is the meaning of the verbal root. This is because, in a verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*), the presence of the meaning of an inflectional suffix (*vibhaktyartha*) as the qualificand (*viśeṣyatā*)—by way of a relation consisting of the "qualifierhood" (*prakāratā*) residing in the meaning of the verbal root—is a necessary cause. Nor should it be argued that the qualifierhood is specified by the condition of "occurring in something other than the meaning of a particle" (*nipātārthabhinnavṛttitva*).

In cases such as "The pot does not see" (*ghaṭo na paśyati*), there would otherwise be the undesirable consequence of the absence associated with the pot being construed with the act of seeing through the relation of objecthood (*karmatā-saṃsarga*). However, if—as is established by experience—the connection of similarity (*sādṛśya*) with the meaning of the verbal root is indeed possible due to the force of intention (*tātparya*), then one should simply postulate that the cognition produced by the negative particle (*nañ*) acts as a blocker for a cognitive relation where the qualifier-role (*prakāratā*) is determined by the qualificand-role (*viśeṣyatā*) residing in the meaning of the verbal root. Thus, in "The pot does not see," such a [similarity-based] understanding should be considered as the result of deliberation.

That which was stated has been refuted; furthermore, because there is no sense of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) when [the negative particle] is co-uttered with another action, this will become clear later. Since there is no way out whatsoever in the case of compounds except for the aforementioned method, and since that [method] is necessary there, it is appropriate to apply it likewise even in the previously mentioned uncompounded state for the sake of uniformity. He justifies what was stated there with the words "This alone is proper," etc. He states the reason for that with the word "ghanā" (dense), beginning with "yataḥ" (since). Regarding the phrase "in the analysis" (*vigrahe*), the meaning is "in the non-worldly analysis" (*alaukika-vigrahe*).

Otherwise, since that [word *iva*] would have a different meaning, it would result in being a *vigraha* (analytic compound), and consequently, there could be no compound with it by including that other meaning within it; for even there, *iva* is absent, and because of the lack of grammatical coreferentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*). This is the intended sense. He states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) with the words "by way of being the object of comparison" (*upamānatvena*). Otherwise, because it possesses a correlative relationship, the compound would be obtained simply by the rule "with words expressing a common property" (*sāmānyavacanaiḥ*), and thus its [separate mention] would clearly be redundant. He states the general principle based on the inherent force of the wording: "with words expressing a common property. He mentions what is not included [in the rule]: "with words in grammatical coreferentiality" (*samānādhikaraṇaiḥ*).

With the intention that, since there is an absolute absence of being directed toward a comparison (*upamāna*), there is all the more no capacity to convey it as such, he says: "by the word *ghana*. By the word "also" (*api*), the inclusion of the word *śyāma* is intended. He says "not even" (*na ca*) according to the maxim "in the absence of the present. "As stated" means that even in that case, the necessity of its being directed toward that [comparison] has already been stated.

Even though there is a worldly analysis (*laukikavigraha*) for this [compound], it is necessary for it to have that [quality] as its primary referent in order to achieve grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*); thus, even in that case, there is an absence of that [quality]. Suggesting this, he says: "by the word *ghana*" (dense). The word "dark" (*śyāma*) is to be supplied. "Even though that is the case" means: even though it conveys the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) by way of density (*ghanatva*), it does not constitute its analysis because it is not in grammatical coreferentiality (*vyadhikaraṇatva*). Now, one might object: even if it does not constitute its analysis, that very [quality] located therein must be accepted out of necessity; to this he replies: "due to proximity" (*pratyāsatti*).

In that context—meaning "in that [compound]. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*atiprasaṅga*) of over-extension to cases such as *nīlotpala*. For this very reason, he says: "of that" (*tasya*). The point is this: where there is a compound, there is a requirement for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*); however, this is not the case in the ordinary analytical sentence (*laukikavigrahavākya*). Therefore, even when there is a lack of coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), one must, out of necessity, accept that status based merely on the capacity to convey that meaning. And thus, the fault of resulting in a compound does not arise. For this very reason, he says: "as in the case of the masculine form" (*puṃvattve*). Now, one might object: "But even that [masculine form] shares the same properties as a compound. To this, he replies: "in the derivative formation" (*vṛttau*).

For this very reason, in expressions such as *darśanīyamātā* ("the mother of a beautiful woman") and *darśanīyamātā*, even though there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) because both words generate a single cognition having the same referent, the substitution of the masculine form (*puṃvat*) does not occur. For this very reason, the failure of the *puṃvat* rule in this alternative is stated in the Bhāṣya. Suggesting this, he says: "by this. The meaning is: "by the non-establishment of the *puṃvat* rule. He states another intention of Kaiyaṭa: "merely" (*kevala*). This is the prior state [of the word], and not the state of being a constituent of the analytical sentence (*vigrahavākya*).—The word "in every respect" (*sarvathā*).

Even though that [word] possesses the capacity to convey meaning as a *śastri* (an indicator), it does not convey it in its capacity as such in the absence of a restrictive co-utterance (*asamabhivyāhāra*), for otherwise an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) would result.

By this [argument], it is shown that the word "like" (*iva*) is employed in the popular analysis (*laukika-vigraha*) to indicate that the preceding member bears a secondary sense (*lākṣaṇika*) directed toward something similar; hence it is called "possessing a secondary sense. For this very reason, there is masculine concord (*puṃvattva*) in compounds such as *mṛgacapalā*, due to grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). If it is asked, "How then is the status of being subordinate to the object of comparison (*upamāna-paratva*) established?", understand it to be so by taking the primary meaning (*śakyārtha*) through the perspective of what was previously the case (*bhūtapūrvagatyā*).

To avoid over-extension and to ensure the necessary grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) in both cases, even in that sentence, the particle *iva* indicates the very same meaning through a similar metaphorical function (*lakṣaṇika*). Dīkṣita and others have stated that in all such instances, the cognition is "the dark one is similar to a cloud. However, in the compound *aravindasundaram*, the cognition is: "the face is non-different from that which possesses beauty identical to [the beauty] which is the cause of the similarity as characterized by the lotus."

Some maintain that because partial inherence (ekadeśānvaya) is impossible, the word *aravinda* alone indicates all meanings through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), while the word *sundara* merely grasps the intended meaning (*tātparya*). This claim has been refuted; for by the aforementioned methods, the formation of a compound and so forth would be impossible, and such a cognition could not occur. He extends the two aforementioned defects to the alternative view on the grounds of non-co-referentiality (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the words "In this way" (*evam*). The sense is: "in that [other] view. The point is that similarity appears as a relation (*saṃsarga*), and not, as in the former case, as a qualifier (*prakāra*).—"That"—refers to both.

Having accepted the compound according to the opinion of the ancients in the manner stated, the fault of the absence of *puṃvadbhāva* (masculine gender substitution) was pointed out. However, in reality, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), even that [fault] does not exist; thus he says "Moreover" (*kiñca*). The words "in such a cognition" (*tathābodhe*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis. He says "Dark" (*śyāmā*) because it is the object of comparison (*upameya*) itself that is perceived as qualified by the attribute of darkness. "Of that"—meaning of the cloud (*ghana*). Thus, the sense is that since it does not convey that [meaning], there is no compound. 1.26.

With the intention that the attainment of the understanding of the meaning [is primary] and not the attainment of the understanding of what has been stated by another, he states the following verse in accordance with that point: "Tad uktam" (It has been said). Kaiyaṭa also [notes] that the word "uktam" (stated) is to be supplied [to the previous sentence]. He explains that very point with "na ca" (and not). "Uktam" means that the nature of being a single object of determination consists in its possessing a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) according to Śastryā. The sense is that there is indeed a dependence on that for the sake of the true nature (*tattva*). He states what was not mentioned in the Bhāṣya and other works: "śyāmetyādi" (dark-complexioned, etc.). Femininity (*strītva*) belongs to the individual instance of the quality (*guṇavyakti*) by virtue of its being the substantive (*viśeṣyatayā*).

[Objection: But what is the proof for the statement "it is similar" (*tādṛśam*) on the grounds that it possesses a common property (*sāmānyavattvāt*)? To this he says: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). The meaning is: "precisely because it has that nature. [Regarding the phrase] "in the subject" (*pakṣe*): the intention is that there is a syntactic connection (*anvaya*) through the relation of similarity (*sādṛśya*). He says "therein" (*tatra*) to preclude the error of regarding it as a mere means of comparison (*upamāna*); the meaning is: "in our established doctrine" (*siddhānta*). By this, its having that nature is stated quite clearly. He says "even though" (*api*) in order to dispel an objection.

[Objection: Even so, since similarity must be stated to have another basis, and because—as shown by the aforementioned method—it is impossible for it to have this [the object] as its basis, and since such a "state of being an object" (upānatva) is not obtained due to the lack of mention [in the Bhāṣya], the cited Bhāṣya would be inconsistent; therefore, he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). This means "in the object of comparison" (*upameye*). "Of this very thing"—that is, of blackness (*śyāmatva*) itself. By the phrase "tantra, etc.," the repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the cognizer is intended. Thus, in this context, *tantra* should be understood as referring to the application of the same case-ending (*vibhakti*) to objects intended to be expressed simultaneously.

The meaning is that because of the presence [of the word] within the apprehended object (*upāttadharma*) and the sentient being (*sattva*), that very cognition is established by experience (*anubhavasiddha*). Regarding this, he states the consensus with the words "it has been said" (*taduktam*). He provides the indicator of the intended meaning (*tātparyagrāhaka*) with the words "by the elders" (*vṛddhaiḥ*). Here he also cites the consensus of the *Bhāṣya* with the words "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). The phrase "of that alone" (*tasyaiva*) means "because of its concomitance (*anvaya*) therein. This [phrase] connects with both [preceding statements].

It has been indicated that this subsequent [passage] is not intended as a restrictive definition (*avadhāraṇa*) in the Bhāṣya; therefore, he says: "even by the word *śastrī*. But if this is so, the doubt [raised] would be irrelevant; hence, in accordance with the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he says: "of many. The meaning is that the status of being a universal (*sāmānyatva*) belongs only to a property residing in many [individuals], whereas in that [case of *śastrī*], because it conveys a property residing in only two [entities] within a compound, it lacks that status. The explanation of the term "in both cases" is: "in the *śastrī*," and "of many" means "of those very many."

But surely, although the existence of the quality [of being] and, in the case of the word, its denotative power are obtained in both cases from this commentary, the co-occurrence (*anvaya*) in both is not obtained; therefore, he says: "here. This means: in the *siddhānta-bhāṣya*. Otherwise, since the point would be established simply by saying "and because of possessing that," the statement as it stands would clearly be redundant.

Furthermore, if that were the case, since the word *śyāmā* would in reality denote many properties, the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) argument found in the Bhāṣya—beginning with the words "not necessarily" (*nāvaśyam*)—would be rendered groundless. Therefore, the intended meaning of the Bhāṣya is simply this: that as many objects as are connected in the cognition produced by a word, so many are denoted by that word. Having thus established the agreement of the Bhāṣya, he states the agreement of the Sūtra as well: "ata eva" (for this very reason). This means: precisely because both [the object and its property] are verbal (śābda) [in their cognition].

This being the case, he states the meaning obtained through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*) with the words "And that" (*tac ca*). All of this pertains to the domain of *vigraha* (analytic dissolution). However, in the actual compound (*vṛtti*), it should be understood that its presence arises by force of the formation of a single referent (*ekārthībhāva*), as indicated by the rule "the standards of comparison" (*upamānāni*). Although there is indeed a difference between the two in their essential nature (*svarūpa*), nevertheless, because non-difference is also perceived according to the method described, the grammatical agreement (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and the masculine substitution (*puṃvadbhāva*) required for the compound are established.

By this commentary, it is stated quite clearly that the cognition is "Śyāmā Devadattā is non-different from Upamāna-Śyāmaśarman. With this in mind, he says in the present context: "Śyāmā," etc. By the word "eva" (only), there is an exclusion of [the view] that it denotes properties residing in many things. By this, the common worldly usage is refuted. And thus—"And so being"—[verse 1.27].

Thus, in order to show that even the consensus of the Alaṅkārikas (theorists of poetics) does not contradict this established conclusion (*siddhānta*), he says: "In poetry... (*kāvyeti*). Suggesting that the suffix *vati* prescribed by the rule "tatra tasyeva" is also included in the preceding [category], he says: "Equal to that" (*tena tulyam*). Likewise, regarding the sentence—meaning, in a sentence containing the *vati* suffix prescribed therein—he says: "That which follows immediately," because the meaning would be incoherent in a *bahuvrīhi* compound. And since there would be a contradiction if it were merely implied (*ārthatva*), he says: "By means of the standard of comparison" (*upamānatayā*).

"Of these"—namely, *yathā* and so forth—"qualifiers of the standard of comparison" (*upamānaviśeṣaṇāni*). By the etymological derivation that they "qualify their own standard of comparison," meaning they cause the standard of comparison to be understood as being characterized by the property of being a standard of comparison, the sense is that they indicate the status of being a standard of comparison. He states this with the words "the standard of comparison. Regarding "of this"—that is, of that cognition (of similarity). "Of this" (*asyāḥ*) is a corrupt reading. He refutes the view of the ancients—that "the status of being a standard of comparison" (*upamānatā*) means similarity (*sādṛśya*)—by stating "the standard of comparison" (*upamāna*), as that is the position favored by the author of the *Prakāśa*.

In this regard, he refutes the acceptance of the desired position—that there is such a distinction in the reading and so forth—by stating "upamāna" (the standard of comparison) and "pradīpa" (lamp). For in that case, this division is untenable, because the cognition of similarity is indistinguishable in both instances. Nor can it be argued that there is a distinction such that the connection with the common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is conveyed in both cases by words like *iva* and the like, but not by words like *tulya* (equal) and the like; for since words such as *yathā* (as) convey the status of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) for that very thing immediately following them, they function as qualifiers of the standard of comparison.

If it is argued that [the genitive] makes known the relation to the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and not to the object of comparison (*upameya*), because one does not observe a word qualifying one thing making known a relation to another, we say no. This is because it has already been stated [in the verse] beginning with "śabdaśakti. Furthermore, the example "like the genitive" (*ṣaṣṭhīvat*) is given to refute the claim that such a capacity to make known a relation to another is something never before observed, even when [the word] is a qualifier of something else.

Just as in expressions such as *rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ* ("the king’s man"), the genitive suffix conveys a relationship such as that between owner and owned, and indicates that the meaning of the base (*prakṛti*) is a qualifier; for a qualifier requires a relation in order to qualify another [qualificandum]. Thus, although it conveys ownership (*svāmitva*) residing in the [king], who is the qualifier, it nevertheless conveys the property of ownership (*svatva*) which constitutes the relation, because a relation by its very nature resides in both relata. In the same way, through the word "like" (*iva*), the state of being a standard of comparison (*upamānatva*) is conveyed there.

The meaning is that the connection with common attributes, such as being delightful and so forth—which sustain that [similarity]—is also understood from the aforementioned reason. He states this with the words "elsewhere. This means in the *Kāvyapradīpodyota*. Thus, regarding the scope of the rule "upamānāni" (Pāṇini 2.1.49), if one were to accept [the application of the suffix] in the same way in cases like *ghana-syāma* (dark as a cloud), he points out the fault regarding the scope of the rule "upamitam" (Pāṇini 2.1.56) with the word "puruṣa" (man). [He says] "in a compound. Furthermore, in that case, the rule "sāmānyāprayoge" (Pāṇini 2.1.57) would also become redundant.

Because the doubt (*śaṅkā*) is equal even in that case. With the intention that it is improper to state that the rule [Pāṇini 2.1.56] is redundant on the grounds that there is the possibility of an alternative application (*gatyantara*) common to the *adhyarddha-sūtra*, he says: "By the word 'upamāna'. This is because of the natural force (*svārasya*) of the term "upamitam" (that which is compared), and because that term always requires a correlate (*nityasākāṅkṣatva*), and because it is applied only when *vyāghra* and so forth function as the standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and because its usage is conventional (*ruḍhatva*). "That" refers to such a status of being a standard of comparison. "By way of that" means by way of possessing a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*).

And thus, since that [quality] is already established, the sense is that it possesses a constant requirement [for a correlative]. Now, with the intention that even if the preceding sūtra is thus meaningful, the subsequent sūtra might not be, he raises an objection: "Even though... — its "nature" (tattvam) is the state of being the object of comparison (upameyatva) for the thing compared; this is indeed what is to be predicated (vidheya). Regarding the cause of its incapacity [to form a compound] in that case, he says: "precisely because of its possibility. He states that the qualification itself indicates this: "for this very reason. The meaning is: precisely because there is no lack of capacity in that regard.

[Objection: "But even if [the word] was not previously perceived as something to be enjoined (*vidheya*), its state of being eternally dependent (*nityasāpekṣatva*) upon what is perceived from it is unavoidable; therefore, the aforementioned works of the ancients would indeed be inconsistent. To this he says: "Let it be so" (*astu*). Here he states the distinction in this view: "But... (*parantu*). — *Tattvam* means "the state of being eternally dependent. — *Gamakatvam* means "the capacity for making the meaning understood. He states that otherwise there would be a fault: "Thus, in the case of a compound... (*iti samāse*). — "Of that" (*tasya*).

In examples such as "rājapuruṣaḥ sundaraḥ" (the king’s man is handsome), the meaning is that the principal member [of the compound] conveys the sense. Here too—even when there is connection with a general property—he says "this," as before; the meaning is that it is precisely the aforementioned qualifier. In that case—namely, in a compound where the principal member is necessarily dependent [on another word]—for this very reason, compounds such as "puruṣavyāghraḥ" (tiger-like man) are established; otherwise, since the connection with an implied common property would be necessary in both cases, there would be no compound even in those instances. (1.28)

He states the purport of the *Prakāśa* in order to explain the distinction: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). This means: "and likewise in the established doctrine" (*siddhānte*). Regarding the term "implied" (*ārthī*): the sense is that it is through suggestion (*vyañjanā*)—by virtue of the necessary connection between cause and effect, and by the excellence [of the object] such as the face—that there is the cognition of that [similarity]. Now, one might object: this is incorrect, because similarity, being of the nature of a property (*dharma*), is not distinct from it; to this he says: "But similarity... He states its producer: "common" (*sādhāraṇa*). He states its indicator according to the established doctrine: "resembling" (*sadṛśa*).

He states [the following] even from the perspective of the opponent’s view: "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍam*). Because it cannot be included within any [of the established categories], he says: "distinct" (*atiriktam*). Regarding "number" (*saṃkhyā*): the meaning is the number sixteen or seven. He says "prameya," etc., because that is not the case since the first contradiction is possible. He resolves the second contradiction differently by means of the initial statement: "furthermore" (*kiñca*). The meaning is: it is based on the number residing in the categories (*padārtha*) themselves.

In this regard: "Now, these are the dogmatic views regarding number: everything is one, because there is no difference in its existence as *sat*; everything is twofold, due to the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal; everything is threefold, due to the distinction between the knower, the instrument of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; everything is fourfold, due to the distinction between the subject of cognition (*pramātṛ*), the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), the object of cognition (*prameya*), and the act of cognition (*pramiti*). Thus it applies to other categories as well, according to the circumstances. Regarding that, [the critique of] the dogmatic view concerning number: if there is a difference between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the probans (*sādhana*), then the dogmatic unity is not established, because of their distinctness."

"Now, if there were no distinction between the probandum (*sādhya*) and the proof (*sādhana*), even so, the [conclusion] would not be established with certainty due to the absence of a proof; for nothing whatsoever is established without it"—thus says the *Vātsyāyana-bhāṣya*. He states this with the words "padārtha... etc. Regarding the "upapatti" (logical justification)—it applies there as well. By this, those modern Naiyāyikas who provide an interpretation and refinement of that [text] by treating it as being intent upon establishing a restrictive rule (*niyama*) are refuted, because it contradicts the root text. To state another specific argument proving his own position in order to refute all opposing views, he says "kiñca" (furthermore).

He states that exclusion by negation (*paryudāsa*) is more logical than absolute negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*), saying "as if with *nañ*" (*nañiva*). Whatever is seen joined with *nañ* or joined with *iva*, the words "from that" (*tasmāt*) are to be supplied there. And the application (*yoga*) should be understood according to the distinction in usage. Thus, *ca* has the sense of "or."—"In a similar [thing]"—that is, in a substance (*dravya*) which is the locus (*adhikaraṇa*).—"For instance" (*tathāhi*)—for (*hi*) because, in common worldly experience, there is indeed the cognition of such a meaning; this is the meaning. He states that very point: "For example" (*tadyathā*).—"A clod" (*loṣṭam*) means a lump of clay.—"And thus" (*evaṃ ca*).

The meaning is that [the result] is obtained through exclusion (*paryudāsa*). By this, Sīradeva and others, who assert other results and other meanings, are refuted. [Objection: But if this is so, how can there be a statement of negation? To this he says: "Because of the negation of the agent. He states this according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*): "Superimposed," etc. By this, it is indicated that this [negation] is verbal (*śābda*), whereas that [result] is implied (*ārtha*). He states its utility for the present context: "For by this," etc.; for since similarity is something distinct. "In that very way," etc.

The meaning of "tathā" (in the same way) is that just as in the case of the use of the negative particle (*nañ*) regarding the aforementioned subject, there is the comprehension of difference (*bheda*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*)—which are conveyed by technical convention (*paribhāṣā*)—through the non-verbal sense (*aśabdārtha*). The underlying intention is that they are presented with equal status. Regarding the phrase "tadvācye": it means "when 'iva' is expressed. An objection is raised: "In this case, there would be no possibility of examples involving *iva*, because in instances such as 'the face is like the moon,' just as non-difference is verbal (*śābda*), difference is likewise verbal."

For this very reason, neither the suffix *vat* prescribed by the rule *tatra tasyeva* (Pāṇini 5.1.116) applies, nor does [the suffix] apply alone in expressions such as *candra iva*, because even when that [suffix] is used in its well-known sense, there is no usage by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) in that specific sense; therefore, he says: *iva*. Regarding the term *adhikāre*, the word *paṭhitena* (by what is recited) is to be supplied. Since the cognition of the superimposed moon is verbal in nature, he says: *tadbhinnaḥ* (different from that). — *pratīyate* (is perceived).

[Objection: "But since a means of cognition (*gamaka*) is impossible there, even if the stated meaning is unestablished, let similarity alone be the expressed meaning; however, it was previously stated that 'difference' (*bheda*) is indeed its [the particle *iva*] meaning. Anticipating this, he says: "But not *soma* itself," and so on. Thus, in the technical definition (*paribhāṣā*), *iva* has a meaning that belongs to the same class as the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in such cases. It should be understood that the connection with that [meaning] also pertains to the meanings themselves, and not to the words. He refutes the view of the Naiyāyikas and others with the words: "By this," etc.

The meaning is: "in contradiction with the Bhāṣya of the commentator on the Paribhāṣā which contains other words. To include both views, he says: "restricted by distinction" (bhedaniyatam). For this very reason, he says: "of this" (asyāḥ) || 1.29 ||

One might object: "But surely, even the view that similarity exists in non-difference is untenable, because there is an absence of a connection with common attributes (*sādhāraṇadharma*) which are the basis for it; for the quality of being 'common' to a property is necessarily dependent upon difference. With this intention, he raises the doubt with the words "And not... (*na ca*). The word "only" (*eva*) serves to exclude what has been stated [previously]. In that context—namely, in the case of non-difference—and thus the identity of "mouth-ness" (*mukhatva*) and so forth is established, the aforementioned fault does not apply. He states the proof for this with the words "For this very reason" (*ata eva*); the meaning is: precisely because its identity is admitted.

Indicating that in the phrase "a thousand sages" (*ṛṣisahasram*) there is a *karmadhāraya* compound, he says: "a thousand. Likewise—by [the word] "one tawny cow" (*ekakapilayā*). By [the word] "thousand," the meaning is: "yielding the fruit of the gift of a thousand cows as a sacrificial fee" (*sahasragodakṣiṇādānaphala*). To indicate its Vedic character (*chāndasatva*), thereby suggesting the rejection of the status of being a commentary accepted by others, he says: "according to the Śruti" (*śrautena*). He states the clear Vedic usage: "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). The meaning has been explained. The same applies further on. The word "thus" (*iti*) connects with the phrase "the state of being seventeen" (*saptadaśatvam*).

The connection [of the word] "śrutau" is with "paṭhitā" in this very context. He states another point: "ata eva" (for this very reason). He explains the meaning of "etena": "mukhya" (primary). He states yet another point: "uktareti" (by what has been said); the sense is that it refers to that very same position. He mentions a relevant point: "evaṃ ca" (and thus); the meaning is "if its [the simile's] status as secondary. He states accordingly regarding the subject at hand: "evam" (thus); the meaning is "in that manner. The word "ekasya" (of one) is to be supplied as an ellipsis—[meaning] of the property, namely, "mukhatva" (the state of being the face). Anticipating the objection that this would lead to the undesirable consequence of the disappearance of the *ananvaya* (non-comparison) figure of speech, he says: "na caika" (nor is there one...).

—By "through difference" (bhedena), it is meant "even by that. By this, the exclusion of non-connection (ananvaya) is established. —"Non-contact" (asaṃsparśaḥ) means being expressible by words. That [non-contact] is restricted to words other than those uttered by the speaker who expresses the reality (tattva). Now, one might object: "Just as the superimposed identity (āropitābheda) is understood through words in the case of simile (upamā), let it be so there as well. To this he says: "For this very reason" (ata eva). The meaning is: "precisely because of its lack of contact with that [identity]. This connects with the phrase "having stated this, the final conclusion (siddhāntita) was reached. Regarding the position that the relationship of subject and object of comparison (upamānopameyabhāva) consists solely in identity (abheda), he says: "That which... (yad iti).

By the phrase "just this, just that" (*yadeva-tadeva*), the absolute non-difference (*atyantābheda*) between the two things established by those [words] is indicated. He states the intended meaning of the doubt with the words "with the object" (*sārtham*). The word *upamā* (simile) is used figuratively (*lākṣaṇika*) at the end of the compound; the word *artha* signifies the result (*phala*), such is the sense. Regarding the word "action" (*karma*): the word *rūpa* (form), like the word *bhāva* (state), refers to a property (*dharma*). There is non-difference between those two. The meaning is: of the cognition of that which constitutes the state of being the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*), namely, the nature of being the object (*karman*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*).

But if there is no difference in the property (*dharmin*), the non-existence [of the comparison] is quite evident, because the number "first" (*ādyatā*) cannot apply to something already excluded, and because it would be grammatically incorrect (*asādhutva*). The reading "in the form of instrumentality" (*karaṇatvarūpā*) is easy to understand. Now, one might object: "Even so, let there be a similarity with something else. To this he says: "of *iva*. The sense is that it is impossible for it to be a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) or the like. As for "nor... (*na ca*): even in the absence of that [similarity], it is due to the capacity of the employment of that word (*iva*). And thus, the purport of the question is: since it is seen to be so in that case, why should it not be exactly so everywhere?

Although there is no conventional usage of terms such as "similarity" (*upamānatva*) in that case, nevertheless, since there is no other way [to explain it], he says "gosadṛśa" (cow-like) even while accepting that [usage]. This is because of its possibility—that is, because the cognition of the exclusion of that [other] is possible. And in the alternative reading "tadbodhe ca," the meaning is the same. To dispel the doubt, "What [is the point]? by showing that this [usage] is also necessary, he answers the doubt regarding how it can be employed with the words "abhede 'pi" (even in the absence of difference). "Abodhaka" means not conveying the stated meaning.

He states the purport of the objection with the words "If this were so": the meaning is that because there would be an absence of a result (*phala*), there would follow the non-employment [of such expressions]. On this view, since this very [expression] would serve as the example (*udāharaṇa*) here, and since the status of being a standard of comparison (*upamāna*) and so forth is not perceived therein, there would be an absolute impossibility of a primary expressive usage consisting of *iva* and other particles; thus, there would be an impossibility of examples for simile (*upamā*), and the rule "upamānāni" (Pāṇini 2.1.41) would be rendered useless—this is the intended sense. By this, the intention stated by Kaiyaṭa is refuted, as is clear from the Uddyota.

The meaning of the word *evam tarhi* occurring there [in the commentary] is "therefore" (*tasmāt*). The word *tatra* refers to the *praśnabhāṣya*. Regarding the difference between individuals (*vyaktibheda*), he says "distinct" (*bhinna*). The word *tat* means the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object of comparison (*upamānopameyabhāva*). Regarding the non-difference of individuals (*vyaktyabheda*) as well, he says "based on superimposition" (*āropita*). This refers to the case of the word "cow" (*gaur*). The word *tasya* refers to either one of the two. He states the reason for this there: "because of the universal" (*sāmānya*). The sense is "because of the identity of the word. Now, one might ask: how is the possibility of stating both [positions] possible in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*)? To this he says "here" (*atra*). This means "in the established doctrine."

"—and so forth—" means "of a usage not joined with the particle *iva*. For this very reason, he states the interpretation there: "like a cow" (*gaur iva*). He concludes what was stated starting with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*) by saying "Therefore" (*tasmāt*). Here, he also cites the consensus of the Alaṃkārikas (theorists of poetics) with the words "In poetry" (*kāvyeti*), because in that context the word "difference" (*bheda*) is stated for the purpose of excluding non-repetition (*ananvaya*). He states the purport of the aforementioned Bhāṣya, which constitutes the established doctrine, with the words "Wherever" (*yatra*). "By a common attribute" (*sādhāraṇadharmeṇa*) means by [qualities] such as dark complexion (*śyāmatva*). "Sāmānya" means non-difference (*abheda*). "Pratyeka" means...

The meaning is "by means of [the property of] being a swordsman" and so forth. "Viśeṣa" (particularity) means "difference. He refutes the statement of the Naiyāyikas with the words "etena" (by this). In examples such as these—which are illustrations of *ananvaya* (non-correspondence)—the word "eva" (only/itself) serves to exclude that [other comparison]. He states the meaning of "etena" as "tasya" (of that). Now, even if this is so, what poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is there in the previously mentioned example "A cow is like a cow"? To this he replies: "mukhādi" (face, etc.). He states it by way of an illustration: "gauriva" (like a cow). Since that [similarity] is not perceived there, the meaning is that because it is likewise not perceived here, it is that very same [figure].

The sense is that, according to the method already stated, it is impossible to describe the comparison where one [element] is not perceived in relation to the other. Now, one might ask: how can that be so? For, in the absence of a word expressive of "like" (*tadvat*), there is no perception of "comparison-ness" (*upamātva*) and so forth, and thus it would not fall under the definition of comparison. To this, he says: "Upamā... and so on. The phrase beginning with "yataḥ" indicates that the term *ananvaya* (non-comparison) is an "etymological" name for the ornament, based on the analysis: "that in which there is a connection with comparison" (*upamāyā yatreti*), referring to a comparison consisting of a common property (*sādharmya*) that is co-referential with a difference touched upon by words. Thus, it is shown that the name of the ornament is significant.

And that absence [of another simile] is caused by the absence of difference, since there is similarity in the manner described. For this very reason, the exclusion of other similes is established as the result. Having grasped that very point, it is stated in the *Prakāśa*, the *Pradīpa*, and other works that "ananvaya" (non-concordance) is the absence of connection with any other simile. This has been explained in exactly the same way by my venerable teacher in his commentary (*Uddyota*) on that work. For this very reason, there is no contradiction with those [other authorities].

And thus it is established that the state of being the object of comparison (*upamāna*) and the object of comparison (*upameya*) resides in a single locus consisting of mere phonemes, which have as their result the cognition of the exclusion of a second similar thing; such is the case here. Consequently, in the domain of *ananvaya* (non-comparison), for the sake of accounting for the initial verbal comprehension and for the cognition of the exclusion of another object of comparison, there is a metaphorical attribution (*upacāra*) of a similarity qualified by difference, even though no actual difference exists. Therefore, in that context, particles such as *iva* indicate a similarity qualified by a difference from the subject itself—which is expressed in co-utterance with them—and [they indicate] that which is without comparison (*nirupama*). Thus, [the phrase] "different from a cow" (*gobhinna*)...

The cognition occurs in the manner of "the cow is similar to a cow," "incomparable," and so forth. And thus, even in cases such as "the face is similar to the face," although there is an absence of the two types of simile (*upamā*) due to the actual absence of difference—just as in "the cow is like a cow"—because the indicator (*dyotaka*), such as *iva*, exists in the example (*dṛṣṭānta*), its verbal nature (*śābdatva*) is established; whereas mere similarity (*sādṛśya*) alone is of the nature of the meaning (*ārthatva*). In the first case, since the word "similar" (*sadṛśa*) and so on conveys only similarity, and because that [similarity] exists even in non-difference according to the aforementioned method, it is possible to exclude [mere similarity] from that [verbal expression]; therefore, it is merely...

The sense is that the non-connection (*ananvaya*) consists in the fact that the connection is not expressed by words but exists only as a matter of meaning. Now, one might object: if this were the case, then in instances such as "the face is like the moon," since that [connection] is not perceived through words and its absence would thus exist, there would be the contingency of *ananvaya*, which would contradict the established doctrine. To this, he says: "In that case" (*tatra*). This means: in the domain of simile (*upamā*) and *ananvaya*. "In reality" (*vastutaḥ*) refers to the actual state of things. "Because of the perception" (*pratīteḥ*): and so, since the relation itself exists, there is no absence of that [relation], and therefore no *ananvaya*. This is the underlying point. "In every respect" (*sarvathā*).

The meaning is that there is no apprehension of a simile (upamā) either through the word or through its sense; the intention is that there is no difference [between the two cases]. Now, if one objects: "If the simile is verbal (*śābda*), then given the presence of the cause, the presence of the effect is necessary; thus, even if the apprehension of similarity is based on the intended meaning (*ārtha*), how can the simile itself be understood (*gamya*) when the similarity is verbal? If you say it is so by the logic of inferring the cause from the effect, then the same consequence would apply to cases such as 'the face is similar to the face,' which would contradict what was stated previously. To this, he says: "In that case" (*tatra*).

The meaning is: "in its application to a domain where there is difference. And thus, the intention is that there is no over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). Now, one might object: if there is multiplicity (*anekatva*) there, how can the definition—which involves oneness (*ekatva*)—be applicable, given that [oneness] has been stated by Prakāśa and others? To this he says: "non-connection" (*ananvaya*). The intention is that, in such a case, the word *eka* has the same meaning [as non-difference] and does not refer to numerical oneness. He states another passage from the Bhāṣya as evidence for the existence of similarity (*sādṛśya*) in non-difference (*abheda*), saying: "for this very reason" (*ata eva*). The meaning is: precisely because similarity exists in non-difference.

Regarding the first sentence as it stands, he says "only *ū* and *aj*" in order to prevent the over-extension (atiprasaṅga) that would result from the application of the rule *aṇudit* (Pāṇini 1.1.69). He says "by implication" (*sāmarthyāt*) because, if there were a non-distinctive connection, the word *ac* would be redundant. By this very [word *eva*], the inclusion of those things grasped by the *aṇudit* rule is excluded. The plural number is intended to refer to individual instances (*vyakti*). He states the intention of the phrase "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) as being "only in the case of difference" (*bhedaeveva*). If one were to accept a distinction based on differences such as usage and so forth, and then attempt to justify it, that justification would be useless; for since such a distinction would be universal, there would be nothing to exclude, and thus his statement would be fruitless. Therefore, he says: "enough of this. (1.30)

He confirms its distinctness with the words "by similarity" (*sādṛśya*). He states what is excluded by the particle *eva* with the words "but not" (*na tu*). For this very reason—namely, because of its distinctness—he says "and so forth" (*ityādi*), meaning that even such [expressions] are included. He says "directly" (*āñjasyena*) because there is no difficulty in explaining [the usage] through the third case of non-difference (the *abheda-tṛtīyā*), as it belongs to the class beginning with *prakṛti*. [Objection: Even so, if it were one, there would be the consequence of many simultaneous errors; to this he says "and that" (*tac ca*), meaning "and similarity. He states that its establishment is likewise [as follows]: "by the manifestor" (*vyañjaka*).

This is not in contradiction with the previous [statement] because it is based on the position that [similarity] is eternal. Now, one might object that the existence of the standard of comparison (*upamāna*) within the object of comparison (*upameya*) is contradicted; therefore, he says: "by similarity" (*sādṛśya*). Indicating the meaning of the phrase "for this very reason," he says: "common" (*sādhāraṇa*). [He gives the example: "of mine. The intention is that when it is said, "dark as a sword-blade" (*śastrīśyāmā*), [the similarity is perceived]. By this, the Sāṃkhya Sūtra statement—"Similarity is not a distinct category [of reality], because it is perceived through direct perception"—which implies that what is perceived by direct perception is only the form of a common attribute (*sādhāraṇadharma*), is refuted.

Because it is established by the aforementioned means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); and because, since "jar-ness" and the like—which are distinct from possessing a conch-shaped neck and so forth—are not perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), they too would fail to be established as distinct categories (*tattvāntara*). Thus he says: "Enough of this. Regarding the portion [of the verse] beginning with "like arrows," he states the distinction by reversing the order: "māteva" (like a mother), etc., such as "O King, eat the *harītakī*," and so on. — "The counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*), etc.

By this, it is indicated that the view—that the meaning is "as if pure similarity" (śuddhasādṛśyamiva)—is indeed untenable because, as previously stated, it would result in the occurrence of a genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*), which cannot be avoided; otherwise, this [usage] would be grammatically incorrect (*asādhutva*). For this very reason, the claim that the connection of similarity with the object of comparison (*upameya*) occurs through a distinction—on the grounds that the rule of word-meaning application (*nāmārthayoḥ*) applies to cases other than particles (*nipāta*)—is refuted. This is due to the reasoning already stated: because that [similarity] is a noun-meaning (*nāmatva*), and because, according to the maxim "the word-meaning [connects with the principal]," when connection with the principal is possible, connection with a single part [of the principal] is impossible, leading to the aforementioned defect.

Announcing this very point, he says: "possessing similarity. For this very reason, he says: "of one part of that. The sense is that, because a connection with the primary [meaning] is impossible, there is a diversity of linguistic derivation (*vyutpatti*). Stating his lack of approval as indicated by the word "some" (*kaścit*), he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "this is indeed incorrect. The sense is that it is difficult to prevent such a usage for one who has acquired that particular linguistic proficiency. Regarding the term "Vārttika," the singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jātāvekavacanam*). He states the general rule regarding the aforementioned distinction between the two positions in the case of particles (*nipāta*) with the word "therein" (*tatra*).

The meaning is: "in a place where there is no *nipāta* (indeclinable) other than those that convey a specific distinction regarding the action."—"Of that"—refers to such a *nipāta*. The word "of them" (*teṣām*) is to be construed with both [the preceding and following clauses]. In examples such as "Caitra’s wealth is like Maitra’s wealth," the genitive case is used in both instances because of its connection with "wealth. In examples such as "He studies from Caitra," the term "from Caitra" (*caitrāt*) has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) referring to a study for which Caitra is the source (*apādāna*), or else follows the aforementioned method; however, it does not connect with the verb "studies" (*adhīte*). This is because that which is denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) cannot function as a standard of comparison (*upamāna*), and so forth—this is to be inferred. || 1.31 ||

Now, as an incidental discussion, he provides an example for the meaning of the specific particle *nañ* (negation) mentioned in the passage beginning with "there, [the word] *gamaka*," etc., namely: "the jar does not exist. This means in the context of absolute negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*). How this is so will become clear immediately below. He states the context of relative negation (*paryudāsa*) with: "not in the *anuyāja* offerings. He establishes the truth of his own position with: "superimposed..."

He states that [the word *tadādi*] is established by the meaning of the scriptural passage to be cited later—"In sacrifices (*yajatiṣu*), one performs the *yeyajāmahe* [formula]"—by saying "in sacrifices" (*yajatiṣu*). Thus, its validity is established through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [word]. He states the subverting argument for the opposite case (*vipakṣe bādhaka*) with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*); this means: if such a meaning were not accepted. He says "in difference" (*bhede*) because, on the view that difference is the expressed meaning, it is understood precisely as the qualificand (*viśeṣyatayā*).

Even if [the absence] is a qualifier by virtue of being that which is to be illuminated (*dyotyatva*), there is still an inconsistency because the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) is construed with the counter-correlate (*pratīyogin*); consequently, it cannot be co-referential (*asāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [counter-correlate]. Bearing this in mind, the author states "superimposition" (*āropa*) and so forth. This is because the statement in the *Dīkṣitabhūṣaṇa* and other works—that the meaning of the negative particle is merely superimposition and that its relation is identity (*tādātmya*) due to parsimony—is inconsistent; for, according to the previously mentioned method, without a suffix, it is impossible to have a cognition [of the object] through that relation. Thus, he states exactly what was said regarding the first position: "In that case"—meaning, in the context of exclusion (*paryudāsa*).

Since there are two defects in accepting [the view] in that manner, he states "tasya tatra" (of that, therein) to show that this [view] is absolutely necessary and thus possesses uniformity. The meaning is: "precisely because it is expressed by that. "Primacy"—this is what was stated in the Bhāṣya. "All," etc.—this refers to the effect beginning with that. Now, one might object: the "secondary" nature (*gauṇatva*) required for the application of the principle of primary and secondary [meanings] is not present here; therefore, he says "itara," etc. Furthermore, his statement—that the words "jar" and so on have their denotative power (*śakti*) directed toward the locus of superimposition (*āropaviṣaya*), while the negative particle (*nañ*) is merely indicative (*dyotaka*)—is also incorrect.

Since postulating two functions (vṛtti) involves the postulation of a qualified power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*) and the assumption of what has not been previously established—both of which entail complexity—the author states the more parsimonious conclusion according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), namely that "metaphorical indication" (*lakṣaṇā*) is the superimposition of the delimiting factor of denotability (*śakyatāvacchedakāropa*). He says "or else" (*yadvā*). The word "nañ" (the negative particle) is to be construed with the phrase "is a grasper of its own [referent]. Regarding the statement "elsewhere they have power over that which possesses a non-superimposed ground for application" (*anāropita-pravṛttinimittavati śakteḥ*), he explains: "its own" (*sva*); the meaning is: when there is a cognition by way of that form which constitutes the superimposed ground for application (*āropita-pravṛttinimitta*).

Alternatively, the meaning is that a *bahuvrīhi* compound [functions] in a cognition where the ground for its application (*pravṛttinimitta*) is superimposed. Thus, indicating that those [words] are metaphorical (*lākṣaṇika*) when applied to that which possesses [the quality], he says "just as" (*yathā*). For this very reason, it was stated previously that [the word] does not denote its primary meaning. The sense is that such a method is established in this case. And so, the intended meaning is that there is no doubt whatsoever that secondary usage (*gauṇatva*) does not arise merely from being metaphorical. This being the case, the six meanings mentioned by the ancients—beginning with "the state of possessing similarity to that"—are logically consistent.

Since the example of similarity, "non-Brahmin" (*abrāhmaṇa*), was stated previously, he speaks [now] disregarding that sequence, beginning with "anudara," etc. The words "jāyamānayā" (by that which is being produced) are to be supplied as the complement to "āropya" (having superimposed). There is a variant reading: "āropitodarabuddhyā" (by the cognition of a superimposed belly). There is also a variant reading: "viśramaḥ" (resting place).

The meaning is as follows: since the superimposition of identity (*tādātmyāropa*) occurs only when difference (*bheda*) and similarity (*sādṛśya*) are present, whereas the superimposition of relation (*saṃsargāropa*) occurs precisely when those two are absent, there arises—after the cognition of the superimposed nature and by virtue of context and other factors that grasp the speaker's intention—an understanding, through implication, of the absence of similarity and so forth, which is mental in nature. Pointing out that the example of "non-horse" (*anaśva*) cited by the ancients as an instance of difference is no different from "non-Brāhmaṇa" (*abrāhmaṇa*), and thus its status as such is to be questioned, he says: "up to 'dvija'. This means the superimposition of the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta*). The word "iti" is used in the sense of a reason. And [the phrase] "and in cases such as this" refers to the aforementioned.

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "the superimposition of another [property] as the cause for its application, rooted in contradiction with that [original property]. The word *viśrāntiḥ* (resting) is to be supplied later [in the text]. Examples of negation (*abhāva*) and censure (*apraśasti*) are to be understood in the cases of *apāpam* and *apaśavaḥ*. Now, one might object: "Even if it is thus denoted (*vācya*), since it is a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*), the previously mentioned defects do not apply; so why is it said to be merely indicative (*dyotaka*)? To this he says: "superimposed," etc. He provides the consensus of the Bhāṣya on this point: "therein," etc.; the meaning is: "in all cases where there is the co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) of the negative particle (*nañ*)."

"This alone"—that is, precisely the state of being a grasper preceded by the abandonment [of the former]. By this, the previous view is excluded. Now, one might object: "In this way, since there is no separate meaning, there is an absence of a single unified meaning; how then can there be a compound? To this he says: "By this much alone. The meaning is: "Precisely by virtue of its indicating that [state]. Just as in the case of the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member (*uttarapada*), by this very point the status of being a direct denoter (*vācakatva*) is excluded.

[Objection: Even so, since the meaning of something other than the meaning of the final member is not perceived, and because there is no expressive power (*śakti*) for a qualified entity, how can it possess the status of a nominal stem (*prātipadika*)? To this he says: "viśiṣṭa... [etc.]. He states the reason for that: "dyotya... [etc.]; the meaning is "indicated by the final member.
