Since it is accepted that there is expressive power (*śakti*) in every compound, he says: "śaktau... [etc.]. [Objection: Let there simply be a difference in meaning for the sake of establishing the form; to this he says: "samāsa... [etc.]. The intention is that this is for the sake of having a single word-form (*aikapadya*) and a single accent (*ekasvarya*).

[Objection: But if that is so, since there is no difference in their being indicators (*dyotaka*), then in cases such as *prajayati* ("he conquers"), it would follow that the composite form alone possesses meaning. To this, he says: "In *prajayati*... He dispels the objection regarding the lack of authority for the grammatical treatise (*śāstra*) by stating: "The parts... This is not only the case here, but it is also necessary elsewhere. Furthermore, the utility of the treatise should be understood even by way of the analogy of the "line-drawn cow" (*rekhāgavaya*). Thus he says: "This is the direction [of the argument]. (1.32)

In accordance with the maxim of the lion’s glance (*siṃhāvalokananyāya*), he says "asandeha" in order to indicate a specific distinction regarding the example of non-existence (*abhāva*) presented hereafter. "Bheda" means by way of a connection rooted in that [distinction]. The particle "ca" is used in the sense of "but. It is clear elsewhere that in the expression "rakṣohāgaladhvasandehāḥ," the cognition of the prior absence of doubt occurs only as a last resort. Now, he clarifies what was stated in "there is no jar" and so forth with the words "asamaste tu. The particle "tu" indicates the difference from what has been discussed regarding compounds. "Nañarthaḥ" means that which is expressed by the negative particle (*nañ*). "Tatra" means between those two.

As for the Naiyāyikas’ claim that absolute negation (*atyantābhāva*) is an eternal non-existence, or a non-existence whose counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitā*) is delimited by a relation other than identity (*tādātmya*), while mutual negation (*anyonyābhāva*) is a non-existence whose counter-correlativity is delimited by the relation of identity—that is not correct. For, according to the method previously stated, such a [negation] lacks eternity, and because it would involve unnecessary complexity (*gaurava*). Intimating this, he says: "other than identity" (*tādātmyetara*). This is intended to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) regarding mutual negation. "Absence of relation" (*sambandhābhāva*) means a non-existence whose counter-correlate is a relation; the same applies hereafter.

Now, one might object: "Is identity (*tādātmya*) here not the nature of the substratum (*dharmin*), since it is not the meaning of the word? For this very reason, it is not the nature of a relation either, because it does not fall under the definition of a relation; and for this same reason, it is not even the nature of non-difference qualified by difference. To this he says: "Identity. The meaning is: "a specific kind of relation. Then, for the sake of parsimony (*lāghava*), he says: "subsisting therein" (*tadvṛtti*). Since a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) is not present there, and because [the former definition] would be over-extensive (*atiprasakta*), he says: "uncommon" (*asādhāraṇa*).

For this very reason, it is stated that there is an absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāva*), and not an absence of relation (*tatsambandhābhāva*). [Objection: If this is so, how can these two possess the universally accepted counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitva*) with respect to jars and the like? To this, he says: "co-extensive" (*samaniyata*). This means in cases such as the absence of substanceness, the state of being a substratum of qualities, and the state of being a substratum of action. Since the opponents accept their identity, he says: "of one" (*ekasya*); that is, of the absence. Because of the co-extensiveness (*samanaiyatyāt*) of the jar, its existence, and its relation, he says: "of these two" (*anayoḥ*).

The meaning is: "of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) and mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*). And thus, the implication is that there is no such thing as the non-existence of a jar or the like that is distinct from those two. He states [the definition of] *kṛdanta* (words ending in *kṛt* suffixes) with the word "tiṅ" [in the verse]. To exclude the fruit (*phala*) and so forth, he says "action" (*kriyā*). By this very term, substances (*dravya*) and the like are excluded. Regarding the propriety of using that [term *kriyā*] in that very context, he states the reason: "not compounded" (*asamasta*). Its nature (*tattva*) consists in being distinct from words that constitute a compound name (*samāsa-saṃjñaka-śabda*).

[Objection: But then this qualification is redundant, because in a compound such as *asaṃdeha* (non-doubt), there is no such cognition at all. Nor can it be argued that the qualification is necessary to avoid a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding the cognition of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) that arises later, even though it was absent previously; for even so, since compounds are optional, in their corresponding colloquial sentences—such as *na saṃdehaḥ* (no doubt)—the same cognition occurs, and thus the problem of deviation remains as it was. [Reply: This is not so.

This is because the intended meaning of "tattva" (the nature of the thing) consists in its being a constituent of a group that is not capable of forming a compound. Now, even if one were to state merely "the meaning of the non-compounded *nañ*," there would still be a deviation (*vyabhicāra*) in cases such as "not twice-born among the *anuyāja*s," where although no such cognition occurred previously, such a cognition does arise later; therefore, he says "absolute" (*atyanta*). In that case, however, the compound has "difference" as its qualificandum (*bhedaviśeṣyakatva*). Thus, the intended sense is that the *nañ* here is a "prohibitive negation" (*prasajyapratiṣedha*). In that instance, however, for the reasons already stated, it is indeed an "exclusionary negation" (*paryudāsa*).

Even though there is semantic capacity (*sāmarthya*), the compound does not occur in the first case because it is optional. By this, the objection that—given a doubt regarding both [the presence and absence of the capacity]—there would be the contingency of compounding, and thus it must be a prohibitive negation (*prasajyapratiṣedha*) rather than an exclusionary negation (*paryudāsa*), is refuted. For, according to the stated method, even in the case of an exclusionary negation, the absence of compounding occurs; furthermore, the statement of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) in the *Bādhalakṣaṇa*—that "optionality" (*vibhāṣā*) applies only to the grammatical operation itself—shows that there is no rule restricting it to connection with a verb, since its application elsewhere is established. Moreover, the fact that the term "optionally" (*vibhāṣā*) would otherwise be redundant is made clear in the *Mahābhāṣya*.

Regarding this, he states the underlying reason: "ata eva" (for this very reason). The meaning is: because its correctness (*sādhutva*) is established only when it follows that [specific] sequence. Its connection is with the word "upapadyate" (is justified). He speaks out of order, saying "aham" (I); since its establishment occurs through the default singular number, he says "ghaṭau" (two pots). He speaks according to the sequence of the sūtras prescribing personal endings, saying "yuṣmad-ādeḥ" (of *yuṣmad* and so forth). He speaks according to the stated sequence, saying "mad-ādeḥ" (of *mad* and so forth); the meaning is: and in the connection of such expressions.

[Objection: But surely, according to the view of the opponent (*paramata*), just as the number denoted by the verbal suffix (*ākhyātārtha-saṃkhyā*) is connected with the productive urge (*bhāvanā*), so too the number of the object (*arthasaṃkhyā*)—which is connected with the productive urge—is connected even with that which is the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of the productive urge, due to the diversity of linguistic usage (*vyutpatti-vaicitrya*). And thus, since co-referentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) consists precisely in having that [productive urge] as the locus for the connection of its number, the systematic distinction between person (*puruṣa*) and voice (*vacana*) is established; therefore, he says: "The meaning of the verbal suffix... This is said while provisionally accepting [the opponent's position]. In reality, however, that is not the case, and so he says: "Furthermore (*kiñca*)."

Now, one might object: even if from a statement such as "the jar does not exist" there arises a cognition of the absence of existence (sattā) whose agent is the jar, there still arises no cognition of the absence of the jar itself; consequently, doubt regarding the jar and the like would result, and it would follow that a cognition of the jar's presence would not be an obstacle [to the cognition of its absence], because there is no contradiction between them. To this, he says: "The existence of the jar," etc. By the word "etc. (ādi), the inclusion of the fact that [such a cognition] is not an obstacle is intended.

By this, the established distinction between the two cases is proven: just as in "Caitra does not cook" (*na pacati caitraḥ*) and so forth, there is the cognition that Caitra possesses the absence of the act of cooking (*pākakṛtyabhāvavān*), so too in "the jar does not exist" (*ghaṭo nāsti*) and so forth, there is the cognition that the jar possesses the absence of being a locus of existence (*sattāśrayatvābhāvavān*). The Naiyāyika claim—that the determinant of agency is simply being the locus of the meaning of either the verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*) or the negative particle (*nañ*) occurring in its vicinity, and that there is no fault because number (*saṃkhyā*) can indeed be construed with that which is construed with the meaning of *nañ* which is itself construed with the productive operation (*bhāvanā*)—is thereby refuted.

Because it is impossible to account for the cognition of the absence of a jar as established by universal experience [if that were merely the absence of existence]. For me, however, since the absence of existence whose agent is the jar is co-extensive (samaniyata) with the absence of the jar, the cognition of that [absence] is possible; furthermore, because of the fault that will be stated later. To state a distinction, he says "evam" (thus), which arises from the context due to the application of the same reasoning. The meaning is "like an absence that is co-extensive. By the words "sandehādi" (doubt, etc.), the cognition of its absence is included. To refute [the opponent], he states the Naiyāyika view: "sama" (equal). The meaning is "of absences that are co-extensive."

In some places, the reading is exactly as it stands. Regarding that, he states the subverting argument: "And not... He says that it does not constitute a subversion because its object is something else: "On account of parsimony (lāghavāt). Even though there is an intrinsic difference in their essential natures, he provides an example for their identity: "Pot-ness (ghaṭatva)... The sense is that in one and the same [locus], there is a counter-correlativity with respect to the pot in the capacity of being a difference (bheda), and a counter-correlativity with respect to pot-ness in the capacity of being an absolute non-existence (atyantābhāva). He provides an example for the identity of existence and non-existence: "Pot-ness..."—and also for two positive entities: "pot and its existence," and so forth.

—*Tattvam* means identity (*aikyam*). —*Hetoḥ*: of the reason stated as "due to parsimony" (*lāghavāt*) and so forth. He states the defect by taking up the lack of co-occurrence (*asamanaiyatyam*): "only one," meaning by the postulation of both. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of other doctrines, such as those asserting the ultimate reality of the substratum (*dharmitāttvikatva*). The particle *api* is used for the purpose of including the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). How that is the case has been explained previously. For this very reason, when the undesired consequence is accepted, he states another defect by taking up the co-occurrence (*samanaiyatyam*): "of that form" (*tadrūpa*). Precisely by the reasoning already stated.

However, this is not accepted by them, because the distinction between those [qualities] is necessary to avoid the occurrence of the aforementioned defect by assuming the unity of their collection. Here, he refutes the second defect with the passage beginning with "tatra" and ending with "kecit. Regarding the phrase "therein"—that is, in that color, taste, and so forth—[the opponent might argue] that since such [a universal] is not applicable there, the cognition "color appears" and so on does not exist at all, because the manifestation of every color is impossible; rather, it is a cognition of a particular [color], and thus that [universal] exists as the delimiting factor (avacchedaka) of that particular, namely as "being that color" and so forth. To this, he says: "tadrūpam" (that color).

[The objection is: "In that case, there would be no co-occurrence (*samanaiyatyam*) between those absences and those two—existence and non-existence—as well as between those two existences, because the delimiters (*avacchedaka*) of the appearing [properties], such as 'absence-ness,' 'difference-ness,' and 'existence-ness,' would be over-extended (*atiprasakta*), just like 'form-ness' (*rūpatva*) and so on. To this, he says: "Of the action" (*kriyāyāḥ*). "In that regard"—that is, among those [absences]. And thus, in that case, the delimiter of the appearing [property] is the specific form of each respective "absence-ness" or "existence-ness," and not the aforementioned general form; therefore, there is no fault.

The phrase "some [say]" contains the seed of dissatisfaction even with that view, because the nature of that [universal] and so forth must be the delimiting factor (*avacchedaka*) of its manifestation; otherwise, it would result in the fallacy of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Furthermore, even the form belonging to that [universal] appears only as embraced by a particular substratum. Moreover, the manifestation of that [form] unembraced by it, and of that [substratum] unembraced by it, was previously established; thus, one is caught in the maxim of the "rope that binds from both ends. And in this way, the second objection remains firmly intact.

He refutes the views of others, both his own and those of others, with the words "by this" (*eteneti*). Because that [term] requires a correlate, he says "of the substrata" (*adhikaraṇānām*). Since it would not be possible to establish the distinction between the speaker and the person if one were to say merely "the absence of a jar," he says "the counter-positive of the absence" (*abhāvapratiyogī*) in order to establish that. He explains the meaning of "by this" as "in what is about to be said"; the sense is that it occurs in this very context. "Of that"—that is, of the absence. "Because of the lack of expectancy"—because of the absence of such expectancy. Since there is no direct connection with that, he says "agent and object" (*kartṛkarma*).

"—it is not incorrect. This is the intended meaning of the phrase beginning with "here" (*iha*). He states "absolute... (*atyanteti*) because of the aforementioned relationship between cause and effect. By this, the view that there is no inconsistency [in the cognition] because of the understanding that "such a jar is the locus of existence" (*sattā-āśraya*) is also refuted. If its connection is with existence (*sattā*) or with its agent and so forth, then even if the jar—which is the counter-positive of an absence residing in something—connects here [with the location], there is no fault, because it is accepted that the negative particle (*nañ*) co-occurring with it has a secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) in the sense of the absence of that which possesses it.

Because, in the case of a jar which is the counter-positive of the absence of existence in this location, there exists the certainty of the absence of existence residing in this [jar]; therefore, the cognition of its being the locus of existence residing therein is untenable. He refutes the aforementioned view of the opponent from the *Nañvāda* with the words "by this" (*eteneti*), meaning "by the final defect. The phrase "the elaboration of this" connects with the word "refuted" (*apāstam*). "Otherwise"—that is, if one does not accept it in that way, or if one accepts such a cognition by supplying an ellipsis for a verb.

Now, it might be argued that according to the method already stated, the understanding—"the absence of existence whose locus is the pot-participant"—is indeed well-established; therefore, he says "tathāhi" (for instance). "Krameṇa" means in the order of expectancy. For this very reason, he says "ghaṭasattā" (the existence of the pot). Regarding its being existent, he says "sataḥ" (of the existent); regarding its being illusory, he says "asataḥ" (of the non-existent). This has been stated by the author of the *Khaṇḍana*.

That [is] a negation. He states its purposefulness regarding the second [alternative] with the words "na ca" (and not). The sense is: because of its existence and because of its momentariness. Even though a contradictory cognition causes the cessation of that [prior] cognition, he states the impossibility of the other [alternative] because the cessation expressed by the employed negative particle (*nañ*) requires a referent (*vācya-sākāṅkṣatvāt*). With the words "buddheḥ" (of the cognition), he [shows this]. By this—by the aforementioned reason—the reading "ity apy apāstam" (thus also refuted) is [to be understood]. He states another fault common to both [alternatives] with the words "ghaṭābhāva" (the absence of a jar). By the word "ādi" (etcetera), the absence of subsistence in the ground (*bhūtalavṛttitvābhāva*) is included.

Therefore, there is no such cognition [of the jar]; rather, by necessity, it is established that its cognition is only occasional. Regarding this, he provides authoritative support with the words "Kaṇāda," etc., where the reading is "pratīti" (cognition) regarding the relation (*saṃsarga*). He states "of the existing jar" (*sato ghaṭasya*) as containing a reason, implying that [the cognition] is fruitful only in this way and not otherwise; thus he says "of the existing. [The phrase] "gehasaṃsarge" means "in the relation with the house," which signifies "subsisting therein" (*tadvṛttitva*). 1.33.

In this view, following the manner of Dīkṣitabhūṣaṇa and others, he raises an objection regarding the removal of the fault that arises: "And not" (na ca). He states "avyayībhāva" to show that there is no fault resulting from that [compound], because the negative *tatpuruṣa* is optional. Indicating both alternatives, he says: "There is no jar on the ground."

"—because there is no *avyayībhāva* [compound]. This is because of the usage in the *Bhāṣya*, "that afterwards," under the rule *acaḥ parasmin*; and because of the statement in the *Bhāṣya* on the rule *yathā'sādṛśye*: "it would follow that 'similarity' (*sādṛśya*) and 'attainment' (*saṃpatti*) [are included]. The meaning is this: in that [former] rule, there is no compound with a word that is understood as being a constituent part of a word expressing those respective meanings; however, it does indeed occur with the word *yathā*, because of the commencement of the subsequent rule.

Regarding this, he states another interpretation of the commentary as a supporting argument: "For this very reason" (*ata eva*). This means: precisely because that [absence] is admitted. Thus it is said in the second [section]. "It was not introduced"—if this were so, there would be the fault of incompleteness (*nyūnatā*). To this he says: "For this very reason. The meaning has already been stated. "In that case"—that is, in the view that the compound is *pūrvapadārthapradhāna* (where the meaning of the first member is predominant). "Of the word" (*śabda*)—the meaning is that although the negative particle (*nañ*) in a sentence denotes a non-existent entity (*asattvabhūta-artha*), in a compound it denotes an existent entity (*sattvarūpa-artha*). Therefore, [the objection does not apply].

If, however, the *avyayībhāva* were not intended [in this context], then because its connection with that [suffix] would be established by it, the impossibility of reaching up to that extent would be quite evident. Now, one might object: "This is not the final conclusion (*siddhānta*) of the Bhāṣya; since a *tatpuruṣa* is generally dominated by the meaning of the final member, how can the stated point be established for you? To this he says: "But here, [it is] otherwise. The word "but" (*tu*) indicates the absence of the two aforementioned defects; the sense is that in this respect, it attains the status of a final conclusion. — "Not established by the statement"—referring to what will be said later. — "The state of being predominant."

Alternatively, let it be that [the compound] is one in which the meaning of the final member is predominant; this is the intended sense (*bhāva*). But if this is so, how is it that [the rule] says, "In the absence of *adruta* (short vowel), there is no *saṃhitā*"? Its meaning is that the proximity (*saṃnikarṣa*) of the subsequent [vowel] is merely superimposed (*āropita*). Regarding the term "sūtra": the meaning is that by virtue of the authority of both [these sources], it possesses the gender of both feminine and neuter. The reading is "the word *saṃhita*. Here he also provides the consensus of others: "for this very reason" means precisely because of the acceptance of its neuter gender.

By this, the claim of Dīkṣita and others—that the negative compound (*nañ-tatpuruṣa*) is optional with the indeclinable compound (*avyayībhāva*) based on the usage in the Sūtra and Vārttika—is refuted. The resolution for the term *asaṃdeha* has already been stated. He says "elsewhere" (*anyatra*), meaning in the *Śekhara* and other such works. He clears away the fault mentioned therein by saying "by existence" (*sattvena*), because that [existence] alone is the counteragent to that [doubt]. Now, if it is asked whether there is no proof for that very point, he says "Kaṇāda," etc. He states the reason for obtaining that [result]: "of the relation also" (*saṃsargasyāpi*). By the word "also" (*api*), existence (*sattā*) and so forth are included.

And thus, since that [position] is indeed untenable according to the manner previously stated, it should be understood that the presentation of the example earlier was made according to that [opponent's] way and not according to our own way; therefore, there is no contradiction with our final conclusion (siddhānta).

Furthermore, even based on the aforementioned commentary, since the negative particle (*nañ*) signifying absolute non-existence conveys the absence of a counter-correlative such as an action, it cannot be syntactically connected with the meaning of a subsequent word (such as *uttara*). Due to this lack of semantic competency (*asāmarthya*), an *avyayībhāva* compound is not possible—just as in the case of *na nirmakṣikam*. Thus, even if the formation of the sentence were otherwise possible, such a cognition would simply not be obtained; therefore, such a cognition is indeed improper. However, in cases such as *na saṃdehaḥ*, because doubt (*saṃdeha*) is a quality (*guṇa*), the negative particle can indeed convey its absence, and thus there is semantic competency.

This too is stated by means of *atyaya* (cessation/absence), and thus there is no fault. This will become clear immediately hereafter, so there is no contradiction with what was said previously. By this, it is established by experience that in cases such as "there is no jar on the ground," based on the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), there arises a cognition of the absence of the occurrence of the word-base "ground" (ending in the locative case) in the jar, etc., just as the locative sense of "inherence" (*ādheyatva*) connected to the ground, etc., occurs in the absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*) of the jar.

Otherwise, it would be untenable for the cognition of absence—produced by such a sentence and unassailed by the cognition of its own invalidity—to possess a state of opposition toward the cognition produced by a sentence such as "there is a pot on the ground," which has the pot as its qualificandum and the property of being located on the ground as its qualifier.

The view expressed by the *Vyutpattivāda* and others—that "in a case where a certain qualifier appears as qualifying a subject (*dharmin*) in the absence of a negative particle (*nañ*) due to a particular co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), the absence of that qualifier is cognized in that same subject when the negative particle is present in such a co-occurrence"—is also rejected. This is because it would entail the denial of experience, for the aforementioned reasoning establishes that [the negative particle] acts as a counter-agent (*pratibandhaka*) in the manner described; furthermore, it is because the cognition having the action as its primary object (*kriyāviśeṣyaka*) alone exists according to the stated method. Thus he says: "This is the direction [of the argument]. (*iti dig iti*)

As for the objection that in your view the experience of a single qualificandum (*viśeṣya*) in cognitions such as "in the earth" would be contradicted—and therefore what I have said alone is correct—that is refuted by the words "In the earth. Due to the speaker's intention (*tātparya*), there may sometimes arise a cognition whose qualificandum is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*), namely, the absence of the function of the case-ending. This is why he says, "of the cognition being one. Otherwise, in the expression "not in water," there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the word "smell" not functioning [as a qualifier]; such is his intention.

As for the claim that the meaning is "water possesses an absence whose counter-positive is the odor residing in earth," that is not correct; for the locative case in "in water" (*jale*) would be untenable. If the cognition were "that absence resides in water," then the locative in "in earth" (*pṛthivyām*) would be untenable, and the word *tat* (that) would become redundant. Therefore, according to the established doctrine, the two cognitions have different substrata (*viśeṣya*).

By this aforementioned method, the view that there is an understanding—even without non-inherence—that "smell is the counter-positive of an absence residing in water" (occurring in the locus "on earth") because the absence conjoined with the locative case-meaning functions as a qualifier and is construed with the counter-positive, is also refuted; for this would be like the cognition "the jar is the counter-positive of an absence residing on the ground. This is the direction of the argument. Thus he says: "This is the direction. (1.34)
In the established doctrine, he removes the objection that has arisen: "One should not look at [the sun] as it is rising," nor ever when it is setting;
nor when it is eclipsed, nor when reflected in water, nor when it has reached the middle of the sky.

This is its inclusion. And this [rule] is part of the *snātaka-vrata* (vows of one who has completed his studies), belonging neither to Manu, nor Yājñavalkya, nor Āpastamba; rather, it is included within the *prajāpati-vrata* (vows of Prajāpati) which constitute the duties of a religious student (*brahmacārin*). Regarding its abandonment, he says "of that" (*tasya*), referring to the subject matter of the fourth sūtra of Jaimini beginning with "actions are for the sake of human ends" (*karmāṇi puruṣārthāya*). Its explanation is as follows: "Brahman," and "in the absence of contemplation."

For this very reason, Āpastamba’s statement in the section on the observances (*vrata*) of a *snātaka*—"One should avoid looking at the sun as it rises or sets"—is consistent [with this view]. Thus, the sense is that because of the aforementioned restrictive rule (*niyama*), there is only a prohibitive negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*) in that context. He refutes the opinion of the Mīmāṃsakas, Vijñāneśvara, and others regarding that sūtra with the words "But as for... (*yattu*). There—meaning in the case of a preclusive negation (*paryudāsa*)—the word "observance" (*vrata*) and so forth refers to that which expresses such a thing. For this very reason, there is the application of the general rule; taking what is obtained from the prohibition therein, he says: "other than that" (*tad-bhinna*).

He says "of the action" (*kriyāyāḥ*) according to the maxim of the connection with the negative particle (*nañivayuktanyāya*). And [he says] "and by means of attainment" (*prāptyā ca*). When there is a desire to know its specific nature, the remainder [of the sense] is that it is because the mere action of a person is preceded by volition (*saṅkalpa*), and because of its proximity through association with that [volition]. Otherwise, the contradiction with the introductory statements made by Manu, Āśvalāyana, Āpastamba, and others would be quite evident; such is the intended meaning.

Suggesting that the daily *saṅkalpa* (resolution) at the times of sunrise and sunset mentioned in the *Tantraratna* and other texts is inconsistent, [the author] states—based precisely on Āpastamba—that "I shall not look," and so forth. How this is so is clearly explained in the *Sūcī* commentary on the *Mitākṣarā*. For this very reason, Vijñāneśvara also demonstrated the same *saṅkalpa* in accordance with the single context of the rules regarding the prohibition of eating meat and the like. This too was stated as a concession; in reality, however, that is not the case, as he says: "Furthermore," and "Where... etc.

The meaning is: "contained within its own sentence. By this, the view that "its existence must be considered because of this vow" is refuted, since that [existence] pertains to a different sentence. This being so, because there is only the connection [of the word] as it is, there is an absence of even the mere expectancy for it. Since the connection is already established, he says "expectancy"; the meaning is "that alone."

The point is this: even when there is a cognition of that [word] which has a different meaning, the expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) for it is possible by virtue of the grammatical rule "between the meanings of two nouns with the same case-ending. This is because such [expectancy], even when its object is non-existent, is frequently observed. And it is not so—that is, it is not the case that [the rule fails]. For, since there is no sublation (*bādha*) due to the absence of that [object] as its domain, and because there exists another grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*) whereby the syntactic relation (*anvaya*) occurs precisely through the relation of difference (*bheda*), that expectancy for it remains. Furthermore, in cases such as "the pot is not blue," according to the method to be explained later, there is indeed a cognition of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), but not a cognition of difference.

In that case, since the positive concomitance (*anvaya*) exists even in the absence of that [negation], and because there is no presence of the mere expectancy for it, there can also be no contrary cognition (*viparītadhī*) arising from the passion (*rati*) to be described hereafter. By this, the view of the Naiyāyikas and others is refuted, who claim that: "Where there is a sublation of the connection by identity (*abheda*) in the absence of the negative particle (*nañ*), there the negative particle produces the cognition of absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*); where there is a connection by identity in the absence of that [non-existence], there the negative particle produces the cognition of difference (*bheda*); and in those cases, the specific knowledge of the respective expectancies (*ākāṅkṣā*) and so forth is the regulating factor."

Suggesting this very point, he says: "ata eva" (for this very reason). The meaning is: "precisely because of the rule stated. However, according to the opponent's view, since "the pot is not a cloth" is equivalent [in structure], that [negation] would also apply here; such is the sense. Concluding, he says: "ata eva" (for this very reason). The meaning is as stated. For this very reason, from the sentence "Caitra does not cook," there is no cognition of "cooking by an agent other than Caitra. To state the distinction, he says: "abādhya eva" (only non-sublated). The meaning is: "only absolute negation (*atyantābhāva*) is what is conveyed by the *nañ* occurring in co-utterance with that [verb]. This is the meaning of the term *prasajya*.

—Having stated "vidhāya" (having prescribed), he says "vihita" (prescribed) to explain the meaning of the resulting specific qualification. The prescription (*vidhāna*) is not to be understood from a sentence that does not co-occur with that [negation]. He states that very distinction in the words "in the *nañ*-sūtra. By that—that is, by the statement made thus in the *Bhāṣya*—"not one beloved" is what is stated there. He explains by implication that this intends the duality of the negative particle (*nan*), saying "not for us. He does not say "na" as in the rule *yenanāprāpte*, because here the word *bahupriya* belongs to the *pātrādi* group. The reading *bahupriyata* is indeed easy to understand.

He states another example for the sake of strengthening what was previously mentioned: "nasandeha" (no doubt). He resolves the contradiction with the statement of the learned authorities: "prasajya" (having applied). Thus, the causal relationship is not exactly as [previously] stated; rather, it should be understood that in that case, the cause is the cognition produced by something other than the foot [of the verse] which denotes such a verbal root and its quality. || 1.35 ||

Having thus defined the absolute non-existence of that object, he defines difference (*bheda*) with the words "yantya" (which means "they go"). The meaning is "difference. He refutes the views of the Mīmāṃsakas and Naiyāyikas in order to demonstrate that this [difference] also pertains only to the sense of the compound and is not expressed by the word itself—introducing the phrase "yattu" (as for what...). "The meaning of the negative particle" (*nañarthaḥ*) refers to that which is denoted by it. The phrase "evaṃ tarhi" (if that is so) is to be connected with "yataḥ" (since), etc. He speaks by way of indication (*lakṣaṇayā*) with the words "paṭapadam" (the word 'cloth'). "In difference" (*bhede*) means in the sense of the negative particle. "Non-difference connection" (*abhedānvayaḥ*) means connection by way of non-difference.

[Objection: But surely this final view contradicts grammatical derivation (*vyutpatti*); therefore, he says, "non-difference" (*abhedena*). [Objection: In that case, there would be no cognition of the first [element] either; therefore, he says, "or else" (*yadvā*). The term "difference" (*bheda*) implies "qualified by its counter-correlate" (*pratiyogiviśiṣṭa*), and so forth. Thus, because there is a syntactic expectancy (*sākāṅkṣatva*), the cloth is construed with non-difference in relation to its counter-correlate, while the qualified [cloth] is so construed in relation to the jar. Therefore, the sense is that even if it were otherwise, there would be no fault whatsoever here. The opponent refutes what was stated by the partisan of a single position (*ekadeśin*): "possessing difference" (*bhedavatī*).

The meaning is that when there is a distinction [between the primary and secondary senses], since the word is capable of exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there is indication (*lakṣaṇā*) therein in order to conform with grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*). He states the refutation according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) with the words "of particles" (*nipātānām*). He states the fault mentioned by the opponent with the words "merely" (*kevala*). Having accepted the opponent's position regarding the correctness of expressions such as "the pot is not cloth" (*ghaṭaḥ paṭo na*), he says "not by non-Brahmins" (*na brāhmaṇaiḥ*). For this very reason, because a further common fault has already been demonstrated previously in the case of compounds, he says "in the case of compounds and sentences" (*samāsa-vākyayoḥ*).

"Even here"—that is, even in that [author's] sentence; by the word "even" (*api*), the inclusion of compounds is intended. For this very reason, he says: "And thus. However, it is not correct to say that the nominative case is used for the sake of grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*); because there is no such rule [to that effect], and because even the default singular number (*autsargika-ekavacana*) occurs only when there is a signifier [of plurality]. Now, if this is so, how is the cognition of difference between them well-known to all people? To this, he says: "The difference of the jar," etc.

Since the view that things co-extensive with one another are identical—such that in a single entity there is the relation of being the counter-positive of a jar in the form of difference, and the relation of being the counter-positive of "jar-ness" in the form of absolute non-existence—has been refuted, he says: "because of its co-extensiveness with that. He states that difference does not possess ultimate reality by saying: "even though," and so forth. He adds: "in the form of difference," in order to exclude such [absurd] propositions as "a jar is different from a jar."

The meaning is that it is preceded by the knowledge of those two—the locus (*āśraya*) and the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*)—which are grasped as they truly are; that is, it is preceded by the knowledge of both the counter-correlate and the locus. In this context—"therein" refers to that prior knowledge. He says "the Self" because [knowledge] exists within itself directly through its own dependence upon itself. He rescues this point by saying "another difference. "If that"—meaning, if it were the third difference—"it would be only the prior difference"—meaning, only the very first difference. He says "mutual" because, without one, there is no existence within itself through its own dependence upon itself.

This also refutes [the objection]—by the words "by the third. Since the fourth [case-ending] has the nature of being the beginning of all [suffixes], there is a mutual dependence within itself through various means; therefore, he says "due to circularity" (*cakraka*). This is clear from the rule regarding the verbal root (*dhātu*); even assuming that "ātaḥ" is a qualifier for proximity (*āntarya*), once the elision (*lopa*) is effected, the *jum* suffix does not apply. Thus, in the resolution of the difficulty in forms such as *alunvan*, the elision is sublated by the *īt* [augment], which is sublated by the state of being *ant* [suffix], which is sublated by the state of being *jus*, which is sublated by the elision, and which is sublated by the *īt* [augment] ending in *ant*, and that [elision] is sublated by the *jus*.

Having set aside the objection regarding the "wheel" (cakraka), the proponent of a partial view (ekadeśin) has resolved the issue by stating that because the substitution of *āt* and so on occurs through the status of being taught (*upadeśivadbhāva*), it is internal (*antaraṅga*), and thus the rule of elision (*lopa*) applies first. However, the problem of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) is well known from the Bhāṣya on the *vṛddhi* sūtra and other sources. To avoid this defect, he says "bhedā" (due to difference), accepting that even the fourth vowel and others are distinct. He states "antima" (final) to provide the seed for why this [mutual dependence] is a defect; for if that were the case, there would be no possibility of reaching a final resting point anywhere, so he says "paryanta" (limit).

As it has been said: "Even so, there would be an infinite regress that destroys the very root. For this very reason—that is, precisely because it is impossible—[it is stated] "in Kaiyaṭa and elsewhere. Regarding the phrase "it has been stated": the meaning is "because of that impossibility. He says "regarding objects such as jars" to show that this is not only the case here, but everywhere else as well. He establishes this with the words "otherwise," meaning: if the aforementioned method is not accepted. [He says] "due to mutual dependence," meaning: because that [unwanted consequence] would follow, and consequently, even the establishment of that [proposed solution] would be impossible.

He summarizes [the point] with the words "padārtha" (the nature of things), etc., beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore). "Mātra" means "in its entirety. The nature of indeterminability (*anirvacanīyatva*) has been stated previously. The reading is "prayojakatvam" (the state of being the cause). By the qualification "samasta" (all) and so forth, the absence of disagreement regarding the object and its cognition and linguistic usage is indicated. Furthermore, dancing [in this context] is precisely the connection with all locations. To the question, "What would be the status of those two according to your arguments, and why?", he says: "upapādayitum" (to establish). When such a question is posed, he states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): "anirvacanīya" (indeterminable), etc.

Now, one might ask: "From what [source] does reality itself arise? To this he says: "Just as..."—of the existent, namely Brahman; "thus"—in that manner; "of the non-existent"—such as a human horn and the like; "not"—indeed not. Even in the reading *naiva* (not at all), it is the same. The reason for both cases has already been stated. Regarding the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), however, he says: "only the state of being produced. Having spoken thus in general, he states the consensus of the present context in particular: "In the same way... The words *satya* (truth/reality) and *māyā* (illusion) refer to their respective attributes; between those two, he says: "difference..."—for it is indeed non-existent (*asan*).

—From contradiction: the suffix *tasi* is added to a word ending in the fifth case (ablative) to form adverbs expressing cause or reason. He states this very point with the words "by the knowledge of one" (*ekavijñānena*). The meaning is that this is also because of the previously cited scripture stating that through the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all. —And from scripture: and from the sacred texts as well.

Although the scriptures are twofold—those establishing non-difference, such as "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*), and those establishing difference, such as "The eternal among the non-eternal" (*nityo 'nityānām*)—nevertheless, by the force of the non-difference scriptures supported by the reasoning of parsimony (*lāghava*), those [scriptures on difference] merely restate the empirical difference imagined through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Furthermore, the very Śruti itself effects the rejection of difference: "There is not even the slightest diversity here"; and the passage beginning with, "He who perceives therein even the slightest difference, for him there is fear; he goes from death to death, for he sees as if there were diversity," is also intent upon censuring such a view. There is no Śruti regarding non-duality that is primarily concerned with the ultimate reality (tattva) such that, out of deference to the statements on difference, the statements on non-duality would have to be interpreted as referring to a difference characterized by non-distinction (*avibhāga*) and so forth—thereby resulting in the aforementioned pure [non-duality] being sublated.

Furthermore, what is called "non-separation" (*avibhāga*) is merely the absence of separation (*vibhāgābhāva*); it is not the opposite of conjunction (*saṃyoga*). Since the absence of separation is of the very nature of conjunction, the absence of that [conjunction]—which is the absence of separation—is even more clearly of that same nature. Consequently, because there is no conjunction in the form of an attainment preceded by non-attainment between the two all-pervading entities, Jīva and Brahman, such [non-separation] is impossible. Therefore, for eternal entities, "non-separation" is indeed synonymous with "non-difference" (*abheda*). It is precisely to indicate this that another reason, beginning with "not here" (*neha*), has been stated.

And thus, it should be understood that identity is merely superimposed, whereas difference alone is the real nature of things; even the conventional usage [of identity] is nothing but the play of ignorance (*avidyā*). He says this with the words "iti" and "alam. He establishes that same cognition in another case as well with the word "evam. There, the meaning is "that which lacks the nature of a jar" (*ghaṭatvābhāvavat*). This is by implication (*ārthāt*); for the verbal [cognition], however, is the perception of the jar itself as superimposed. By the phrase "by the non-existence of the absence," it should also be understood that it is due to the absence of the perception of that [jar], as well as the absence of the perception of anything different from it.

"—and this" means that in the compound, there is ignorance of that [distinction]. Regarding the first [point], it was explained by relying on the intention to express [the two] simultaneously in the rule: "The negative compound (*nañsamāsa*) with *tva* and *tal* takes precedence over the previous [rule]. However, that would be incoherent if the particle *eva* were included therein. Furthermore, the unreality of difference is also clear from that Bhāṣya and other such works.

Regarding the second [instance], the prohibition of a quality (*guṇapratiṣedha*): commentators have explained this in order to justify the counter-example *agārdabharathikaḥ*, which means "other than one who deserves a donkey-cart" (*gardabharatham arhati*), formed with the suffix *ṭhak* according to the rule *tadarhati*. It should not be argued that the meaning of this word is "one distinct from the agent who is fit for a donkey-cart," because even there, by implication, the absence of fitness (*arhatvābhāva*) is understood, and thus there is indeed a prohibition of a quality; just as when one says "distinct from a jar" (*ghaṭabhinnah*), it is understood that "he possesses the absence of jar-ness. This is what must be said.

In the case of *na gardabharatham arhati* ("he does not deserve a donkey-cart"), when there is a desire to express the simultaneous co-occurrence (*ekārthībhāva*) of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) and the sense of "deserving" (*arha*) with the word *gardabharatha*, the compound is formed with the derivative (*taddhita*) ending first—relying on the semantic connection (*sāmarthya*) through its constituent part—and thus results in the meaning "one who deserves a superimposed donkey-cart. This is for the purpose of avoiding the over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*) [of the rule]. Otherwise, the inconsistency of this [explanation] would be quite evident. (1.36)

He refutes the first view—that of Dīkṣita, Bhūṣaṇakāra, and others—with the words "nañ-dyotya" (expressed by the negative particle). This [view] pertains to both sentences and compounds. The meaning of *nañ* is simply difference (*bheda*). Precisely because of that [difference], it functions as a pronoun (*sarvanāma*), its predominance [is established], the determination of person (*puruṣavyavasthā*) in cases such as "you become" (*atvaṃ bhavasi*), and the restriction [of number] in cases such as "many" (*anekam*). As for the form "anekāḥ," it is correct by means of *ekaśeṣa* (retention of one from a group of identical forms). However, the [form] to be mentioned later regarding compounds is different, so there is no tautology; for the sentence and the compound have the same meaning.

For this very reason, he says: "not a jar" (*aghaṭam*). Since capacity (*sāmarthya*) exists in both cases, there is no decisive factor for selection; hence he says: "the cognition of something or other" (*yatkiñcitpratīti*). This is because it is observed that when the meaning of the subsequent word is predominant—as in "bring the king’s servant" (*rājapuruṣam ānaya*)—it is so. For this very reason—that is, because that consequence would follow in that alternative—he says: "the negative particle" (*nañ*). [The word *nañ*] connects with what precedes. By the word "only" (*mātra*), there is the exclusion of a Brāhmaṇa who is devoid of purity, proper conduct, and so forth, as well as Kṣatriyas and others. Since even that much would not suffice to exclude [such persons] if the meaning were merely the sense of the negative particle (*nañ*), he asks: "But who [is meant]? (*kaḥ punar iti*).

This question does not concern the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) alone, because it is a general rule that pronouns refer to the primary subject; therefore, he states [the answer] for that purpose: "qualified by the meaning of the negative particle" (*nañarthaviśiṣṭa*). Since it is well known that the meaning of the negative particle is simply non-existence (*abhāva*), the sense is: what is this object of the subsequent word (*uttarapadārtha*) qualified by the negative particle, which is distinct from the previously established meaning of that subsequent word? He explains the meaning indicated by the suffix *ka* and suggested by the *bahuvrīhi* compound: "ceased" (*nivṛtta*). The intention is that the suffix *kta* is used in the passive sense (*karmani*).

Since a qualifier would not be appropriate at all if the meaning of the word were entirely negated, he states the intended sense [of the sūtra] as "through similarity, etc. By "etc.," [he means] concomitance and so forth. The literal meaning of the *bhāṣya*—that one who possesses the superimposed [quality] when primary Brāhmaṇahood has ceased—is expressed by the words "nañ" (the negative particle). Thus, the purport is that the negative particle (*nañ*) serves as the indicator of the intended sense that the meaning of the subsequent member of the compound possesses its own cause for application (pravṛttinimitta) as something superimposed. He then states the literal meaning based on the predominance of the meaning of the subsequent member: "nañ."

The intended meaning (*tātparya*) here is that the negative particle (*nañ*) indicates the purport that the referent of the subsequent word (*uttarapadārtha*) possesses its own applied basis of application (*svapravṛttinimitta*). It should be understood that this very point also constitutes the predominance of the referent of the subsequent word (*uttarapadārthaprādhānya*). He refutes that very statement with the words "As for what [was said]... (*yattu*). Regarding the word "that" (*tat*): because of the reasoning already stated, and because the very thing mentioned [by him] is what is accepted in the Bhāṣyas according to the preceding and following context, there is no possibility at all of such a meaning being intended. This has been made clear in the *Uddyota*. Having [provisionally] accepted [the opponent's position], he states another fault with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*).

The "Tantrikas" refers to the Naiyāyikas and others. He speaks from the perspective of the opponent [the Mīmāṃsakas] with the words "nañ-vācya" (denoted by the negative particle). He says "yatra" (where) because there is an absence of equality regarding the well-known application and security [of the term]. An objection is raised: "In that case, the cognition of a jar or the like would not be an obstacle to [the cognition of non-existence], since it does not bring about the absence of the apprehended object"; to this he replies with "bādhā" (sublation). An objection is raised: "But for the opponents, the experience is exactly like that"; to this he replies with "ṛṣyanubhava" (the experience of the sages), because of its superior authority. He states another meaning of that [term] with "anenaiva" (by this very [statement]); the meaning is: "because it has been stated that [non-existence consists in] the counter-positive and its absence."

The sense is that there is a lack of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanā*). Furthermore, by taking the cognition of that [object] as the object of desire, it is possible for even such a sublation-cognition (*bādhadhi*) to function as an inhibitor. In reality, however, it has been stated previously that a sublation-cognition does not at all function as an inhibitor with respect to knowledge.

By this [principle], the presence and absence of the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) share the same status of logical necessity (*tulyayogakṣema*). Therefore, where the cognition of the relation of the counter-correlate presented by a given word with its substratum (*anuyogin*) occurs solely through the relation of locus and located (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), there the absence of that relation also occurs in the same way. For example, in cases such as "Caitra cooks" (*pacati caitraḥ*), since the meaning of the verbal suffix (*tiṅartha*), such as the action (*kṛti*), is related only to that which is presented by the nominative-terminated word, so too is the absence of that relation there. Having thus restated this established doctrine as the view of the ancient grammarians (*jīrṇaśābdika*), therein...
The Naiyāyika claim that "the cognition of the absence [of an object] everywhere is based on experience" is also refuted. Thus he says: "This is the direction [for further argument]. (1.37)

By means of the *siṃhāvalokana* (the lion’s glance) method, he refutes what was stated by the Mīmāṃsakas regarding the definition of sublation (*bādha*) in the subject matter already mentioned—beginning with the words "But as for... and so forth. The phrase "not in the *anuyāja*s" refers to the statement in the Āpastamba Sūtra and other texts: "One does not perform the *yeyajāmahe* [formula] in the *anuyāja*s. He explains the first fault therein with the words "For instance," and so forth. He uses the term "counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*) because that very [negation] is the counter-correlate of the absence. In this context—"therein" means in the *anuyāja*s; "and thus"—means when that [negation] is the object to be enjoined (*uddeśya*). The word "by passion" (*rāgeṇa*) [is used].

The sense is that, at times, the disease is observed to increase due to consuming those [foods] as prescribed by a physician, and because [the rule] is for the purpose of removing hunger. By the word "kvacit" (in some cases), he indicates that this is not universal, as established by the mention of the *sūta* (the smelter). He says "and in the present case": regarding the matter of the *anuyāja* offerings, all authors of Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya works maintain that there is an application from the preceding sentence, namely, "In sacrifices, one performs the *yajāmahe*. That is not so, because that [application] is as non-existent as a sky-flower. If it is asked, "In that case, how is there an application?"

"Listen: 'Ośrāvaya' has four syllables; 'Astu śrauṣaṭ' has four syllables; 'Yaja' has two syllables; 'Ye yajāmahe' has five syllables; and the *vaṣaṭ*-utterance has two syllables. This seventeen-syllabled Prajāpati indeed knows the sacrifice as it is attached [to him]. Thus, by this statement taught as an independent injunction (*anārabhyādhīta*), that [mantra] is taught; from that, its application [is established]. Having this in mind, he says: "Ye yajāmahe. Although by that [statement] everything [regarding the mantra] is obtained, nevertheless, because of the context (*prakṛtatva*), only that much is mentioned.

The meaning is that this attainment [of the fruit] occurs solely through the scripture (śāstra) fashioned from the Vedic texts (śruti) that declare it. Now, one might object: since a prohibition possesses greater force because it uproots an injunction, [the author] says: "upajīvyeti" (by virtue of being dependent). The intention is that for that reason, the [prohibition] also possesses greater force. Again, one might object: if there is an option (vikalpa), then the desired consequence is accepted, as in the case of the [optional] taking of the Soma cups; therefore, he says: "vikalpeceti. This [option] is associated with defects. Now, one might ask: how can these two be identical, given that the former has a different purpose? To this he says: "vedeti. Because in all those cases, according to the stated method, they possess the status of authoritative words (pramāṇa-śabda).

[Objection: But if this is so, then there is a contradiction with the established doctrines of the Mīmāṃsakas and others, who maintain that [the Veda] is tainted by eight defects; therefore, he says: "in whatever way. This is their intention: although the abandonment of validity (prāmāṇya) is indeed the acceptance of the absence of validity, and the acceptance of invalidity (aprāmāṇya) is also that very same thing—since it is impossible for the Veda to produce a cognition in the form of an error—there is no difference between these two. Nevertheless, when accepting the absence of validity, the seed of its being a defect is twofold: [first,] regarding validity, because of the [Veda's] being free from defects and so forth...

One [form] consists of existence (*sadbhāva*), while the other consists of non-existence (*abhāva*), namely the non-perception of validity in the absence of validity in the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the intention to express a twofold division is that the first is conditioned by the existence of a positive means of knowledge (*bhāvapramāṇa*), and the second is conditioned by the absence of a negative means of knowledge (*abhāvapramāṇa*). However, in reality, it is not proper to accept a distinction between different defects based on this much; rather, the fourfold set of defects alone is essential. It should be understood that the phrase "in whatever way" (*yathākathañcit*) indicates that the conceptual alternative (*vikalpa*) is defective in every respect.

"When there is observation" (*ālopane sati*). The phrase beginning with "firstly" (*prathamam*) and so forth [is used]. The word "only" (*mātra*) has the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). By this, there is the exclusion of that [observation] when [the object] is situated in a different location at that time. He says "error" (*bhrama*) because it is impossible for it to be a valid cognition (*pramā*) in every respect due to the possibility of a sublation (*bādhaka*). He says "cognition" (*bodha*), which means "valid cognition" (*pramā*); for this very reason, he will later say "valid cognition" and so forth. He says "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*) because it is precisely due to its being an error; the point is that validity is established only in relation to that [non-conceptual] [perception].

Revealing his intention, he refutes the aforementioned fault with the word "nanu" (but surely). He states "niṣedha" (negation) because [the object] is perceptible. With the very same intention, he says "śāstrasyaiva" (of the scripture itself). "Tādṛśa" means "consisting of error. "Pramā" refers to the absence of that [error], and so forth. If one objects "na cet" (if not), the ellipsis is "because that very thing is impossible. He explains that very point with "niṣedha. In accepting that [position], he strikes at the root with "kiñca" (furthermore); the intention is exactly as stated. "Vikalpa" means that its impossibility is precisely what is being argued.

Now, since it will be stated later that [the opponent] accepts a cognition of non-existence even when its counter-positive is not established for them, there would indeed be a fault in saying "nanu" (surely) because, in their view, the prior knowledge of the negation is impossible; therefore, he says "or else" (*yadvā*) according to that very view. "In such a case" (*tādṛśe*) means: in the object of the first observation of the scripture of negation. He says "artificial" (*āhārya*) because desire acts as the stimulant (*uttejaka*) therein. He says "it must be exactly so" (*evameva*) to show that this is necessary elsewhere as well. By this, the claim that [the counter-positive] is established through partial [cognition] is refuted.

For the "establishment of the counter-positive" (pratiyogiprasiddhi) means, by implication, the establishment of the locus where the counter-positiveness is fully resident; thus, even in your own view, there is no establishment of its subsistence therein [in the absence of such a locus], otherwise an over-extension (atiprasaṅga) would result. To include all other views held by the opponent, he says: "by all. Now, since only a non-artificial (anāhārya) cognition of the counter-positive is the cause of that [non-perception], how can the desired conclusion be established by that much alone? To this, he says: "the counter-positive..."

[Objection: But surely this is not a distinct relation of cause and effect, since it is subsumed under the general relation of cause and effect; and since that [general relation] is established in such a way as to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), [the author] says: "that which has a correlate" (*sasambandhika*). From that too, he states the general pervasion: "the qualifier" (*viśeṣaṇa*). [Objection: But in this way, there would be the undesirable consequence that a non-impelled cognition (*anāhāryajñāna*) could arise from an impelled cognition (*āhāryajñāna*); therefore, he says: "impelled" (*āhārya*). It is precisely the object of a cognition produced by a desire existing at the time of a sublation (*bādhaka*). "That"—namely, the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*).

And thus, the meaning is that there is no qualified cognition (viśiṣṭabuddhi) due to the absence of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) in that manner; for in that very way, the causal complex (*kāraṇasāmagrī*) exists. Now, one might object: "Even if perception is thus established, this does not apply to verbal cognition (*śābda*), because that [causal relation] is absent there. And so, since it is necessary to include that [relation] there to avoid over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), the aforementioned defect remains. To this he says: "The superimposed" (*āhārya*). The sense is that it is "lacking justification" (*niryuktikatvāt*). He states the opponent's view, which is what is excluded by the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "in this very way" (*evameva*): "In the lake," etc. This means: "but other modes such as these," and so forth.

[Objection: "In that case, the statement of the Naiyāyikas and others—that what is prohibited is that which has been previously established—would be inconsistent. To this he says: "prasaktam" (what is established). He states [the view] of the Arhats themselves with the words "yadi" (if). He points out another defect in their system with the words "kiñca" (furthermore). From the word "tasmāt" (therefore), it follows [the conclusion]. With the words "etadeva" (this very thing), the meaning is that they are even stronger than those [others] because of that [fact]. He says "kiñca" (furthermore) to show that the argument—that in the case of absolute sublation, the contradiction of a foundational premise (*upajīvya*) results in establishing an option (*vikalpa*), which then functions as a sublater—is not the actual basis for their strength.

— *yatra* means "in which. He states another defect with the words "avacchedaka" (delimitor). [Objection: But in that case, what is the status of that which is non-co-referential (*tadvyadhikaraṇa*)? To this he says "anuyāja" (after-sacrifice), because the second alternative is more appropriate. It has already been stated that there is no compound because it is optional (*vaikalpikatvāt*). For this very reason—namely, precisely because there is no option (*vikalpābhāvāt*) in cases involving general and particular [terms] according to the aforementioned method—otherwise, since an option would result from both the positive and negative rules, the desired result would be established by the rule for *jas* alone, making the rule "vibhāṣā jasi" redundant.

But is it not for the purpose of restriction (*niyamārtha*), since even if it serves a subsequent purpose, the status of being a "distinctive rule" (*sāmānyabhinna-sūtra*) is possible? However, without one of the two terms, the other term does not possess that status, as it is not perceived through the literal force of the words (*akṣaramaryādā*). Therefore, he says: "at the beginning" (*ādau*). By this, there is a summary of the four sūtras beginning with "the first" (*prathama*).

Although it is possible for the three rules beginning with *pūrva* and for *tayap* and *nema* to function as restrictive (*niyāmaka*) rules as before, and while the optionality (*vibhāṣā*) regarding the first case and so on remains unestablished, nevertheless, the intended meaning is that it is more appropriate for those rules to be meaningful solely by indicating the absence of such restriction through parsimony (*lāghava*). For this very reason—because there is no occasion for an option (*vikalpa*) in your view, as if it were an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)—otherwise, its inconsistency would be quite evident. (1.38)

In this context, he also cites the agreement of another commentary, stating "etadeva" (this very same thing). The meaning is that everything stated [in the verse], beginning with "tanniṣedha" (the negation of that), is intended. Regarding "sañjñitve" (in the state of being the named): this refers to the position where that [status] is not established. Regarding "vidheḥ samānaviṣayasya" (of an injunction having the same scope): [this refers to] within its domain. Regarding "vibhāṣāyām" (in the case of an option): [this refers to] within that same domain. Regarding "kṛtā": the meaning is "exhausted. This being the case, he avoids the contradiction with Jaimini by saying "api tu" (but rather). Regarding "abhyuccayaḥ" (an additional argument): even though there is no difference in terms of being a Vedic tradition (*ārṣatva*), the meaning is that it is improper according to the stated method because it lacks logical justification (*niryuktikatva*). He states this with the words "yuktisiddhā" (established by logic).

For this very reason, that [attainment of the nature of a sentence] was mentioned later; for the primary means of establishing reality is precisely the accomplishment of the nature of a sentence. For this same reason, it was mentioned earlier; thus he says: "The sentence... Therefore, although there is no option (*vikalpa*) in cases involving general and particular [means], in cases where the objects are identical, even a defective [means] must be accepted out of necessity; thus, it is not to be discarded. For this very reason, Jaimini formulated the sūtra: "But those having the same purpose should be treated as options. Regarding that, because of the context of the commentary on the sūtra beginning with *na veti*, he says otherwise: "Now, however..."—namely, "that and that... etc.

The meaning is "by those which prescribe an option. The intention is that this refers to the position where the scripture directly prescribes correctness (*sādhutva*). And thus—when there is a conflict regarding the same object and when that [conflict] is abandoned. He states that it indeed has the same object with the word "atīti" (beginning with 'ati'). Regarding "the *ṣoḍaśin*": because it is so clearly stated in the Taittirīya Śruti in the mantra and other parts. And thus, the reading "gṛhṇāti ṣoḍaśīm" should be understood; it should be noted that its occurrence in certain texts is indeed questionable. As for "by the sentence" (*vākyena*): the meaning is "by the injunctive sentence" (*vidhivākya*).

Regarding that [prohibition] of the *ṣoḍaśī* libation: as for the claim that the meaning there is not "the *ṣoḍaśī* libation is not a means to the desired end"—because that would contradict the injunction for the libation—but rather "the absence of the *ṣoḍaśī* libation is a means to the desired end," this is incorrect. For the Naiyāyikas and others maintain that when a negative particle (*nañ*) is used in conjunction with a verbal root, the syntactic relation of the case-ending applies to the absence of the root's meaning. This is not so; for it would result in a contradiction with the maxim "of suffixes" (*pratyayānām*), and because another fault will be stated later in the discussion on injunctions (*vidhi-vāda*).

Making this very point clear, he says: "In both cases as well. Therein, he states the rule for performance with the words "of those two," meaning that it applies at the very beginning of all [rites]. He says "likewise" (*evam*) to show that the acceptance of rice and other materials is also exactly so. The Smārta [rite] is mentioned first because it has fewer syllables. For this very reason—namely, because there is no other restrictive factor in those cases—he says "from the beginning," meaning from the first commencement according to one's own choice. This is clearly stated in the *Trikāṇḍamaṇḍana*, where it is said: "If any optional material has been resolved upon in a particular case..."
In its absence, that which is similar should be apprehended, but not another conceptual construct.

And thus, it should be understood that such a performance by the followers of Kātyāyana is to be considered [as valid]. The word "iti" marks the end of what has been stated. He speaks [the following] as a digression: "Therein"—meaning, in a case where the objects are distinct. "[In the case of] a prohibition"—meaning, regarding that [prohibition]. The word "paścāt" (afterwards) is to be construed with "graha" (taking/accepting). The word "utsargasya" (of the general rule) is to be construed with "abhāve" (in the absence of). The reading is "prāmāṇye" (in the validity) when knowledge has arisen previously; "aprāmāṇye" (in the invalidity) is a corrupt reading. He says "evam" (so too) because the same logic applies. "Śrutiḥ"—meaning, as the recipient. "Dadhni"—meaning, in the case of curd.

[Objection: But in that case, the subsequent sentence would be redundant; therefore, he says "Māṭhara" [in response]. In such instances, the form *tadviṣayavarjam* ends in a *ṇamul* suffix. The word *kālam* is an adverbial modifier (*kriyāviśeṣaṇa*). For the very reason stated, he says "apavāda" [etc.]. [The phrase] "of the prohibitions" has "mutually" as its ellipsis (*śeṣa*). Regarding the statement "that has been said," the meaning is: "that too has been stated by him [the author] himself. He explains the sense of the expression "as if of a different form": "at first sight" (*āpātataḥ*). [The phrase] "upon obtaining that" means: when that [distinction] is attained. For this very reason, he says "then" (*tadā*).

By the word "aneka" (many), since it is not pervaded by those characteristics, the absence of sentence-unity (*padaikavākyatā*) is established; thus he states that "sentence-unity" (*vākyaikavākyatā*) is intended here—this is what he means by saying "eka" (one). In this way, because there is no *sāvarṇya* (homogeneity) between *a* and *jña*, that [rule] applies only to others; and since the elision of *n* (*nalopa*) is considered non-existent (*asiddha*) only in the context of the prescription of *svādi* suffixes, it should be understood that it is not non-existent elsewhere. By this, the claim that "because an option would arise regarding the prohibition of the instrument (*karaṇa*), it must refer to a distinction" is incorrect.

In the case of a specific prohibition, the general rule is understood to refer to others than that [specific case], as in "curd is to be given to the Brāhmaṇas; but [it] is not to be given to Kauṇḍinya," which means [it is to be given] to those other than him. This is because the word *kauṇḍinya* is occupied by a singular number (*ekavacana*) that is contradictory [to the plural sense required]. Indeed, just as in the expression "not of the great king" (*na mahato rājñaḥ*), one does not perceive both non-difference and difference from greatness in the king—as one might in the expression "of the great kings" (*mahatāṃ rājñām*)—so it is here.

Even if one were to somehow justify [the use of the singular] on the grounds that "one is not two," this would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the lack of syntactic connection (*ananvaya*) with the phrase "to the second [person] it should be given. Thus, the argument of the Naiyāyikas is refuted, because a usage involving a second person contradicts direct experience (*dṛṣṭānubhava*). For this very reason, the Bhāṣya states only: "Let curd be given to the Brāhmaṇas; but buttermilk to Kauṇḍinya. This is what he says: "Thus, enough. (1.39)

In the Siddhānta, he says "na ca" (and not). The word "ca" (and) is out of its proper order; the connection follows the sequence [of the items]. Since that [meaning] is not obtained from the literal reading, he says "tatra" (there), meaning "in the first half-verse. He states what is appropriate, which is obtained through the conjunction of things to be understood therein: "ete" (these). The phrase "ity adhyāhāraḥ" (thus there is an ellipsis) is to be supplied. By "etena" (by this)—namely, by the possibility of the stated method—he says "natam" (bowed to). This belongs to the Vaiṣṇava [tradition]. For the word "yaḥ" (who), the word "labhyate" (is obtained) is the ellipsis. By the word "api" (also) in "ity api," [it is implied]: "Neither Viriñca, nor Bhava, nor even Śrī, who rests upon his body..."

"The cowherd women obtained that grace which bestows liberation from worldly existence"—thus says the *Bhāgavata-samuccaya*. Having indicated the intended meaning (*tātparya*) of the previous verse, he states the intended meaning here with the words "of those who have gathered together. Thus, the hidden purport (*gūḍhakūtam*) is that such a statement is made to indicate the extreme desirability [of devotion] by way of suggesting the extraordinary greatness of the worship of the Lord through devotion and so forth. He provides another internal example of difference with the words "this belongs to Maitra. He refutes the Nyāya position with the words "as for what [they say]," namely, "the possessor of ownership."

Because that [ownership] is also a subordinate element (śeṣa), and not the possessor (svāmitvavat). For if it were the possessor, since ownership does not reside in wealth and so forth, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even with respect to wealth belonging to Caitra, one could say, "This is not Caitra’s. The point is that relations such as being a qualifier (*nirūpakatva*) do not serve as the delimitors of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitānavacchedaka*). — Regarding "Caitra's": the meaning is that the cognition is that "this [wealth] is distinct from that which possesses the ownership related to Caitra; it possesses the ownership related to Maitra."

By this, the view that—because the absence of ownership (*svatvābhāva*) is understood here—the negative particle (*nañ*) expressing prohibition must necessarily connect only with the verb is refuted. [The author] says "that which resides in" (*yanniṣṭhe*) because there is no decisive reason [to prefer one interpretation over another]. "Of its meaning" (*tadarthasya*) means "of the meaning of that case-ending. Regarding the first [alternative], he says "by that very [word]"; regarding the last, he says "in that very [place]. The intention is that it is due to proximity (*pratyāsatti*). "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means if proximity is not accepted. "In oneness" (*ekatva*)—for when there is an intended meaning, such a cognition is possible, just as in the case of "one who possesses the absence of a single action" (*ekakṛtyabhāvavān*).

He states another defect with the words "kiñca" (furthermore). He says "viśeṣa" (particular) because [the meaning] is obtained even through generality (*sāmānyatas*). He says "svākāṅkṣā" (its own expectancy) because it is based on the logic of internal expectancy (*antar-aṅga-nyāya*). With the words "evaṃ ca" (and thus), there is a refutation of the Naiyāyika view. Indicating that for its sake, he says "na pacati" (he does not cook). "Tadabhāve" means in the absence of the *kṛtya* suffixes and so forth. "Sa ca" refers to what is accepted by them. According to the first method, he says "prathamānta" (ending in the nominative case); according to the second method, he says "niyamataḥ" (necessarily). "Pratyayaḥ" refers to the verbal suffix (*tiṅ-vibhakti*).

He states that even what is asserted by the Naiyāyikas and others is accepted because it is established by reason—thus he says, "The positive concomitant" (*anvayī*). Regarding absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) therein, he says, "Blue" (*nīla*). He expresses their very consensus by saying, "And this has been made resonant" (*dhvanitañcedam*). For in that context, the fault in the two definitions was given as: "Because it arises immediately after the cessation of the [preceding] entity, the definition of 'cessation' does not apply to the word. The meaning of the statement "the non-existence of phonemes" (*varṇānāmabhāvaḥ*) is "non-existence whose counter-positive is delimited by the property of being a phoneme" (*varṇatvāvacchinnapratiyogitākābhāvaḥ*); and its purpose is that such [non-existence] does not occur while the phonemes are present.

"Precisely for that reason"—namely, because it is obtainable therein from that very [source]. Although in the final system (siddhānta) there is no verbal expression of the absence of its existence, nevertheless, according to the method stated, since that [absence] is implied (ārthatvena), the proof of the absence of the universal form (*rūpasāmānya*) is also established; this is the meaning. For this very reason, it was stated in general terms. Now, one might object: "Since a particular is understood through a universal, and since the cognition derived from that [universal] is of the aggregate of absences of those particulars, there is no proof of that [universal]. To this, he says: "viśeṣa... [particular...].

The sense is that, such being the case, there would be cognition for only one person and not for all, and thus there would be no attainment [of the result]. Now, even if this were so, there would be no such conventional usage as "there is no yellow pot" in that context; for since the pot itself is the delimitor of the relatum (anvayitāvacchedaka), the cognition of the absence delimited by it would be sublated. To this he says: "the relatum" (*anvayitā*). He says "the meaning of the negative particle" (*nañartha*) because of proximity. Since the pot, like existence (*sattā*), is also an implied relatum of the meaning of the negative particle, he says: "yellow color" (*pītarūpa*). "Yellow pot" is a part of that sentence.

But if one says "delimited by the counter-positive-ness" (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*), the aforementioned fault remains; thus he says "pratīti. By the word *api*, there is a simple conjunction (*kevalasamuccaya*). Nor can it be argued that even so, because that [counter-positive-ness] resides only in the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), it is not "delimited by the delimitor of the correlate" (*anvayitāvacchedakāvacchinna*), and thus the aforementioned fault persists; therefore he says "tadavacchinna.
