This means "delimited by a property residing in the qualificand. Now, even if the qualifier exists, since the qualified (*viśiṣṭa*) is something distinct [from the mere qualifier], how can that which resides only in the [qualifier] reside in that [qualified]? To this he says "viśiṣṭaṃ ca."

Since the abundance of defects is evident if [the universal] were not distinct in every respect, he says "sarvathā" (in every respect). And thus, because it resides in the individual qualified by the qualifiers, that concomitance is delimited by the delimitor of the concomitance; therefore, when stated in that way, the aforementioned defect does not arise—this is what he means by "ata eva" (for this very reason). Now, since the apprehension of the word's denotative power (*śaktigraha*) and so forth have the same object, how can there be a cognition of a specific individual even by that much? To this he says "yathā" (just as). Thus, the rule is that the indicator has as its object the absence of [other] indicators; hence there is no defect.

In the same manner, having stated that for absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*), he states [the rule] for mutual non-existence (*anyonyābhāva*) with the word "evam" (thus). By the word "api" (also), there is an inclusion of such cases as "the pot is not a blue pot. The intention is that [negations] such as "the blue pot is not a yellow pot" certainly do occur. Because the ancient [author] cited that [case] there, he says "adharma" (unrighteousness) etc. [to provide a counter-example]. If it is objected: "Even so, let that [unrighteousness] be of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), since it too possesses that character," we say no. This is because there is a common experiential cognition (*sāmānyīya-anubhava*) that "there is some such thing which is the meaning of this sentence."

For if it were of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva*), then since the cognition of that non-existence—such as through perception—is a qualified cognition (*viśiṣṭabuddhi*), the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) as delimited by its counter-positiveness-restrictor (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*) must necessarily be a cause for that cognition in some way; thus, there would be a dependence on the cognition of the counter-positive. However, that is not possible, because at that time, the general cognition (*sāmānyajñāna*) [of the word-meanings] being present, the status of being a sentence-meaning-cognition (*vākyārthajñānatva*) cannot serve as the restrictor of counter-positiveness.

This is because only a property that does not reside in the locus of the absence (*abhāva*) and does reside in another object can serve as the delimiting factor of counter-correlativity (*pratiyogitāvacchedaka*). However, such a specific nature of knowledge (*viśeṣajñānatva*) cannot be known prior to the apprehension of the particular objects themselves. Therefore, ignorance is a positive entity (*bhāvarūpa*) that possesses an object. Indeed, there is no rule that for a cognition with an object, there must necessarily be a dependence on the knowledge of an object delimited by its delimiting factor (*viṣayatāvacchedaka*), since this is contradicted in the case of the knowledge of a desire to know (*jijñāsājñāna*).

This is because there is an experience [of the desire] "I wish to know the meaning of the scripture" conditioned by the apprehension of its general form, which arises from a desire for knowledge regarding the specific meanings of the scriptures that have not yet been understood. For this very reason, the followers of the Upaniṣads have accepted ignorance (*ajñāna*) as being superimposed upon the witness (*sākṣin*) and as being manifested by the witness; thus they have stated: "It is said elsewhere. This means "in the *Gurumañjūṣā* and other works. By the word "even" (*eva*), the exclusion of its having negation as its object is intended. The sense is that if that were the case, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*). By the same word "even," the exclusion of its being the counter-correlative (*pratiyogin*) of negation is intended.

For this very reason, he says: "non-existence" (*ābhāva*). Now, one might ask: what is the status of such expressions as "the non-existence of a jar does not exist"? To this, he says: "the non-existence of a jar. Furthermore, one might ask: even so, what is the status of passages such as "by which [something] is not reached" (*yenāprāpte*)? To this, he says: "by which" (*yena*), and by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he includes such statements as "one who is not Rudra is not a reciter of the Krama-text. He says "pertaining to the subject at hand" (*prakṛta*) because it serves as a qualifier; for particles (*nipāta*) have multiple meanings, whereas a single [word] does not, since there is no such usage. Making this very point clear, he says: "it has been said"—namely, that the negative particle (*nañ*) expresses negation.

Because the aforementioned understanding would be impossible due to the absence of two negative particles (*nañ*), and because since non-existence itself is non-existent, it is impossible for that [negation] to be conveyed by a single negative particle alone; [the author] removes the objection raised against his own position with the words "I shall crush" (*mathnāmi*). This is a statement by Bhīma in the *Veṇīsaṃvaraṇa* addressed to Sahadeva. By the word "etc. (*ādi*), there is an inclusion of such statements as: "I shall not drink the blood from Duḥśāsana’s chest," "I shall not smash Suyodhana’s thighs with my mace," and "Let the king fulfill his wager for you."

*Kākū* is a specific modification of sound. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the author intends] such statements as "there is no genus in a genus," "there is no fire in a lake," and "one does not offer oblations in the atmosphere. This is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*); however, what was stated previously was according to the system of others, so there is no contradiction. Indicating this very point, he says here as well: "by way of being fire" (*vanhitvena*). The true nature of this matter will become clear in the section on *kāraka*.

By this, the view held by some—that the negative particle (*nañ*) conveys the absence of the qualifier in every case with respect to the qualificand—is refuted; for the fault of non-comprehension arises in cases such as "there is no existence (*sattā*) in the universal (*jāti*)," because inherence in the universal is unestablished there, and because existence in the universal through any other relation does not obtain there. Thus, what was stated by the Naiyāyikas is rejected. 1.40.

Revealing the inconsistency of [the opponent's] ornaments and so forth, he states the essence of his own established doctrine (siddhānta) with the words "In this case, this... and so on. Regarding the first [point], he says "the fitness of the counter-positive" (pratiyogyatā). Regarding the second, he says "in the case of a mustard seed" (sarṣape). He refutes the first reason with "and not" (na ca). He explains the very lack of establishment [of that reason] with "in the rule concerning the negative particle" (nañ-sūtre). "Thus" (evam) means "of such a kind"; it connects with the word "is seen" (dṛśyate). By the word "if" (yadi), it is implied that there is simply no perception. "It is indicated" (sūcitam) means it is indeed indicated by Kaiyaṭa.

Having thus stated the non-perception of that which would establish [the existence of the negative particle], he states the perception of that which establishes it, beginning with "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). "Contrary" (*viparītam*) is an adverbial qualifier of the action of seeing. Regarding "if *na* were not uttered": the meaning is "if it were uttered as a subsequent element. Regarding "doubt" (*sandeha*): because there is no expressive word co-uttered [with it], the expectancy for a counter-correlate (*pratiyogi*) for the meaning in the form of cessation is not satisfied; and because it would thus lack expressiveness, the particle would simply not be employed. However, if it were expressive, there would be doubt—this is the meaning.

He states its form with the words "of what? (kasya). The meaning is: "of which word is this the word-meaning" (padārtha)? The term *padārtha* is intended here to refer to the denoted object (*abhidheya*). The point is that by using the expression "as if in doubt," the absence of a definitive determination is intended. With this very intention, it was previously stated that "for this very reason, it is not so. By this, the objection that "this must be considered because such [a view] is accepted there" is refuted. Having stated the positive concomitance (*anvaya*), he states the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) with the words "this very [point]. This was stated by Vardhamānopādhyāya. "For this very reason" means: precisely because that [word] is the cause of that [cognition].

[Objection: But in this way, a separate requirement for a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) for negation (*abhāva*) arises, which contradicts what was stated previously; therefore, he says: "As for the locus" (*ādhau*). This being so, just like a negative particle (*nañ*) not co-referential with an action or a quality, a negative particle co-referential with those [action or quality] also has only the sense of superimposition (*āropitatva*); thus, there is uniformity everywhere. With this intention, he says: "Of the superimposition" (*āropasya*). And so forth, beginning with "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). "The meaning of *nañ*" means that which is expressed by *nañ*. Regarding this established doctrine, he states the cognition produced therein: "In this case" (*atrety*). This refers to a constituent of the sentence.

By the word *api*, [the author] includes such [statements] as "not even one beloved" and so forth. By the word *ādi* in "doubt" and so forth, [the author] includes such cases as "the yellow conch does not exist. [Objection: Since a qualified existence (*viśiṣṭasattā*) is unestablished, how can there be a superimposition (*āropa*)? [Response: This has already been answered. By this very [point], the previously mentioned cognition is excluded. [Objection: But how can the cognition of non-existence, which is established by experience, be denied? [Response: To this he says: "But it is objective" (*ārthastu*). Taking that [objective non-existence] alone, the obstruction of the cognition of the counter-positive (*pratiyogijñāna*) and so forth is to be reconciled.

Or rather, it follows the method already stated. "For this very reason" means precisely because it is accepted in that manner even there; the sense is that this is according to the maxim of "the negative particle (nañ) and 'iva'. Here, he refutes the charge of being unauthoritative by saying "for this very reason," which means: simply because such a cognition occurs.

[Objection: But in this case, if there is no compound (*asamāsa*), since there would be no regulating factor (*niyāmaka*) as to where the connection with a substance (*dravya*) occurs and where the connection with an action (*kriyā*) and so forth occurs, you would face the consequence of total lack of restriction (*avyavasthā*). For me, however, when the meaning is that of difference (*bhedārthakatva*)—that is, when the meaning is superimposed (*āropitārthakatva*)—there is a connection with a substance; whereas when the meaning is absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāvārthakatva*), there is a connection with an action and so forth. Thus, a restriction is possible. Therefore, he says: "And thus" (*evañca*). This means: "and when the object is established by a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇasiddhatve*). [The word] "relation" (*saṃsarga*) is followed by "other than that" (*taditara*) and so forth. He supports what has been stated with: "This very... (*idameva*).

"Otherwise" means if it has the sense of non-existence (*abhāva*). He states that very point with the words "If... [etc.]. Nor can there be metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) there, for *nañ* would then be merely indicative; for if that were the case, it would fall under the status of a qualifier, resulting in the aforementioned fault. Indicating this, he says: "Therefore... [etc.]. The meaning of the injunction (*vidhi*) is the state of being a means to a desired end (*iṣṭasādhanatva*), whereas upon the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) with *nañ*, it is the state of being a means to an undesired end (*aniṣṭasādhanatva*); thus, the aforementioned fault does not apply. Therefore, he says: "The undesired... [etc.]. By this, the claim of the Prābhākaras—that the effect (*kārya*) has as its object the non-existence of eating *kalañja*—is also refuted.

Precisely for this reason—that is, because that very [entity] is the referent of that word—otherwise, its inconsistency would be evident. By this, it is shown that this [objection] is to be considered; for there is no evidence for the denial of the cognition of absence established by experience. Furthermore, according to the aforementioned method, a lack of systematic determination (*avyavasthā*) would result therein. It is not the case that systematic determination does not occur according to the stated method, because it is possible for that which restricts the superimposition of a relation (*saṃsarga-āropa*) to be precisely what restricts absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*).

Furthermore, since the two absences are always cognized, it is logical that the occasional nature of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) arises from the force of the desire to engage in such transactions. Moreover, after the cognition "the jar does not exist," there would be no inhibition of the cognition of the jar's presence [if the absence were merely a non-existence]. It should not be argued that for me, the first case concerns the superimposition of relation (*saṃsarga-āropa*) while the second concerns the superimposition of identity (*tādātmya-āropa*), and thus there is no fault; for it is possible that the very factor which governs the superimposition of relation and so forth is what governs that [inhibition], and because superimposition functions as a cause only in the context of ordinary perception (*laukika-pratyakṣa*).

For superimposition (*āropa*) is precisely the cognition of a relation with the locus of the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*). It is for this very reason that the *Bhāṣya* states that there is a cognition of negation (*abhāva*) in the word "not" (*na*). By this, the view expressed in the *Līlāvatyupāya* is refuted; thus it is stated in the *Bhūṣaṇa* and other works that superimposition alone is the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) in a compound, whereas in a non-compound, it is simply negation, since there is no evidence to deny the cognition of negation established by experience. Having thus restated the opinion of the modern grammarians (*navya-śābdika*), [the author] says: "That is not so, because the cognition of negation is experienced in all cases."

Furthermore, since a common property of superimposition (*āropatva*) is difficult to define even for Brahman, and because it would be unnecessarily cumbersome (*gaurava*) to treat that [Brahman] as the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*), this view is rejected. By this, the claim that "it is similarity to that" and so forth is also refuted. The Naiyāyika argument—that since the cognition of similarity and the like can be accounted for through secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*), the meaning of *nañ* must be non-existence alone—is cast aside due to the aforementioned collection of reasons. Thus, in accordance with the cognition of both the object and its absence, perception itself also has that [non-dual reality] as its object.

It does not have as its object an absence residing in the ground whose counter-positive is the existence of a jar, nor does it have as its object an absence whose counter-positive is a jar qualified by having the ground as its locus; for, since the case-factors (kārakas) are construed with the verbal root (bhāvanā), it is difficult to maintain that such a word has this kind of meaning. And thus, the superimposition of such an identity upon the ground is established. In the case of "The jar is not a cloth" as well, both [factors] are exactly like this; therefore, the superimposition of the identity of the counter-positive upon the locus is established.

For this very reason, [the reason] is unestablished in both cases. Its establishment should be understood through the following positive concomitance (*anvaya*): "That which is the case that 'there is a jar on the ground' is not so; that which is the case that 'the jar is a cloth' is not so. Thus he says: "The direction," etc. (1.41).

He states the refutation of the alternative view as expressed by Bhūṣaṇa: "As for [the claim] that..."—[this refers to] the quality residing in the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Since that very thing is the quality in that context, he says: "by the counter-correlate" (*pratiyogin*). [This applies] to valid cognition (*pramā*), and not to mere cognition (*jñāna*) in general. Thus, the stated [position] is incorrect; this is the sense. "Residing therein" (*tadgata*) means residing in the eye (*cakṣus*). The valid cognition of the bamboo occurs in that very [place].

[Objection: In that case, the causality of non-existence (*abhāva*) would necessarily follow, because its nature consists precisely in being the counter-positive (*pratiyogin*) of the existence that serves as the cause; and thus, by parsimony (*lāghava*), the quality (*guṇa*) alone would be the cause. To this he says: "When [the excellence] exists. By the word "even" (*eva*), that [non-existence] is excluded. For it is observed many times that even a cognition which is not directly contradictory may act as an obstructor (*pratibandhaka*) by destroying the cognition that produces [the effect]. He states the absence of technical "quality-ness" (*guṇatva*) in the phrase "in the case of superimposition" (*ārope*). When there is no apprehension of that [superimposition] as being produced by a quality, he says: "In perception" (*pratyakṣe*).

By this, the view that—on account of such conformity—the [negation] must be the cause in every instance because its causality is implied there, is also refuted. It should be understood that, according to the reasoning already stated, since there is no cognition of an absence unqualified by its counter-positive (*pratiyogin*), the perception "not not" would necessarily follow; therefore, even out of fear of that consequence, it cannot be the cause in that context. He refutes exactly what was stated by the *Bhūṣaṇa* and others with the words "As for what... (*yattu*). By the word "etc. (*ādi*), the violation of the grammatical rule "the meaning of two nouns [is connected by a case-ending]" (*nāmārthayoḥ*) is included. — "Different from a jar" (*ghaṭabhinnah*).

The meaning is that [the rule] applies only to those where the object of qualification (*viśeṣya*) possesses a distinction consisting of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*) which has become the prior member (*pūrvapada*). He states that the indicator (*jñāpaka*) is with reference to the general case—namely, "in the subsequent [rule]. He states its result: "for this very reason. The meaning is: precisely because of the indication of that [fact] there in a general sense. Regarding the word *sub*—it is the term *sub* that is carried over (*anuvṛtta*) from the rule "a *sub*-ending [word] and a vocative" (*subāmantrita*). "On account of the requirement"—that is, solely on account of the non-contradiction of what is expressed by the word *yoṣā*. This is the justification for this view; it has been established by [the author] himself.

As for the view set forth and established in this manner by the author of the *Bhūṣaṇa* and others—that in examples such as *atvaṃ bhavasi*, because the negative particle (*nañ*) functions as a dyotaka (indicator), the word *yuṣmad* is used with a lakṣaṇā (metaphorical indication) to mean something other than that [the person denoted by the finite verb]; and because there is no grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the meaning of *yuṣmad* (which is different in form) and the [verb], the rule for the person endings (*puruṣavyavasthā*) applies; and for this very reason, in forms like *asaḥ*, the operations of a pronoun (*sarvanāmakārya*) occur because, despite the indicated singularity, there is no status as an apasarjana (subordinate member); and for this very reason, the rule "in a compound not containing *nañ*" (*anañsamāse*) is consistent—[the author] refutes that with the words "naña iti. By the word "ādi," [words like] *yuṣmad* and so on are included.

He states another objection: "savagateti. For this very reason, even though there is the rule "guṇavacanānām," there is no fault, because that [rule] has a different scope. [Objection: But if this is so, what is the status of the expression "patantyaneke"? To this he says: "patantīti. [Objection: It is established by means of *ekaśeṣa* (the retention of one from several); since that has already been stated by them in that context, he says: "ekenaiva. By the word "aneka. The same applies further on as well. Non-attainment is the reason for its rejection. "Pṛthak": this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound.

This is precisely the point: the defect consisting in the non-establishment of the stated rule cannot be avoided in any other way. Regarding the statement "aneka" and so forth, he says "superimposition" (*āropa*), because unity is superimposed upon many; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Bhāṣya—this is the intended meaning. By this, the argument of the Naiyāyikas—and likewise that of others—is refuted, which claims that since the rule of primacy for the first member does not exist in a *tatpuruṣa* compound, the operation of a pronoun (*sarvanāma-kārya*) is established in cases such as *asaḥ* by the aforementioned indicator (*jñāpaka*), and therefore it is logical that the negative particle (*nañ*) has the meaning of non-existence (*abhāva*).

Therefore, it should be understood that the first position mentioned is indeed more reasonable. He states this with the words "this is the direction. He provides a qualification with the words "not anywhere. He states the proof for this with the words "for this very reason," meaning: precisely because it possesses the aforementioned sense. He states the result of the mention of "prior" in the passage beginning with "not anywhere," etc. Regarding the fault of producing a contradictory cognition (*viruddhamatikṛttva*), he states what is included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) as an example cited by Prakāśa and others, namely: "the garland" (*srajam*). Now, one might ask: why is this contradictory? To this he says: "water," etc.

The intended meaning may indeed be understood here even through a reversal of the sequence; however, because it produces a contrary cognition instantaneously, it is considered defective. For this very reason, the purport is that this constitutes an occasional defect (*anityadoṣa*). Thus concludes the examination of the meaning of the negative particle (*nañ*). 1.42.

Now, he explains the meaning of the particle *eva* with the words "the word *eva*. As for what the ancient Naiyāyikas maintain—that the meaning of *eva* consists of the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*), the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*), and the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*)—among these, the first [exclusion of absolute non-connection] is the exclusion of that which is qualified by an absence characterized by the absence of pervasion of the delimitor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka*). And this occurs in cases where *eva* is connected to a verb; for in such a cognition, the knowledge of that specific word-order is the cause.

And thus, in cases such as "the lotus is indeed blue," there arises a cognition such as: "the lotus possesses the locus-hood of blueness, which is qualified by the absence of the absence of being a pervader of lotus-ness. The second [type of exclusion] is the exclusion of the absence of identity (*tādātmyābhāvavyavaccheda*). And that occurs in instances where [the particle *eva*] is connected with the qualifier, because the knowledge of that [exclusion] is the cause for the cognition thereof. Thus, in cases such as "the conch is indeed white," there arises a cognition such as: "the conch possesses the exclusion of the absence of identity with whiteness. The final [type of exclusion] is the exclusion of identity with anything else (*anyatādātmyādivyavaccheda*).

And that [negation] is indeed connected with the qualificand (viśeṣya), because the knowledge of that [negation] is the cause for the cognition of it. Thus, in cases such as "Pārtha alone is the archer," the resulting cognition is "Pārtha is non-different from the archer who possesses the absence of identity with anyone other than Pārtha."

That is not so; for, according to the literal limits of the words, that meaning is not obtained there, as in the case of "knowledge grasps the object," where only the exclusion of non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*) is perceived. Furthermore, in cases such as "this person cooks indeed," the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) is perceived. In the first instance, there is no perception of the absolute exclusion of connection (*atyantāyogavyavaccheda*) everywhere, because—according to the reasoning stated previously—the nature of being a lotus (*sarojatva*) and so forth lacks the status of being a delimitor of the correlate (*anvayitāvacchedaka*).

In expressions such as "the face is similar only to Caitra," even regarding the second object (the non-Caitra), there is a cognition of the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*); therefore, such a restriction is difficult to maintain. Furthermore, according to the method previously stated, this is because the absence of an absence is a positive existence. If, however, it is argued that "this is a general rule (*utsarga*), but not an absolute restriction (*niyama*)," and that consequently—according to experience and the intended meaning (*tātparya*)—there may be a different understanding in those cases because the knowledge of the respective sequence (*ānupūrvī*) serves as the cause [of that specific understanding], and thus the aforementioned fault does not apply; even then, the entire remaining host of faults persists.

Furthermore, the assumption of multiple specific powers would result in a greater complexity that is indeed difficult to avoid. Having all this in mind, he says: "In the case of restriction" (*avadhāraṇa*). This means "in the cases previously mentioned. Regarding the phrase "it is so everywhere," he says "from this very [source]" (*asmādeva*) because that statement would otherwise be incomplete; the meaning is "from the aforementioned Vārttika. Otherwise, since the illustrative examples (*lakṣya*) would be impossible, the inconsistency would be obvious. What is included by the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) will become clear immediately below. And "that"—namely, the specific cognition (*jñānaviśeṣa*).

Since it is necessary for that [word] to function as a qualifier according to the method previously stated, he says: "dyotya" (to be indicated). Regarding "sameti" (with the word *sama*): this refers to what precedes it. And since that [word] does not have a single form, in order to explain its nature in its entirety by reversing the previously mentioned sequence, he first speaks regarding non-difference (*abheda*) as connected with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), saying: "tacceti" (and that). This means "and the restriction. Regarding "svaṃ pārthaḥ" (Pārtha himself): regarding "sameti," the meaning is "in the form of an archer co-referential with Pārtha. Now, one might ask: how can there be a rejection of well-known cognition? To this he says: "tadanya-" (other than that).

For this very reason, he states that in your view there is a clear contradiction with the usage of poets, whereas in my view there is not—beginning with the verse "kācit" (A certain woman...). Now, one might object: "In such cases as 'In that matter, Pārtha alone is the archer, none other,' since the meaning is obtained through the aforementioned method, there would be the fault of redundancy for expressions such as 'none other'. To this he replies: "ārthyā" (implied). This means "by suggestion" (*vyañjanayā*). The sense is that such a meaning is understood precisely through the power of the word itself (*śabdamaryādayā*). Having provisionally accepted this, he says "lavaṇam eva" (it is indeed salt), asserting that in reality even that [suggestion] does not exist.

The meaning is that particles (*nipāta*) have multiple significations. This very point is what was previously included under the term "and so forth" (*ādi*). However, in this context, the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) does not apply, because it would be contradicted and because the usage is intended to convey a different purport (*tātparya*). The same applies hereafter. Regarding "where indeed" (*kveva*): when this is said, there arises the understanding that, due to the confusion of locations and other factors, there is no possibility for you to eat. Regarding "of that"—namely, of *eva*—he speaks concerning the subject of difference (*bheda*) in that very context: "in the conch" (*śaṅkhe*). "Its own"—namely, its whiteness (*pāṇḍuratva*). Regarding "together" (*sama*): [the commentary continues].

The meaning is: "the referent of the word *śaṅkha* (conch) as co-occurring with the term *pāṇḍuratva* (whiteness). Regarding the phrase "in the conch" (*śaṅkhe*), it begins with "since," etc. The usage *aneka* is like [the usage of] *asu-vat*. The cognition is that whiteness is the qualificand of the restriction, having the conch as its locus. Now, regarding the second case, he says: "In the conch. Its own form is white (*pāṇḍura*). The meaning is: "the referent of the word *śaṅkha* as co-occurring with the term *pāṇḍura*, which is apprehended as not being the locus of that [whiteness]. [This refers to] the manner of restriction.

[Bahuvrīhi: It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound, because it is employed toward one who possesses the cognition that "the conch has many colors. Regarding the third [type], he says: "action" (*kriyā*). Likewise, there is laughter (*hāsa*). And he says: "by means of cognition" (*buddhyā*), meaning that the other [laughter] is indeed of a specific form due to the force of context and so forth; the meaning is that it is a referent (*padārtha*) in the form of Caitra, which is co-occurrent with an action grasped as not being its locus. The understanding is: "the act of laughing is the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) whose agent is non-different from Caitra. In that very same case, he states another [example] by way of distinction: "blue" (*nīlam*).

In this context, since the qualifier would be redundant if "pure" were taken alone, he says: "blue. The meaning is that it has as its qualifier a lotus which, through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), is not the locus of the absence of that [blueness], being mentioned in co-utterance with "blue garment. The resulting cognition is: "The act of becoming, which is the qualificandum of the restriction, has as its agent a lotus non-different from blue. He says "cognition" because there is yet another distinction even in that very case.

In the view of the opponent (*paramata*), in sentences such as "the touch is indeed cold" (*śīta eva*), the connection must be stated as belonging to that which possesses the exclusion of identity with what is other than cold (*śītānyātādātmyavyavacchedavataḥ*), delimited by the nature of touch (*sparśatva*) which delimits the agency of existence (*sattākartṛtā*) residing in a substratum such as water (*jalādyadhikaraṇaka*). This is due to the diversity of linguistic convention (*vyutpattivaicitryāt*); otherwise, since the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) connected with that which is co-uttered (*samabhivyāhṛta*) is perceived only in relation to that very thing with which it is connected, there would be the following unintended consequence: just as in the case of "smell [is] non-existent in things other than earth" (*gandhe pṛthivyanyāvṛttitva*), there would be an implied meaning (*arthāpatti*) that "the touch residing in water is possessed of the exclusion of identity with what is other than cold," and thus the touch would be cold (*śīta eva sparśaḥ*).

Pointing out another complication by indicating that the same fault would apply even to the term *dravye* (in a substance), he states the second qualification as "only cold" (*śīta eva*). [The full expression is] "coldness is inherent," and so forth. The meaning is: a water-substance expressed in co-reference with a cold touch that does not have that [coldness] as its substratum. The resulting cognition is: "the touch, which is non-different from cold, is the object of determination residing in water."

According to the opponent's view, in expressions such as *caitreṇaivaitayā* ("by Caitra alone with this [action]"), there is—due to the peculiarity of linguistic convention—a cognition of the agent as being one who lacks identity with anyone other than Caitra, delimited by the property of being an action associated with a causal factor other than himself; thus, even though the two cases are similar, such a usage does not occur in the other instance. Indicating this distinction regarding the object-terminations (*karmapratyaya*), he says: "by Caitra alone. To explain that it applies elsewhere, he says: "in all cases" (*sakala*). This means "all those present in the mind"; the meaning is "not by another," as indicated by the counter-references such as "not by another."

The cognition is: "This perception has Caitra as its agent, whose object is not restricted [to this alone], and which has this [jar] as its object. According to the opponent's view, in cases such as "earthness exists in the jar," the word "occurring-in-earth" (*pṛthivīvṛtti*) must be understood as meaning "occurring in that which does not possess identity with anything other than earth," for that is what captures the intended meaning (*tātparya*). This is because, in a compound, it is impossible for the subordinate member (*upasarjana*), the referent of the word "earth," to undergo syntactic connection (*anvaya*). Alternatively, one would have to accept a peculiar complexity in the linguistic rule (*vyutpatti-vaicitrya*). Indicating this, he says specifically regarding that very point: "the cognition having jar-ness as its qualificand" (*ghaṭatvaviśeṣyakajñāna*).

The meaning is that [the cognition] has as its qualificandum (viśeṣya) the category "pot-ness" (ghaṭatva), which is mentioned in grammatical coordination with "residing in earth," and is apprehended as not residing in that [earth]. The reading "having pot-ness as its qualifier" (ghaṭatvaprakāraka) is a corruption. Since "residing in earth" is well-established in pot-ness, the statement is not addressed to one who already possesses the knowledge that "it does not reside there" (in pot-ness); rather, it is addressed only to one who possesses the knowledge that it resides in something else. Thus, he says "not residing in another" (nānyavṛtti) so that it is not directed toward someone for whom it is already known that "it does not reside in earth. This is what is meant by "restriction" (avadhāraṇa).

The phrase beginning with "pṛthivītvasāmānādhikaraṇyena" [is used]. According to the opponent's view, although the word *ṛtau* is syntactically connected to the action, it functions to exclude non-connection (*ayogavyavaccheda*). Thus, the understanding would be that the object of the injunction is the absence of the absence of one's own act of approaching one's wife during her fertile period (*ṛtu-kālādhikaraṇaka-bhāryākarmaka-svakartṛka-gamanābhāvābhāvaḥ*). However, this results in a violation of the grammatical rule that suffixes have as their primary referent the qualificand (*viśeṣya*) of the meaning, and it is also beset by the previously mentioned defects. Therefore, he says: "*ṛtau*". The word *sva* is for clarity; it refers to one's own act of approaching.

The meaning is that the agentive factor (*kartṛ-kāraka*) is understood as not having that [prohibition] as its basis. Regarding "his own wife": it should also be understood as "having him as the agent. Regarding "of that"—this refers to the act of approaching. Now, what is the proof for its being such? To this he says: "Of the desired," with the words "standing in proximity" to be supplied. By that—namely, by hearing of the fault in not approaching. Therefore, even when one approaches during a single *ṛtu*, there is an inclination to do so during other *ṛtus* as well, in order to avoid transgression (*pratyavāya*).

And thus, it should be understood that the absence of approaching one's wife [for intercourse] during her fertile period—residing in the agent through the relation of agency—is the cause of demerit (*pratyavāya*). Now, one might object: "In this way, since there are multiple restrictive determinations (*avadhāraṇa*), would it not follow here too that one must postulate multiple potencies (*śakti*)? To this, he says: "entirely" (*sakala*). Its establishment occurs precisely by the method previously stated. He states it according to the view of others: "indivisible" (*akhaṇḍopā*).

Even in an example where the enumeration is not explicitly stated, because the cognition occurs in that very same manner within that specific co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), he says "five times five" (*pañcapañca*) to indicate "in this very way. The meaning is "even in cases such as these. Because [the definition] would otherwise be over-extensive (*atiprasakta*), he says "of the intellect" (*buddhistha*) in order to delimit it by means of "otherness" (*itaratva*). Both are qualifiers of "fiveness" (*pañcatva*). The meaning is "that form of number. "Self" (*sva*) refers to such fiveness.

The meaning is: that which has as its qualifier an object denoted by the word "edible" (bhakṣya) mentioned alongside the "five five-nailed animals," wherein the state of being edible is not connected to those [animals]. Now, one might object: even if their status [as inedible] is obtained through the sense of the text, there is no cessation of what is prompted by passion (rāga); thus, that [eating] would indeed occur, which is undesirable. To this, he says "eva" (only). This refers to the case where that [prohibition] is employed. He states the absence of that [prohibition] with the words "lakṣaṇā" (indication): passion is the means of proof (pramāṇa) that prompts [the action]. [This refers to] the eating of what has been made known [by the prohibition]. He says "tadatirikta" (other than that) [to mean] other than that [passion].

The meaning is: "those five types of five-clawed animals [that are permitted]. Otherwise, if it were an original injunction (*apūrva-vidhi*) for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*), there would be the consequence of requiring an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for its non-performance; furthermore, the statement regarding the eating of other [forbidden] things would be inconsistent. This is the intended sense, which he expresses by the words "iṣṭa" (desired) and so forth. 1.43.

He refutes the statement of the modern Naiyāyikas with the words "yattu" (as for what [they say]). The word "sarvatra" (in all cases) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Vyavacchedaḥ" (exclusion) refers to that very thing. By means of that, there is the exclusion of both; thus, unlike that [other view], there is no assumption of multiple powers. Furthermore, "anyayoga" (connection with another) is merely a relation with something else.

And thus, in cases such as "the lotus is blue" (*nīlaṃ sarojam*), through the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the verb in its substratum, the exclusion of otherness from the act of becoming blue is cognized as being in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the state of being a lotus. In cases such as "the conch is white indeed" (*śaṅkhaḥ pāṇḍura eva*), there is the cognition of the exclusion of otherness from being white, delimited by the state of being a conch. In cases such as "Pārtha alone [is the archer]," there is the cognition of the exclusion of otherness from being Pārtha, delimited by the state of being an archer. In the case of "at the proper season," there is the cognition of the exclusion of otherness from such an act of going.

In expressions such as "on the earth," the intended meaning is the cognition of the exclusion of occurrence on anything other than earth, as in the case of "fragrance" and so forth. This is what he states: "On the earth" and "in fragrance. For this very reason, it is not the case that [fragrance] exists only on the earth, like space, because [space] does not occur [there]. There is no fault here, because when a certain relation is cognized through the co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*) of a particular word, the cognition of the exclusion of its connection with anything else arises from that same co-occurrence.

[Objection: But how can the earth, which is presented as a qualifier of the meaning of the locative case, be construed with a different object, given that it is unestablished (avyutpanna) for that which is presented as a qualifier of one thing to be construed with another? To this, he says: "vibhakti... The sense is that in such cases, the rule governing that [construal] is restricted.

According to the opinion of the Prācīnas (the Easterners), however, this [mention of *eva*] is not for the sake of its being a dyotaka (indicator), because it is sufficient for the understanding that "odor resides in that which lacks identity with anything other than earth"—where the word "earth" refers by *lakṣaṇā* (secondary indication) to that which possesses identity with something other than earth, and the locative case (*saptamī*) serves to indicate grammatical correctness. It is precisely to avoid this meaning that there is the mention of *eva*; for [the desired meaning] is established simply by the understanding that "odor resides in that which lacks identity with anything other than earth," delimited by the property that delimits the referent of the word co-occurring [with "earth"].

The reason for this writing is precisely due to the force of the meaning itself. It should be understood that, according to the method already stated, there is no [restriction] such as "only residing in earth," because the cognition of its subsistence is understood as being delimited by the qualifiers of the meanings of the words co-uttered with it. He states a defect common to the views of the ancients: "aneka... (in the case of multiple...). There—in the view of the ancients—it has been explained how it is in cases such as "only cold" and so forth.

In cases such as "Pārtha alone," there is a variety of grammatical rules (vyutpatti) stated in the Navya school, based on the cognition: "He is non-different from an archer and possesses the absence of identity with anyone other than Pārtha. I suspect that in cases such as "The conch is white indeed," the same applies, because the cognition is: "The conch is a locus of whiteness and possesses the absence of identity with anything other than what is white."

Even in cases such as "The conch is indeed white," there is the cognition that "the conch is that which possesses the absence of identity with whiteness, delimited by the property of being a conch" (śaṅkhatvāvacchedena); likewise, in cases such as "The lotus is indeed blue," the aforementioned cognition occurs, which is quite clear. Thus, in both views, whether one posits distinct powers (*bhinna-śakti*) for the exclusion of connection with others (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) and so forth regarding words like "other" (*anya*), or whether one posits a single qualified power (*viśiṣṭa-śakti*), there is an equal degree of excessive complexity (*gaurava*).

It should be understood that, as in the case of "different from a jar" (*ghaṭād anya*) and so forth, there is a relation with a single part [of the meaning], and that the mutual relation among the objects presented by a single word also occurs due to the variety of linguistic conventions (*vyutpatti*). By this, the claim of the Neo-Naiyāyikas—that there is a primary denotative power (*śakti*) in exclusion (*vyavaccheda*) and a secondary indicative power (*lakṣaṇā*) elsewhere—is also refuted. He states another common fault: "such... [tādṛśa]. Now, one might argue that here, as in "see the jars" (*ghaṭān paśya*), the matter is resolved through the principle of the stem-repetition (*prātipadika-tantra*); therefore, he says: "the case-ending" (*vibhaktim*).

The point here is that while [the property] exists there [in the earth] as an object of simultaneous predication (*sahavivakṣā*), it does not do so here [in the definition] because it is not an object of simultaneous predication. By this, the redundancy (*gaurava*) resulting from non-repetition is also indicated in this view. This is said while granting the point for the sake of argument; in reality, however, he says "earth" etc., meaning that since there is no fruit [to such a definition], it does not exist at all. [The phrase] "in smell" etc. refers to perception as another means of knowledge (*mānāntara*). Thus, the understanding occurs according to the stated method: "smell possesses subsistence in the earth, which is the object of the restriction."

And the restriction (*avadhāraṇa*) consists of a cognition having as its qualificandum the "fragrance" mentioned in grammatical co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhṛta*), which is grasped by way of exclusion from other things such as earth. Thus, the view that in examples such as *pārtha eva dhanurdharaḥ* (Pārtha alone is the archer), the understanding is of the form "Pārtha is the archer; one other than Pārtha is not the archer," is also refuted by these four defects. For this very reason—because [the restriction] is obtained there [in the word *eva*] from that [word] itself—he says, "only through implication (*ārthyeva*)," since, according to the stated method, it cannot be verbal (*śābda*). And thus—"in its being implied"—means when it is an object of implication.

By the word *api* (also), there is a conjunction with the phrase "the five not mentioned therein. He states its nature: "And that," meaning negation. [Objection: But if this were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (*apatti*) of the elimination of verbal cognition (*śābdī*) in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). However, in the opponent's view (*paramata*), this fault does not arise, because the distinction between existence and non-existence is possible even for that [negation]. Therefore, he says: "But the verbal..."—meaning "only in such cases as" etc. By the word "etc.," [examples] such as "What is the ornament? are included. He states what is to be conjoined by the word *api*: "the five."—"The additional... [is the meaning].

The meaning is that because restating what has already been established would be purposeless, it [the word] functions there through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Now, one might object: "But even so, there is no proof for a secondary indication based on the non-existence of that [restriction] and its inclusion within the definition; how then can there be such an exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*)? To this he says: "For this very reason. The sense is that in this treatise, the term *niyama* (restriction) generally denotes *parisaṃkhyā* (exclusion). He explains this with the words: "In the absence of that," meaning: by accepting the sense in that manner even when that [restriction] is absent. He states that very point with: "For by that," meaning: by the explanation of the *Bhāṣya*.

The Mīmāṃsakas, the authors of the Dharmaśāstras, and others, however, claim that this is a verbal *parisaṅkhyā* (exclusive specification); he refutes their view with the words "As for that which... (*yattu*). He states the fault in rules such as "when *yuṣmad* is the upapada" (*yuṣmadyupapade*) with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). The word "since" (*yataḥ*) is to be supplied. In this way—just so—in that case of presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*), there is the quality of being non-verbal (*aśābdatva*). Because a restrictive rule (*niyama-śāstra*) has the purpose of negation (*niṣedha*), he says "scriptural" (*śāstrīya*). With the question "What? (*kim...*) [he asks]: "In solitude, what pair of feet of the wearer of the Kaustubha gem is to be meditated upon?"

What is to be propitiated? What is meritorious? And what is desirable? [The answer is] compassion (karuṇā), through attachment to which the mind becomes capable of infinite liberation; this is the remainder [of the verse]. Regarding the word "ārtha" (implied): it begins with "praśnapūrvaka" (preceded by a question) and so forth. The same applies further on. By the word "ādi" (and so forth), lamps and other such things are included. "For this very reason"—namely, because it is implied (ārthatvāt). "What is the ornament? and so forth.

"What is the deed performed by the noble? A well-done action, not a fault. What is the unimpeded eye? Intellect, not the physical organ. Who other than you knows how to distinguish between the real and the unreal?"—this is the remainder [of the verse]. "It has been cited"—the meaning is that it was cited by the author of the *Prakāśa* and others. In that context, pointing out even the contradiction with the *Bhāṣya*, he says: "By the *Bhāṣya*. "Done" means "desired. In the phrase "itītītyatrāha," the word "atrāha" (here he says) is to be construed. "Therein"—meaning, between those two. "That"—meaning, its employment.

He states how the point under discussion is obtained from the commentary (*bhāṣya*): "In this [context]" (*atre*). The meaning is "in the *bhāṣya*. This is the intended sense: it is clear in works such as the *Prakāśa* that for a word there are three functions (*vṛtti*), whereas for a meaning there is only suggestiveness (*vyañjakatva*). Thus, where the *bhāṣya* introduces the subject of words, only denotability (*śakyatva*) is intended; however, here, because the subject introduced is meaning, it is suggestiveness alone. And so, even in the absence of the word "is understood" (*gamyate*), since that [meaning] is obtained, its perception is made clear by the mention of that [suggestiveness].

By this, it is refuted that the *Bhāṣya* located in the *Vipratiṣedha-sūtra* is contradictory. He states another defect with the words "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). Regarding the phrase "definition" (*lakṣaṇa*), it refers to the two words and so forth. The meaning is that, since the understanding of a different object from a single meaning occurs in the case of the example (*dṛṣṭānta*)—that which is to be established in the subject under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*)—it is not so [established] through the example. He states the agreement in his own system with the word "necessarily" (*niyamena*). He says "composition" (*sandarbha*) because it is stated as such in the case of the subject under discussion.

With the intention that "instruction" (*upadeśa*) means the first pronunciation, he says: "by another word" (*śabdāntareṇa*). [Objection: But why was it not stated exactly in that way? To this he replies: "by implication" (*arthataḥ*). This implies that it is not only here, but everywhere regarding that subject. He says: "of such a kind" (*īdṛśa*); the meaning is: that which makes known something whose non-attainment is by word, but whose attainment is by implication. The word "in the world" (*loke*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. 1.44.

To establish his own stated definition with greater brevity, he states the established conclusion (*siddhāntatva*) with the words "others, however" (*pare tu*). From the "indicative mark" (*liṅga*)—that is, from the capacity to manifest the mere rope. He says "unprecedented" (*apūrva*) because it is not obtained from another word; the sense is that it is intended exactly so in its definition. "He takes up" (*ādatte*) is in the *leṭ* (subjunctive) mood; the meaning is that one should take it up with this mantra. "Determined" (*niścita*) means that which makes known a determined object. Having thus set forth the opinion of Bhaṭṭa, he also sets forth the consensus of Mammaṭa and others with the words "the rhetoricians" (*ālaṅkārikāḥ*).

The word "they say" (*āhuḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "Sexual intercourse" (*vyavāyaḥ*) means approaching a beautiful woman. Regarding the phrase "one should serve a *mud*": thus says the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*: "One should hire a Brāhmaṇa who will drink the remnants; if one does not find a Brāhmaṇa, one should pour it into an anthill; that is the expiation in that case. For a Brāhmaṇa is indeed the drinker of the remnants when he has offered the oblation. He says "by passion" (*rāgataḥ*) because there is no obligation of necessity (*nityatva*) in the form of an absence of sin (*pratyavāya*) for its non-performance. He says "a living being" (*prāṇī*) because of the natural force of that statement.

The sense is that otherwise, since animals would not be subject to injunctions and prohibitions, there would be no engagement with them. He says "ataḥ" (therefore) to indicate this. The word "hi" here has the sense of "for. To exclude the etymological meaning, he says "vivāha" (marriage). Regarding "teṣu"—meaning in the case of sexual intercourse, meat, and liquor—"viśeṣeṇa śabdataḥ avasthitiḥ prāpaṇam" (establishment or attainment specifically by means of words) is the literal meaning of the term; thus he says "teṣu. Śrīdharasvāmī’s statement that "vyavasthā" means "niyama" (restriction) is refuted by the phrase "rāgataḥ" (by way of passion), which yields the following result.

It indicates the state of being fulfilled—*āsu*, meaning "in those services. Now, one might object that in this view there is no such instruction, which would contradict the *Bhāṣya*; therefore, he says, "even in the *Bhāṣya*. One might further object that hearing of a fault [for non-performance] is redundant, since the sin of omission (*pratyavāya*) is obtained simply by virtue of the injunction; therefore, he says, "having bathed after her menses" (*ṛtusnātām*). And thus—by the re-enactment of what was already established, there is the exclusion of other [options]. For this very reason—due to the lack of a determining factor (*vinigamanā*), it is because of the intended meaning (*tātparya*) alone in all cases. Regarding the first [point], he says in order: "of the householder" (*gṛhasthasya*).

Regarding the second [verse], he says: "one who is not married. Regarding the third, he says: "during her season" (*ṛtau*). And it has been stated—indeed, it has been said—that because the phrase "in the Smṛtis" connects with both [cases], there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*). By this, the statement of those learned in logic, such as Bhāruci, Viśvarūpa, Vijñāneśvara, and others—who claim that in the case of "during her season," a restrictive rule (*niyama*) alone is appropriate and not an exclusive specification (*parisaṃkhyā*)—is refuted; this is clear from my commentary on the *Mitākṣarā* titled *Lakṣmī*.

[Objection: But if this is so, since it does not fall under the definition of verbal cognition (*śābda*) as stated by the Mīmāṃsakas, how can it possess that status? To this he says: "And in that case" (*tatra ca*). The intention is that this is a definition common to both [verbal and inferential knowledge], and not of that [verbal cognition] alone. Here he also cites Kaiyaṭa’s agreement: "of *ijādi*" (*ijādeḥ*). Because it shares the result of excluding the other, even what is called "exclusive specification" (*parisaṃkhyā*) is treated by the term "restriction" (*niyama*) in this system; hence he says: "restriction" (*niyama*). He cites another passage from Kaiyaṭa: "of which" (*yasya*). The phrase "Kaiyaṭa said" (*āha*) is to be supplied here.

He also cites the consensus of the Bhāṣya with the words "anupara" (and so on). There—"tatra" means "from that. Regarding the phrase "when the fruit of the action accrues to the agent"—the word "hi" (since) is to be understood as the ellipsis. By stating the non-difference between the two [the agent and the fruit], having thus established the principle in the case of non-co-occurrence (*asamabhivyāhāra*), he says "even the word 'eva'" (*evakāro’pi*) to show that it is exactly the same even in the case of co-occurrence (*samabhivyāhāra*), based on the previously cited Bhāṣya. "Tadartha" means "for that purpose," i.e., for the exclusion of other resulting fruits. He states precisely what is excluded by the particle "va": "not however" (*na tu*). The particle "api" is used to conjoin the absence of those two.

[Objection: But if this is so, since the threefold suggestiveness mentioned previously would be impossible, how can it be stated as such? To this he says: "That" (*tad*). The meaning is "precisely" (*eva*). Regarding "the state of being a means of knowledge" (*mānatvam*): the reading is "the state of being a suggester" (*dyotakatvam*). Since that object [is understood] in that way, for that very reason there is that suggestiveness; this is the meaning. The sense is that one illustrative example has been stated for the phrase "in the same way, others are to be inferred," and this is the second. [Objection: But if it were thus, in the absence of that [suggestive power], there would be no cognition of it. To this he says: "Precisely" (*eva*). For this very reason, it was stated there [in the *Vivaraṇa*] that "[it is] clearly [so]."

[Objection: But in this way, there would be the consequence of the destruction of verbal cognition (*śābdabodha*); therefore, he states what was previously mentioned: "śābdeti. He states the very reason for this that was mentioned before: "yuṣmadīti. [Note: The reading is *na hi sūcitam*. [Objection: It is undisputed that there are three defects in a restrictive injunction (*parisaṃkhyā*); among them, the first two defects reside in the words (*pada*), while the last resides in the meaning (*artha*). And that is possible only in the view that maintains the secondary signification (*lakṣaṇā*) of the two words, not here; thus, these two positions have not been stated. To this, he says: "pakṣadvaye 'pi" (even in both positions).

Demonstrating the removal of the restriction (*niyamodātaharaṇa*), he says: "Now then" (*nanu*). Regarding "from cognition" (*pratīteḥ*): because when there is such a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*), there is understanding exactly in that manner. By "and so forth" (*ādi*), [actions such as] massaging the feet are included. Regarding "by its own force" (*svarasataḥ*): the meaning is "by its very nature. Regarding "the sublation of what is established" (*klṛptabādha*): this is a *bahuvrīhi* compound. The same applies hereafter. It should be understood that with this very intention, the logicians (*nyāyavidaḥ*) and others have stated that it is indeed a restriction (*niyama*) in that context.

[Objection: "But surely, even if this [act] such as scratching with the nails is impossible, let it be a purely original injunction (*apūrvavidhi*); how then can it be a restrictive injunction (*niyama*)? To this he says: "Because it is already established" (*klṛpta*). The phrase "in cases such as 'one threshes the rice-grains'" (*vrīhīnavahanti*) is to be supplied. Although even in this case where there is simplicity (*lāghava*), the heaviness of postulating three defects still exists, nevertheless, the sense is that in that context it remains exactly so because of compliance with the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). However, in this system (*śāstra*), since both injunction and restriction are possible, the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that the injunction alone is superior; therefore, one should understand that there is a contradiction with that [conclusion].

Suggesting this very point, he says: "from this" (*asmāt*). He states them in their proper order: "beginning with activity" (*pravṛttyupeti*). For this very reason—having intended exactly this—he says: "on level ground" (*same*). The sense is that although a location is obtained by implication because a sacrifice enjoined by the sentence "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām*) cannot be performed without a place, it is nevertheless difficult to grasp both the level and the uneven simultaneously. He says: "the suffix" (*pratyaya*); the meaning is: "the second person is used when [the pronoun] *yuṣmad* [is present]," and so forth. He says: "this" (*etad*).

It should be understood that by this, the application of the rule "vidhiniyama" (injunction-restriction) has also been effectively explained according to the aforementioned method. Concluding, he says: "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). This means: "if the two stated positions are correct. He provides another example of scriptural restrictive enumeration (*parisaṃkhyā*) from this treatise: "The husband... (*patiḥ*). Regarding the first position, he says: "by the restriction" (*avadhāraṇā*). Regarding the second position, he says: "again" (*punaḥ*). This is intended with the thought that [the alternative] is obtained through implication (*arthataḥ*). As for the means of knowledge that establishes the general [rule], they are respectively passion (*rāga*) and scripture (*śāstra*). Regarding the second [position], he says: "not elsewhere" (*nānyatra*).

For this very reason, the elders [state]: "The operation of restrictive rules (*niyama-śāstra*) occurs by way of positive injunction (*vidhi-mukha*), and they serve to restrict general rules (*sāmānya-śāstra*). By this, the statement of the ancients—that these rules also operate by way of prohibition (*niṣedha-mukha*)—is refuted. Furthermore, that [statement] is intended to prevent a contrary restriction even in the case of the word *pati*. Its resolution has already been stated.

[Objection: Is it not the case that regarding the rule "only five [animals]," since the eating of rabbits and so forth is obtained both optionally and simultaneously, then between the two options of restriction (*niyama*) and exclusion (*parisaṃkhyā*), in the first case (restriction), there would follow the fault of sin for not eating rabbits and so forth, whereas no such fault follows from eating dogs and so forth; furthermore, this would contradict the Smṛti texts on expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Moreover, even if the second fault is absent in the case of exclusion, the first fault remains as it was in the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). [Reply: This is not so. There is a distinction: in the case of restriction, the intended meaning (*tātparya*) lies therein, and thus it is so; but here, the intended meaning does not lie therein. Therefore, the cases differ.

It should be understood that there is no fault whatsoever in the claim that the meaning of the particle *eva*—namely, the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*) and so forth—is itself the clear result of employing that very particle *eva*. Thus he says: "iti antre" (in such places), which means in the *Gūḍhamañjūṣā* and other works. This concludes the determination of the meanings of verbal roots and indeclinables.
